While such benchmarks measure how useful a model is, they provide no insight into the biology it represents. We introduce BioScore, a benchmark that quantifies how well an image encoder captures cell identities, with spatial transcriptomics of the same tissue as the reference. A sparse autoencoder splits the encoder's patch embeddings into sparse features, which we cluster into a fixed number of groups. BioScore then measures, for each of 52 cell identities defined by marker genes, how specifically one group follows the identity's expression over the tissue. Because the autoencoder training is fully unsupervised, a match shows that the model represents the cell identity from the image alone. We score 8 pathology foundation models and 3 natural-image models. Every pathology model scores above every natural-image model (0.299--0.371 \vs 0.214--0.232), and paired tests separate three tiers among the pathology models. Unlike a supervised probe, BioScore needs no labels, builds its reference from the data and scores even from few sections, yet it ranks the encoders as a probe does. Its per-identity breakdown indicates which cell identities each encoder captures or misses.
item.dc:creator: Paul Vilars, Vincent Quoc-Huy Trinh, Maria Vakalopoulou, Dimitris Samaras, Stergios Christodoulidis, Mahdi S. Hosseini

item.title: Attack Policy Selection can Mislead Monitor Evaluators
item.description: arXiv:2611.34934v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI monitors, classifiers that flag dangerous behaviour by AI agents, are often evaluated against transcripts generated by attack policies acting as proxies for dangerous behaviour in deployment. We evaluate an ex-production OpenAI monitor as a case study and find that measured false negative rate is highly sensitive to both the method used to generate attack policies and the level of optimisation applied within that method. This rate ranged from 0.5\% to 20.8\% across optimisation levels of a single method (reinforcement learning), and from 6.4\% to 23.0\% across methods at their best observed optimisation level (optimised prompting vs.\ transcript editing). Every attack policy was developed against proxy monitors only: all reported results show attacks transferring to the held-out GPT-5.4 target monitor. Our results suggest that monitor evasion evaluations can easily mislead: an evaluation using only basic attack methods may give false confidence that a monitor is strong. The sensitivity to attack-policy choice raises a problem: interpreting any particular result as evidence about deployment performance requires justification. The transcripts produced by attack policies are proxies for the dangerous behaviour a monitor must flag in deployment. These proxies can introduce visible artefacts, such as reasoning about a ``side task'' absent from the instructions shown to the monitor, that affect monitor judgements. Given the sensitivity above, the choice of proxy can change an evaluation's conclusion. Reading these results as evidence about deployment therefore requires a separate legitimacy argument for why the proxies are informative, including any justification of conservativeness. Making convincing arguments remains an open problem.
item.dc:creator: Charlie Griffin, Oliver Makins, Asa Cooper Stickland, Alessandro Abate, Yarin Gal, Abby D'Cruz, Xander Davies

item.title: Can image generation help visual reasoning? An empirical study
item.description: arXiv:2611.34935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models think in words; then multimodal models might think in images. We test whether a generated helper improves the answer to a visual question. A model describes the helper it needs and then answers using the original and generated images together. Across 13 vision-language model and generator pairs, generation lowers mean accuracy by 3.7 percentage points, with declines on nine of ten tasks. Two unified models, BAGEL and Janus-Pro-7B, each lose accuracy on eight tasks. On VSTAR, adding a generated image to the same planning hint lowers accuracy by 10.47 points. Repeated image edits yield different outcomes across tasks. ChartQAPro and MathVista stay below their no-generation baselines, while ERQA gains three points after ten edits.
item.dc:creator: Xueyang Yu, Yifan Jing, Taiming Lu, Linrong Cai, Zhipeng Cai, Yunyang Xiong, Gabriel Sarch, Zhuang Liu

item.title: Generalizable Equivariant Diffusion Models for Non-Abelian Lattice Gauge Theory: Analytical Foundations and Numerical Scaling Tests
item.description: arXiv:2611.03530v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Gauge-equivariant diffusion models can be used to generate ensembles of field configurations in non-abelian lattice gauge theories. Previously, we demonstrated the feasibility of modeling these theories by combining L-CNN-based diffusion models with the Metropolis-adjusted annealed Langevin algorithm (MAALA). Here we focus on the underlying analytical framework. In particular, we present a rigorous derivation of the reverse-time stochastic differential equation on the group manifold, discuss the gauge invariance of the denoising loss function, and provide extensive numerical benchmarks regarding the scaling behavior with respect to the lattice volume and the inverse coupling $\beta$. Full analytical expressions for arbitrarily sized Wilson loops and the topological charge susceptibility during the forward process are given as well.
item.dc:creator: Gert Aarts, Diaa E. Habibi, Andreas Ipp, David I. M\"uller, Thomas R. Ranner, Lingxiao Wang, Wei Wang, Qianteng Zhu

item.title: The Symmetry Budget: How Much Group Structure Should a Network Architecture Assume?
item.description: arXiv:2611.33169v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A network architecture is, in large part, a symmetry assumption: convolution ties weights across translations, attention ties them across permutations, and a fully connected layer ties nothing. When the data are only approximately symmetric, tying trades approximation error against estimation error, and the right amount of tying is a property of the dataset, not of the architecture alone. We study this trade-off in an exactly solvable model: linear maps on signals over the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_d$, with architectures indexed by the subgroup lattice of $\mathbb{Z}_d$, so that a single integer $k \mid d$ interpolates between an unconstrained layer ($k=1$, $d^2$ parameters) and a fully equivariant one ($k=d$, $d$ parameters). We derive the finite-sample excess risk in closed form, show that for a generic symmetry defect the leading-order risk is affine in $1/k$, and prove that intermediate architectures are then never strictly optimal: the lattice collapses to an all-or-nothing choice with phase boundary $n^\star = \sigma^2 d(d-1)/\varepsilon^2$. Structured defects break this collapse and restore interior optima, and we give a closed-form defect profile for a graded defect. Measurements agree with the theory on $60/60$ cells of a $(\varepsilon,n)$ phase diagram and $48/48$ cells of a second phase diagram at $d=16$, recover the predicted exponent as $-1.92$ against $-2$, and exhibit the predicted $k^\star: 12 \to 4 \to 1$ ladder under graded defects; a two-layer nonlinear control reproduces the crossover. We also characterize when the affine collapse survives for non-abelian groups.
item.dc:creator: Noor Islam S. Mohammad, Mahmudul Hasan, Md. Basim Al Zabir Shammo, Hasan Siddiki, Jakaria Habib

item.title: Feature-Based Explainability of Transformer Scoring Models: A Fidelity-First Framework for Automated Writing Assessment
item.description: arXiv:2611.33175v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Transformer-based automated writing scoring models can achieve strong agreement with human scores while providing limited transparency into the response characteristics associated with their predictions. This study evaluated a feature-based post-hoc explanation approach in which explanatory fidelity was established before feature importance was interpreted. English Language Arts responses from three writing prompts in Grades 6 and 8 were analyzed, with about 12,700 responses per prompt and separate DeBERTa-v3-base research models for Expression and Conventions. Each response was represented by 61 interpretable linguistic and writing-quality features. Four approaches - theory-driven composites, hierarchical feature groupings, exploratory factor analysis, and Random Forest surrogates - were compared in their ability to reproduce DeBERTa predictions. Random Forest surrogates produced the largest observed R2 values across all six prompt-by-trait conditions, with held-out R2 values from .81 to .95. SHAP analyses showed substantial overlap in high-importance features across traits, with 75% to 90% of the top 20 features shared. Trait differentiation occurred mainly through relative feature weighting: Expression showed greater importance for lexical and conceptual indicators, whereas Conventions showed greater importance for sentence-level and syntactic-control indicators. Under researcher-defined mappings, rubric correspondence was 90%-95% for Expression and 12%-18% for Conventions. These percentages are descriptive and conditional on the mappings and available linguistic features. The findings support a fidelity-first framework for examining apparent scoring priorities while distinguishing post-hoc evidence about model behavior from direct explanation of transformer internals.
item.dc:creator: Michael Hemenway, Edward W. Wolfe

item.title: One Neural Operator for Re-planning Low-Thrust Cislunar Transfers after Thrust Outages, at the Original or a Later Arrival
item.description: arXiv:2611.33188v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Safe-mode events causing thrust outages are common in missions with electric propulsion. To demonstrate mission feasibility in such an event, missed-thrust margin studies are performed where thousands of outage scenarios need an exact re-plan solved. We train a neural operator that maps a nominal trajectory with an outage profile to a re-planned trajectory and to the probability that the recovery exists, for 270 low-thrust near-rectilinear halo orbit (NRHO) to distant retrograde orbit (DRO) transfers, at an allowed slip of up to 10 days. On unseen transfers and zero slip, its median control error on the severe half of outages is 1.20% compared to 14.0% for the best cheap re-planner benchmark. With the arrival slip as an input, the error is 1.67% against 23.2%. It also predicts the recoverability of an outage for a given arrival slip with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.997, while the minimum recoverable slip prediction is optimistic by more than half a day on only 6 of the 84 checked outages needing slip. At the original arrival, the ensemble spread of an operator variant with solver inputs has a rank correlation of 0.91 with the actual error, and performing exact solves on the 31% most uncertain severe outages reduces the 90th-percentile error from 8.5% to 2.3%. A query takes milliseconds without a solver, making this a useful tool for large outage studies where the cost of thousands of exact solves outweighs the time to train the operator.
item.dc:creator: Selim Olgu Pilav

item.title: Dynamics of Collective Diversity in Human-AI Co-Creation for Creative Tasks
item.description: arXiv:2611.33192v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative AI systems are increasingly deployed at scale to support human users in creative tasks across a variety of domains. However, as more users adopt the same AI agent, the resulting artifacts may become increasingly homogeneous, leading to a collapse in collective diversity. Prior work has documented this risk, but lacks a systematic framework for understanding how collective diversity changes as AI adoption scales across co-creation settings. In this work, we conduct a large-scale crowdsourcing study to understand and model the dynamics of collective diversity, quality, and effort in human-AI co-creation across two creative domains: Creative Hypothesis Generation and Creative Story Writing. We find that current AI agents used in co-creation can improve artifact quality and reduce effort, but at the cost of declining collective diversity as adoption increases. We further show that more fine-grained human-AI interaction, along with more diverse agent policies, can mitigate this collapse. Finally, we fit predictive models that quantify how collective diversity scales with adoption across co-creation settings, providing insights for designing AI agents that aim to preserve collective diversity.
item.dc:creator: Manh Hung Nguyen, Chao Wen, Sebastian Tschiatschek, Adish Singla

item.title: Extraneous Cognitive Load in Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.33197v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) shows that human problem-solving is affected by both intrinsic load, arising from task difficulty, and extraneous load, arising from how task information is presented. Large language models (LLMs) show analogous effects: presentation alone can affect model performance, but these effects have not yet been systematically isolated from task difficulty. To address this gap, we introduce CogLoadBench, a controlled benchmark that varies five CLT-inspired presentation factors across three reasoning task families. Across models, we find that higher extraneous load conditions often reduce accuracy by either adding competition or complicating the reasoning path. To support diagnosis and mitigation of load-related effects, we propose the Extraneous Load Score (ELS), a prompt-time metric computed from activations that estimates a model's extraneous load, and show that it generalizes across reasoning task types and load levels. We further show that shifting model representations toward lower-load directions at inference time can improve average model performance without changing prompt content.
item.dc:creator: Arushi Gupta, Sheng Liu, James Zou

item.title: Adaptive attention routing multimodal expert graph neural network for drug-drug interaction prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.33200v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate prediction of drug-drug interactions (DDIs) is essential for drug safety in combination therapy. Multimodal methods built on knowledge graphs (KGs) already combine molecular structures, substructures, targets and biomedical relations into drug representations, but they still face three problems: features are heterogeneous across modalities, fusion does not adapt to individual drug pairs, and modality-specific information is diluted during integration. We propose the adaptive attention routing multimodal expert graph neural network (AARME-GNN) to address them. A Feature Adaptive Calibration Module (FACM) reduces within-modality noise in each representation through bottleneck reparameterization and channelwise recalibration before fusion. A Multimodal Weight Router (MMWR) then sets the modality weights of each drug pair, with an entropy constraint that prevents the weights from collapsing onto one modality. A Routing-Aware Weighted Distillation (RAWD) mechanism builds a soft target from the unimodal branches, so that the fusion classifier retains the knowledge held by each modality. On Dataset 1, AARME-GNN improves precision over MKG-FENN by 3.71 and 6.57 percentage points in known drug and known new drug prediction, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) by 4.53 in new drug prediction. On Dataset 2, the advantage is concentrated in the two cold-start settings and in precision.
item.dc:creator: Jingyi Yang, Chengcheng Yan, Hongri Cong, Feifei Zhao

item.title: A Causal Energy Prior for Learning Directed Acyclic Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.33225v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Bayesian learning of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) has long relied on non- or weakly informative priors, on the assumption that the information needed for an informative one is rarely available. In genetics and systems biology, annotation databases now make it possible to assemble a prior DAG before learning from data. Existing informative priors are local: they score a DAG arc by arc and cannot encode how interventions propagate along its paths. Thus, we propose the local-global energy prior (LGE), a Gibbs distribution over DAGs whose energy combines a local divergence from the prior DAG, the Structural Hamming Distance, and a causal one, the Structural Intervention Distance. We derive rules to calibrate its decay and the weight of the two divergences from the prior DAG alone. We quantify how much prior mass stays on the true DAG, and how much data overturn the prior, when the prior DAG is partially incorrect. In simulations, LGE improves both the structural accuracy of maximum a posteriori DAGs and the fit of the corresponding Bayesian networks to the true distribution over non- and weakly informative priors, even when half of the arcs of the prior DAG are wrong. We also showcase LGE on a gene regulatory network learned from single-cell kidney data.
item.dc:creator: Marco Scutari, Noriaki Sato, Shuichi Kawano, Rui Yamaguchi, Seiya Imoto

item.title: Real Package, Wrong Controller: Static Auditing of Vendor--Protocol Mismatches in LLM-Generated PLC Code
item.description: arXiv:2611.33227v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language models can generate Python that drives industrial protocols on programmable logic controllers, yet existing code-grounding checks ask whether an imported package or symbol exists rather than whether it suits the declared industrial target. We define \emph{metadata-conditioned, import-level vendor--protocol incompatibility} and build \textsc{Proteus-OT}, a label-free static verifier over a version-pinned graph of documented bindings. Across 883 generated scripts, 180 carry an import-level mismatch against the declared target (20.4\%); restricting to single-vendor targets gives 16.3\%, and additionally requiring the offending library to reach a protocol communication call gives 14.2\%, which we read as conditional on the corpus metadata rather than on verified intent. None of the 28 adjudicable human control files carries one, a sample too small to estimate a prevalence. Within the balanced subset, 96.6\% of mismatching scripts import packages and call methods that exist, so an existence baseline does not represent them, and every positive ships with an inspectable witness. We also audit machine-versus-human classification on the same corpus, where character $n$-grams reach macro-F1 1.000 under task, model and vendor-disjoint partitions and survive comment removal, an AST round trip and identifier anonymisation. The trailing newline present in 95.2\% of human files and in none of the generated ones separates the classes on its own. Vendor--protocol consistency is a useful static audit target, whereas provenance classification on repository-labelled corpora is not authorship detection.
item.dc:creator: S M Zia Ur Rashid, Sazidul Islam Hira, Suman Rath

item.title: Soft Decentralized Expected SARSA: Equilibrium Selection via Gradual Adaptation
item.description: arXiv:2611.33228v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce Soft Decentralized Expected SARSA (SDES), a modification of Decentralized Q-learning in which agents maintain persistent exploration and update their acting Q-values gradually rather than switching directly to newly learned best responses when updating. We prove convergence to $\epsilon$-greedy Nash equilibria in weakly acyclic stochastic games for sufficiently large batch sizes. We then show, in the repeated Prisoner's Dilemma with memory, that soft updating can reshape basins of attraction without changing the equilibrium set. In the deterministic limit, we derive analytical basin bounds governed by the Q-value differences between actions in the target policies and show that reducing the policy learning rate can favor either cooperative or competitive equilibria. These results suggest that soft updating is not merely a stabilization device but also a mechanism of equilibrium selection in decentralized learning.
item.dc:creator: Giuseppe Martucci, Janusz M. Meylahn, Gurdal Arslan, Serdar Yuksel

item.title: Effect-Driven Skill Abstractions for Offline Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.33229v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We seek to learn discrete skill abstractions to facilitate long-horizon, goal-conditioned reinforcement-learning (RL) tasks. Recent approaches have shown success by quantizing actions via clustering or reconstruction. However, these objectives lead to skills that are not directly related to what the current state affords or what the goal requires. Instead, we argue that goal-directed skills should be driven by \emph{how they affect the state} of the agent. To realize this, we introduce a novel quantization method for action chunks that optimizes next-state predictions conditioned on the current state and action. This objective encourages skills to be distinguished by the future states they lead to, resulting in a vocabulary that spans diverse outcomes reachable from a given state. Our framework can easily be paired with common offline RL methods by replacing their continuous actor head with a discrete one that selects among the learned skills. We can execute these skills in the environment by converting them back to continuous actions using a trained low-level controller. Experiments on benchmark navigation and manipulation tasks largely show substantial and consistent improvements over both the continuous-actor baselines and reconstruction-based discretizations. Our project page can be found at: https://burcukilic.github.io/projects/effect-driven-skill-abstractions/.
item.dc:creator: Burcu Kilic, David Drexel, Emre Ugur, Justus Piater

item.title: How Many Samples Is RL Worth? Best-of-N versus RL Post-Training for Text-to-Image Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.33232v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) on a reward that can be checked automatically has become a common last step in the training of text-to-image models. A simpler way to get more correct images is best-of-N: draw N images from the base model and keep the one that a picker prefers. We ask how many base model samples one RL sample is worth, and call this number the exchange rate. We measure it for Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium and its public Flow-GRPO checkpoint on 398 new prompts in the style of GenEval, the benchmark behind the RL reward, with human labels on every prompt and two automatic judges other than the reward. The answer depends on the prompt. Four fifths of the prompts do not ask for a position (for example, one object left of another). On these, the base model catches up: best-of-16 with an off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM) as the picker is about as good as one RL image. A person who looks through up to 3 base images finds a correct one as often as one RL image is correct. On the prompts that ask for a position, RL is far ahead: a person finds a correct image among 8 base images for only 52% of the prompts, against 92% for one RL image. Over all prompts, our primary test, which we fixed in advance, finds best-of-16 with the VLM picker 9.3 points behind one RL image when both automatic judges must pass an image. People see a smaller gap, 5.5 and 6.5 points in two checks. FLUX.1-dev shows a similar gap in the same test. RL also solves 20 prompts that the base model misses in 128 tries, and 1,024 tries recover half of them. The automatic judges are wrong in opposite directions: a detector-based judge like the reward, as used in our primary test, reports a larger gap than people see, and VLM judges report little or none. Comparisons of RL with best-of-N should therefore check the selected images by hand.
item.dc:creator: Salil Bhatnagar

item.title: Learning the Platform, Not the Learner: Sequencing Shortcuts in the Offline Evaluation of Educational Recommender Systems and LLM Rankers
item.description: arXiv:2611.33240v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Educational recommenders are usually compared offline, by how well they predict the next activity in logs of tutoring systems, learning applications and MOOCs, where the next activity is largely decided by the platform: teachers assign problem sets, tutors draw problems until mastery, engines select questions. On eight public datasets from five platforms, we compare four structural predictors, which use nothing about the learner beyond the last activity, with ten personalised recommenders and with open-weight LLM rankers from 0.5 to 7 billion parameters, under two protocols. The structural predictors reach between 0.81 and 1.00 of the best accuracy of any method (median 0.95), mostly through population transitions rather than the course order; the best personalised recommender is significantly better on five datasets, by 0.007 to 0.102 NDCG@10, and on Eedi in three of four training runs. Every method is far less accurate on steps along transitions never seen in training and on steps chosen by learners. LLM rankers look competent with random negatives but are never much better than a word-matching baseline, and with negatives that are plausible under the course structure they stay close to random or well behind the transition heuristic, whatever their size. In a simulation with known learner needs, the structural share tracks the share of steps decided by the platform, and offline accuracy ranks an oracle of the learners' needs below imitators of the platform. Weighting test steps by how unlikely the structure makes them restores much of the link with usefulness and, on the real data, reveals a significant personalisation signal on seven of the eight datasets. We propose a syllabus-aware evaluation checklist and release a Python package that reports the lift of any recommender over the structure.
item.dc:creator: Youssef Jdidou

item.title: Beyond the Efficiency-Efficacy Dilemma: A Critical Analysis of Transferability in Adversarial Malware Detection
item.description: arXiv:2611.33243v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine Learning (ML) models are already being deployed at scale for malware detection. Therefore there is a pressing need to rigorously study adversarial robustness. To that end, we introduce the Adversarial AI Engine (AAIE): a platform for automated security stress-testing. We performed transfer attacks, via EMBER2018, against a Random Forest target. Counterintuitively, we found single-step FGSM to have the highest attack success rate (ASR) of 52.9% compared to iterative PGD with 45.2% (p < 0.002). Compared to iterative attacks which tend to overfit surrogate networks creating brittle perturbations, FGSM created more transferable examples. We benchmarked our attacks using ASR, transferability score, evasion rate, and resilience index. Through these metrics, proposed in concordance with emerging standards in AI governance, we expose shortcomings as our transferability scores peak at ~0.8 with constrained perturbations. We highlight the practical security implications of these findings and demonstrate AAIE for automated adversarial auditing.
item.dc:creator: Veysel Alevcan, Mohammad Furqan Ali, Teresa Sousa, Lu\'is Miguel Campos, Christoforos Ntantogian

item.title: MonoQPM: Splitting Features into Concepts for Inherent Interpretability and Predictive Performance
item.description: arXiv:2611.33252v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Alongside superposition, polysemanticity is one of the primary obstacles to achieving interpretable deep neural networks. While these phenomena are typically intrinsically linked, the Quadratic Programming Enhanced Model (QPM) naturally decouples them. By representing classes with a sparse binary assignment of very few features, QPM prevents superposition by design on its final features but still exhibits polysemanticity. However, measuring polysemanticity is an open problem. This work proposes a utility-focused approach to measuring polysemanticity by quantifying the decrease in interference-induced activation errors, which yields the practical utility of tighter prediction sets using Conformal Prediction (CP). We explicitly disentangle the polysemantic features of QPM into monosemantic concepts to create the Monosemantic QPM (MonoQPM). Because its features are disentangled, MonoQPM acts as a significantly more efficient Conformal Predictor. Additionally, we introduce CUBCars, a dataset providing ground truth information about shared concepts. Using this and other datasets, we demonstrate that polysemanticity emerges in QPM across all tested architectures, but is effectively alleviated by MonoQPM. For instance, MonoQPM guarantees 88% coverage using Adaptive Prediction Sets on ImageNet with just 66% of the frozen QPM's set size.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Norrenbrock, Robert Zimmermann, Timo Kaiser, Sovan Biswas, Neslihan Kose, Bodo Rosenhahn

item.title: Same Tokenizer, Better Tokens: Choosing Image Tokens by MAP Inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.33261v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Discrete visual tokens encode images for reconstruction and serve as training targets for autoregressive image generators. Vector-quantized tokenizers typically assign each encoder feature its nearest code independently. The decoder uses these codes jointly, so a sequence of individually nearest codes can reconstruct an image less faithfully than an alternative assignment. A local model of the reconstruction loss yields a closest-vector problem with a decoder-dependent target and metric. Reconstruction-only search improves PSNR across the frozen tokenizers we test. Different code sequences can achieve similar reconstruction quality, leaving room to favour more predictable ones. We introduce RecaP (Reconstruction and Predictability), which selects codes for a frozen tokenizer by balancing how faithfully they reconstruct the image with how likely their sequence is under a pretrained autoregressive prior. On ImageNet, LlamaGen GPT-B trained on RecaP tokens achieves lower early-checkpoint FID against training images than GPT-B trained on nearest-neighbour tokens. The difference is smaller against held-out images. On an ImageNet subset, the prior improves generation at comparable reconstruction FID. Our code is available at: https://github.com/gmum/recap
item.dc:creator: Piotr Kubaty (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Jagiellonian University, Krak\'ow, Poland, Doctoral School of Exact and Natural Sciences, Jagiellonian University, Krak\'ow, Poland), Jacek Tabor (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Jagiellonian University, Krak\'ow, Poland, Centre for Credible Artificial Intelligence, Warsaw University of Technology, Poland), {\L}ukasz Struski (Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, Jagiellonian University, Krak\'ow, Poland)

item.title: JetDiffusion: Pushing the Speed Limits of Video Generation with NVFP4 Sparse Attention
item.description: arXiv:2611.33268v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Attention over long sequences is a major computational bottleneck in video generation, which can be alleviated through sparsity and low-bit quantization. We propose JetDiffusion, a video generation system built on trainable Video Sparse Quantized Attention (VSQA), with custom inference kernels that combine native NVFP4 computation and kernel fusion. At 90% sparsity, VSQA accelerates attention by 8-29x compared with FlashAttention on different hardwares. To further accelerate video generation, we combine VSQA with NVFP4 linear quantization and step distillation. Although each technique can individually preserve generation quality, jointly adapting to all three remains challenging, particularly under aggressive NVFP4 quantization. Through empirical studies, we develop an effective staged training recipe that enables stable adaptation to quantization, sparsity, and few-step denoising. On Wan2.1-14B, the resulting model achieves 273x end-to-end video generation speedup on the RTX 5090 while maintaining comparable video quality.
item.dc:creator: Yulun Wu, Zihan Min, Minshen Zhang, Kaiqin Kong, Ji Xie, Will Lin, Junda Chen, Wenxuan Tan, Aryan Kumar, Loay Rashid, Qingyu Yin, Hao Zhang

item.title: Building a Unified Inline Code Editing Model for GitHub Copilot
item.description: arXiv:2611.33314v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI-assisted coding ranges from fully agentic coding to inline code suggestions in the editor. Inline suggestions require predicting a developer's most likely next edit from an editing session. The next edit may lie at the cursor, in nearby lines, or farther away, and one editing intent can span several of these. The preceding system queries separate completion, nearby edit, and long-distance edit models, each with its own output format, in a fixed sequence; it thus cannot express intents spanning distant locations in one response, can require several sequential model calls per suggestion, and prioritizes completion even when a correction would serve better. We present a unified model that predicts all three edit types in one output space: a sequence of anchored diff patches specifying locations, deleted lines, and added lines. This representation permits multiple edits per response, so the client can serve later edits from a cache without further model calls. We train this model in two phases, first unifying next edit and long-distance edit prediction, then adding code completion. We synthesize multi-edit supervision from single-edit data via model pseudolabeling and edit history playback. We use a binary LLM-graded reward, a patch validity taxonomy shared by data filtering, reward, and evaluation, and grader boosting for targeted failure modes. Phase 2 also adapts how the client processes and presents model outputs. In controlled online A/B experiments in GitHub Copilot, Phase 1 significantly reduces time to display by 6.77% and output tokens by 58.93% relative to the three-model baseline. In Phase 2, the 3-in-1 model and client adaptations reduce dismissed suggestions per user by 10.06% relative to the 2-in-1 model paired with the completion model. Throughout this report, we also share our methodology and learnings in evaluation, training, and end-to-end model and system design.
item.dc:creator: Microsoft CodeAI Team, Microsoft VS Code Team, Julia Gong, Benjamin Liggett, Shengjie Ma, Ulugbek Abdullaev, Zhehui Liao, Benjamin Steenhoek, Gaurav Mittal, Fuhui Fang, Satarupa Guha, Hang Zhao, Anand Mooga, Cheng Long, Benjamin Simmonds, Soojin Choi, Luciana Abud, Nathan Halstead, Alexandru Dima, Yu Hu, Elsie Nallipogu

item.title: Large-scale Model Merging via Recovery-aware Task Weighting
item.description: arXiv:2611.33315v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Model merging combines multiple task-specific expert models into a single model. However, merging preserves expert capabilities unevenly across tasks. This imbalance is particularly pronounced in large-scale settings, where some tasks can suffer severe capability losses even when average accuracy remains high. To address this imbalance, we introduce Recovery-aware Task Weighting (RaTW), a model merging framework that assigns larger weights to tasks whose expert capabilities are poorly retained by an initial merged model. We quantify these recovery opportunities as the fraction of a task's labeled validation samples that its expert predicts correctly but the initial merged model gets wrong, and use the resulting task weights to re-merge the experts. To evaluate merging at large scale, we construct CLIPMerge-100, a 100-task benchmark with task-specific experts on CLIP ViT-L/14 and ViT-B/32. Across eleven merging methods with 20, 50, and 100 tasks on two CLIP backbones, RaTW improves both mean accuracy and tail20 (the mean expert-normalized accuracy of the 20% worst-retained tasks) in all 33 ViT-L/14 settings and 32 of 33 ViT-B/32 settings. We further introduce ReForge++, which combines RaTW with iterative model refinement and outperforms all evaluated baselines, including a matched-budget control, in both mean accuracy and tail20 across all settings.
item.dc:creator: Kaiyang Li, Shaobo Han, Boming Chen, Martin Renqiang Min, Shihao Ji

item.title: What Does RL Post-Training Teach Text-to-Image Models? A Skill-Wise Analysis of Flow-GRPO
item.description: arXiv:2611.33316v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has become a standard way to improve text-to-image flow models: Flow-GRPO lifts the GenEval score of SD3.5-M from 0.63 to 0.95, a gain read as the model having learned compositional generation. We ask how much of that gain the base model's own samples already contained, by measuring pass@k over shared noise seeds, one skill at a time, before and after RL, on prompts never used in training. The answer differs by skill. On four of GenEval's six skills, where 32 base samples already solve almost every prompt, the gain is sharpening: one post-trained sample is worth 4 to 10 base samples, and pass@32 barely moves. On spatial relations it is unlocking: pass@32 rises from 0.69 to 1.00, 128 base samples do not match one post-trained sample, and prompts the base model never solved in 32 samples are solved 93% of the time, as often as those it solved. The benchmark average, 31 base samples per post-trained sample, describes no skill. Relations carry 35% of the gain; of the other 65%, selecting among 8 base samples with the judge behind the reward recovers nine tenths. We propose an account of when each occurs: within a prompt, a group-relative update re-weights only the outcomes its samples contain, and a flow policy cannot widen the noise that produces them; across prompts, shared parameters let successes on some prompts repair a deficit common to many. The same anatomy applies to a text-rendering checkpoint. The account's predictions are tested with a checkpoint trained without KL, within-prompt diversity, and controlled training that holds object classes out, where sharpening comes first and transfers, and unlocking follows, on practised objects before unseen ones.
item.dc:creator: Cheng Zhang, Jiesong Liu

item.title: What Must LLM Agents Communicate? From Information Loss to Communication Failures
item.description: arXiv:2611.33318v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When evidence is distributed across LLM agents, a team may collectively possess all the information needed for a decision yet fail to use it effectively. What must agents communicate for accurate joint predictions, and when does interaction help? We study three requirements for effective communication: sufficiency of the information conveyed, selection of relevant evidence, and utilization of received information. Drawing on information theory and communication complexity, we develop a framework that combines theoretical benchmarks with controlled experiments and message-level analyses. We find that local probability reports can discard essential information, with theoretical information loss closely matching observed performance penalties. Query-first interaction improves predictions when relevant evidence depends on a private query, but compact one-shot representations can eliminate this advantage. Even when sufficient information is communicated, agents may fail to select or use it correctly. Together, these findings distinguish fundamental communication limits from failures in how LLM agents communicate and use information.
item.dc:creator: Yi-Yun Chu, Xiaobin Shen

item.title: Do Not Let the Prior Heal the Anomaly: Selective Anchoring for Detection from Incomplete Measurements
item.description: arXiv:2611.33331v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative priors can recover anatomical detail from incomplete medical measurements, but may erase the very lesions that imaging aims to detect, even when the measurements contain evidence of them. We introduce selective anchoring that protects reliably measured image components from prior-driven changes, while allowing expressive generative models to reconstruct unresolved structure. Acquisition uncertainty in the protected components is either added deterministically to the downstream test or carried by the ensemble through stochastic perturbations of the readings. We implement this principle as a wrapper for pretrained diffusion and flow samplers and as AnchoredFM, a fast constrained flow model. Under a linear-Gaussian measurement model, the protected coefficients are unbiased in expectation and achieve nominal interval coverage across repeated acquisitions, independently of the learned prior. Across sparse-view CT, accelerated brain MRI, and photoacoustic tomography, selective anchoring improves lesion contrast preservation and uncertainty reliability, and can reduce reconstruction error within lesions. For tumor detection in accelerated MRI, with a healthy reference estimated from the measurements alone, deterministic anchoring raises mean AUROC across eight samplers from 78.4% to 84.6% and lesion sensitivity at 0.25 false-positive marks per slice from 38.8% to 47.5%, with gains in all four predefined tumor-size groups. At thresholds frozen on healthy validation data, mean sensitivity rises from 20.2% to 44.1% (37.6% with stochastic anchoring). These findings show how expressive generative priors can reconstruct unresolved anatomy without healing away the abnormalities that the measurements support.
item.dc:creator: Nicolas Tricard, Stefan Brandst\"atter, Jason Chen, Zituo Chen, Linzheng Wang, Georg Langs, Sili Deng

item.title: Evaluating Ensemble Methods for Algorithmic Stability Under Data Perturbations
item.description: arXiv:2611.33375v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Standard classification algorithms often exhibit sensitivity near decision boundaries, which can compound instability that already exists from overfitting to a subset of high-influence samples. Ensembling is commonly used to stabilize classifiers, but we show that it can destabilize those that are already stable. The well-established practice of subbagging can yield substantial improvements in stability, as we validate in the cause-of-death classification setting. However, its effect depends on the perturbation level, and for stable classifiers the finite number of bags introduces destabilizing Monte Carlo noise that shrinks only slowly as the number of bags grows. This instability can be mitigated, though, by the recently proposed inflated argmax, which allows for multi-class predictions in ambiguous cases. We further examine the extent to which the Rashomon set, the collection of distinct models that achieve near-optimal predictive performance, can reduce instability by leveraging predictive multiplicity rather than resampling. We find that the Rashomon ensemble can stabilize unstable classifiers, but requires sufficient predictive multiplicity, which is not guaranteed. It is a promising direction, but not currently a general substitute for subbagging. Our results are consistent with an influence equalization interpretation of why these ensemble approaches stabilize unstable classifiers, although their failures on stable classifiers appear to have distinct sources.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (2026), ISSN 2835-8856
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Edelhertz, Simon D. Nguyen, Tyler H. McCormick

item.title: Probabilistic Machine Learning for Total Kinetic Energy Distributions in Neutron-Induced Fission
item.description: arXiv:2611.33379v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The incident-neutron-energy dependence of post-neutron total-kinetic-energy (TKE) distributions, particularly their width in the multichance-fission regime, provides a sensitive test of fission calculations. We investigate how the General Description of Fission Observables (GEF) and probabilistic machine-learning models trained on GEF reproduce measured TKE distributions, emphasizing their width at high incident-neutron energies and extrapolation beyond the training range. Gaussian process regression (GPR), GPR with a white-noise kernel, a mixture density network (MDN), and a Bayesian mixture density network (BMDN) are evaluated on a common calculated dataset. An extended MDN/BMDN analysis uses 1,025 GEF spectra from 20 target nuclei and 60 measured distributions. Training ranges of up to 20, 40, and approximately 76 MeV are compared with matched-size controls extending to 30 or 40 MeV while preserving the number of spectra per target. Above 40 MeV, the BMDN width mean absolute error relative to experiment decreases from 5.63 MeV for training up to 20 MeV to 2.70 and 2.53 MeV for two matched-size 30-MeV controls and 1.77 MeV for the matched-size 40-MeV control. Predictive-interval coverage relative to GEF above 40 MeV rises from 52.3% to 92.3% between the 20-MeV and full training ranges. Agreement with measured mean TKE and widths is target dependent, with no uniform ordering among GEF, MDN, and BMDN. The results demonstrate the sensitivity of high-energy widths to training-energy coverage, with improvements already evident at 30 MeV. The comparatively slow variation of GEF widths at high energies limits the extent to which these improvements can be attributed to learning nontrivial energy dependence. Adequate training-energy coverage is critical for reproducing the calculated high-energy evolution, while agreement with experiment remains constrained by the underlying fission model.
item.dc:creator: Vaia Prassa, Martha Papadopoulou, Christos Bompotas

item.title: Can a Short Video Clip Verify a Model Fix?
item.description: arXiv:2611.33393v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A developer who reproduces a video model's error on a short clip can replay that clip after an update. How often does a correct clip answer mean the original test now passes? On 960 prespecified CG-Bench questions, we updated from Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct to Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct. Accuracy on a 64-frame sample spanning the full video rose from 27.9% to 33.3%. Before scoring the newer model, we froze 388 clips on which the older model reproduced its exact reference error. The updated model passed the reference on 51 of 116 clip passes (44.0%, 95% Wilson interval 35.3-53.0%) and on 16 of 272 clip failures (5.9%). Closing cases on a clip pass would have declared 65 unresolved reference failures fixed. Requiring a clip pass would have missed 16 of the 67 reference fixes (23.9%). In a separate 1,028-video study with different checkpoints and direct option scoring, only 15 clips passed, and the 16-frame reference confirmed one. For the generated-answer update, the short replay identified cases worth checking, while the original input remained necessary to verify individual fixes.
item.dc:creator: Raj Shan

item.title: Confidence scores for gated automation of large language models
item.description: arXiv:2611.33394v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong capabilities in automated decision-making. However, LLMs may produce incorrect answers with high confidence, limiting their applicability in decisions that affect individuals and organizations. Reliable confidence scores are necessary to gate such decisions, and existing estimates are frequently unavailable or too coarse to support effective gating. This work uses supervised learning to train models to predict the correctness of LLM-generated answers, enabling automated confident responses and routing uncertain ones for human review. A linear confidence score head is fitted to the final-layer hidden state of the frozen LLM backbone, and text-only metamodels are trained as an alternative for closed models. All results come from a single 2B-parameter backbone, on graded answers that are about 98% SQuAD and the remainder TruthfulQA. Against multiple baselines, the confidence score head outperforms all baselines and metamodels, automating the largest fraction of the workload at high accuracy targets. Prompted confidence scores can appear well calibrated yet lack the resolution needed for thresholding. Although transferability to unseen datasets is modest, the confidence score head remains the most robust approach. The proposed confidence scoring framework enhances the safety of automating LLM-based agents and can be adapted to gate other properties, including safety or compliance.
item.dc:creator: Luiz G. A. Alves, Aaron Vermeersch

item.title: Best-of-$N$ Test-Time Steering Can Lead to Reward Hacking in Vision-Language-Action Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.33398v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown promise for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but adapting to changing environmental conditions still remains challenging. Recent test-time steering methods have shown promise in enabling adaptive VLA policies by utilizing additional computation during deployment. In this paper, we consider best-of-$N$ test-time steering for VLA models, where multiple action candidates are sampled from a fixed policy and a verifier is used to select the best one during deployment. We show that increasing $N$ does not always improve performance when the verifier is inaccurate, and can favor candidates whose scores exploit prediction errors, a form of reward hacking. We study this effect on 60 LIBERO-Safety task-level cases using a $\pi_{0.5}$ policy, with ten repetitions per case. We introduce controlled errors in a MuJoCo trajectory verifier and show that as $N$ increases, selected candidate rewards diverge from the accurate verifier rewards, leading to reward hacking. We also show that verifier calibration and softmax-based candidate selection can mitigate reward hacking in some settings.
item.dc:creator: Vanshaj Khattar, Jing Liu, Toshiaki Koike-Akino, Ming Jin, Ye Wang

item.title: Gaussian priors from nonlinear PDEs with the semiclassical approximation
item.description: arXiv:2611.33400v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Probabilistic numerical methods for partial differential equations (PDE) combines the governing physics with observations to treat solving the PDE as a Bayesian inverse problem. This allows techniques to quantify the uncertainty in the field reconstruction under model-form error. In the majority of cases, a Gaussian prior is assigned to the field of interest, and Bayes's theorem in the infinite-dimensional setting is used to derive the posterior. While Gaussians have been shown to be well-suited for linear PDEs, a similar treatment for nonlinear PDEs remains open-ended. In this work, study the use of the semiclassical approximation to construct Gaussian priors from variational energies or integrated square residuals for probabilistic numerics. The prior is derived by expanding the PDE energy about a stable solution and uncovering a Gaussian form. We then analyze the different characteristics of the resulting priors as they pertain to the inverse problem. In particular, we find that the covariance operator is given by the inverse of the Hessian of the energy whose associated Cameron-Martin space is the solution space of the PDE. We also find that the prior responds to model-form error by sharpening or flattening itself depending on the distance between the ground truth and the solution of the assumed model.
item.dc:creator: Alex Alberts

item.title: An Adversarial Multi-Agent Pursuit Game for Locomotor Agility Pretraining
item.description: arXiv:2611.33407v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agile humanoid locomotion requires controllers that can adapt to rapidly changing motion demands while remaining stable and robust. Recent locomotion controllers are typically designed with either a dense reward that is carefully shaped to encourage steps and penalize falling, or by using a reference tracking reward which teaches the controller to follow predetermined motions. Once a behavior that maximizes the reward is discovered, the controller ceases to learn. While generally stable, reference tracking methods focus on motor control separately from motion generation. Self-play has been proven as an effective technique for superhuman performance on several multiagent games like Go, Starcraft, hide-and-seek, and capture-the-flag. We train neural networks to play the game of multiagent tag in a physics simulator to study if new motion generation and control strategies can emerge through sparse feedback and competitive self-play. We present MJTag, a task suite for role-conditioned locomotion during competitive pursuit-evasion. Our model is a role-conditioned policy for a low-level locomotion controller and optional planar velocity commands. MJTag's league-based play with sparse feedback enables a locomotion controller to adopt new strategies, including dodging, sprinting, and tackling.
item.dc:creator: Nathan A. C. Hogg, Matt Hyatt, Neil Klingensmith, George K. Thiruvathukal

item.title: A Semantics-First Approach to Multimodal Video Captioning with Frozen Encoders and Stabilized Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.33409v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose the Audio-Visual Query Transformer (AVQFormer), a highly efficient architecture built upon a 2.7B parameter LLM featuring a fixed-length $K=16$ semantic alignment module, stabilized via Adaptive Self-Critical Sequence Training (ASCST) with Entropy Regularization. Multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs) often rely on global audio representations to compensate for inefficient, frame-based visual encoders. While our Phase 1 prompted evaluations demonstrate that the Multimodal Base Model achieves strong deep semantic alignment (scoring 0.889 on BERTScore F1), optimizing this architecture for legacy metrics reveals a performance gap. We explore this gap as a hypothesis we term temporal alignment friction: a conflict where global audio representations disrupt the chronological sequence of visual frames, leading to penalties under visually-focused evaluation metrics. Consequently, by stripping away the audio, our Video-Only ablation conforms more closely to this rigid syntax, achieving 63.0 CIDEr. While trailing larger models such as Qwen2.5-VL (67.4 CIDEr), this establishes a strong baseline for sub-3B parameter LLM-based models. This indicates that CIDEr, as applied to datasets such as MSR-VTT, may exhibit a bias toward visually grounded syntax, limiting its ability to fully capture multimodal semantic richness.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proc. SPIE 14027, Multimodal Image Exploitation and Learning 2026, 140270E (2026)
item.dc:creator: Albert Chiwara, Erhan Guven

item.title: ViCARD: Visual Credit Assignment with Reward-Gated Distillation for Multimodal Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2611.33437v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Visual reasoning requires models to identify relevant visual evidence and use it to derive correct answers. Outcomebased reinforcement learning (RL) faces two key challenges in this regime: it yields no learning signal when perceptual errors cause all sampled responses to fail, and it broadcasts a uniform advantage across every token within a response. Conversely, while visual self-distillation offers dense guidance from evidence-centered image crops, student learning from token distributions alone often fails to elicit correct final answers. Motivated by an audit of training rollouts that exposes these complementary failure modes, we introduce ViCARD (Visual Credit Assignment with RewardGated Distillation), which integrates per-token visual supervision with verified correctness rewards. For each rollout group, we leverage a teacher with its input image cropped to the relevant visual area, and use this to provide per-token supervision to the student while also valuing correctness. If all sampled rollouts fail, ViCARD samples an additional crop-teacher answer and activates on-policy distillation only if that answer is correct. Together, these mechanisms provide fine-grained visual credit within informative reward groups and a learning signal for otherwise uninformative all-fail groups. Extensive comparisons across model scales demonstrate that ViCARD improves fine-grained visual reasoning performance over RL and distillation baselines, while retaining broad visual reasoning capabilities.
item.dc:creator: Zijian Huang, Jiasi Chen

item.title: Centered Kernel Distance: Dimension-Free Error Bounds for Comparing Neural Representations
item.description: arXiv:2611.33447v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The asymptotic error of representational similarity metrics such as centered kernel alignment (CKA) and representational similarity analysis (RSA) has been well-characterized, but there are no realistic bounds on how estimates of representational similarity $\textit{simultaneously}$ depend on the number of sampled neurons ($N$) and experimental conditions ($M$). We study the natural metric counterpart of CKA and RSA, which we call the Centered Kernel Distance (CKD). We show that CKD admits an unbiased estimator, whereas several popular similarity measures including CKA have no unbiased estimator. Under mild assumptions, we show that estimation error of CKD decays in proportion to $1/M + 1/N$. Strikingly, the rate in this bound does not depend on the dimensionality of the space of experimental conditions. Thus, similarity estimation does not suffer from the curse of dimensionality, which plagues similar problems in high-dimensional statistics. We verify our results empirically in random shallow neural networks, trained neural networks, and macaque visual cortex data. Ultimately, this paper advances a framework for predicting the error of similarity estimators in experiments by relaxing existing, biologically-unrealistic assumptions. Our theoretical and empirical predictions produce specific prescriptions on how to most efficiently estimate the similarity between multiple neural systems.
item.dc:creator: Shujun Xiong, Sarah E. Harvey, Jacob Zavatone-Veth, Alexander H. Williams

item.title: HumblePRM: Improving VLM Abstention in Ambiguous Situations through Process Reward Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2611.33452v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reliable deployment of Vision Language Models (VLMs) requires that a model's expressed confidence remain grounded in what it can actually see, and that it recognize when the visual evidence is too ambiguous to commit to a confident response. Standard post-training uses outcome reward models (ORMs) that supervise only the final decision, rewarding a confident answer regardless of whether the image supports one, while existing methods either tend to detect uncertainty post-hoc or assume an objective verdict always exists. We instead split multimodal reasoning into two stages: perception, where the model must factually describe the scene, and calibration, where it must judge whether that evidence is sufficient to commit to a conclusion. We introduce HumblePRM, a lightweight process reward model (PRM) that scores each stage independently, rewarding agreement between evidence and expressed confidence rather than outcome correctness alone. Training with HumblePRM increases abstention due to uncertainty on ambiguous inputs considerably while leaving accuracy on clear images roughly unchanged. We also find that the improvement transfers to Gemma 4 E4B, a larger, popular edge model. Our findings show that process reward supervision is a promising route to VLMs with better calibrated abstention, ensuring more reliability rather than unpredictable behavior.
item.dc:creator: Saket Reddy, Ke Yang, ChengXiang Zhai

item.title: A Realistic End-to-End Runtime Crossover Estimation for Quantum-Enhanced Training of Large-Scale Machine Learning Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.33454v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine Learning (ML) is one promising application domain for Quantum Computing (QC) speedups, but asymptotic complexity considerations often mask the actual engineering costs of actual end-to-end workflows. For the use case of training a linearized Neural Network with a Quantum Linear Solver, a provably favorable quantum scaling has been suggested. We present realistic resource estimates for this problem, accounting for data access, computation, and readout. Our analysis examines three increasingly complex benchmarking scenarios, under distinct sparsity-scaling assumptions, thereby enabling progressively more realistic resource estimates. We identify crossover regimes relative to classical methods and find that crossover points emerge only for very large problem sizes, long computation times, and highly restrictive output requirements. This work provides a blueprint for evaluating quantum-enhanced ML algorithms under realistic hardware constraints and help identifying the bottlenecks that must be overcome to approach industrial quantum utility.
item.dc:creator: Maximilian Alexander Wolf, Alona Sakhnenko, Florian Geissler, Andrea Matic, Jeanette Miriam Lorenz

item.title: PAC Learning to Sample: On Computational Aspects of Language Generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.33464v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The success of language models has motivated theoretical work on learning to sample from distributions on discrete domains. A prominent abstraction is the model of language generation in the limit, introduced by Kleinberg and Mullainathan (NeurIPS 2024), in which the algorithm must generate from the target language after some finite but unspecified number of positive examples. While its positive results are surprisingly general, most guarantees are qualitative. In this work, we seek quantitative guarantees on sample and time complexity, inspired by statistical and computational learning theory. To this end, we study a PAC model of language generation, proposed (in a different context) by De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio (SODA 2015), in which a Boolean concept class $C$ over $\{-1,1\}^n$ defines the target languages: given uniformly random positive examples of an unknown concept $f \in C$, the learner must output a sampler whose output distribution (conditioned on the training data) is close in total variation to the uniform distribution over $f^{-1}(1)$. Their work implicitly gives an efficient algorithm for PAC learning to sample $C$, given three primitives for $C$: an online learner, approximate sampling and counting oracles, and an SQ learner. We ask whether these ingredients, in particular online learnability, are necessary. First, we construct a Boolean concept class $C$ for which online learning is cryptographically hard, yet PAC learning to sample is computationally efficient. Then, we develop new algorithms that use offline ERM oracles instead of online learners, together with approximate sampling/counting oracles for intersections of concepts in $C$ and an SQ learner for $C$. We view our results, together with the work of De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio, as a first step towards understanding the computational complexity of language generation.
item.dc:creator: Alkis Kalavasis, Shuchen Li, Manolis Zampetakis

item.title: SplatWAM: Splatting World Action Models for Real-Time 3D Imagination
item.description: arXiv:2611.33467v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: World models typically predict future observations in pixel or latent space, limiting their ability to directly represent true 3D scene evolution. We present SplatWAM (Splatting World Action Model), a generative world model that learns action-conditioned dynamics directly over compact 3D Gaussian primitives. A tokenizer SplatWAM-T first encodes a variable number of unposed views into a fixed budget of Gaussian tokens. A dynamics model SplatWAM-D then predicts future Gaussian states in a single forward pass per action, using log-Euclidean covariance coordinates and differentiable rendering supervision to facilitate learning in an explicit 3D space. Each predicted state can be rasterized from arbitrary viewpoints, enforcing a shared 3D representation across views by construction. On OGBench Scene, SplatWAM renders novel views 12x faster than video world models (~80 FPS on an RTX 5090) with up to 2.0 dB higher PSNR. We further introduce SplatWAM-P, a lightweight flow-matching policy head jointly trained with the dynamics model. Across 8 task suites, model-free Gaussian-token policies outperform pixel-based counterparts by up to 24.8 percentage points. SplatWAM-P improves over Latent Particle World Model (LPWM) by 12 percentage points and matches HIQL without a learned value function. On LIBERO, our ~1B model outperforms WorldVLA (~7B) and the robot-pretrained OpenVLA (~7B), while matching OpenVLA-OFT when both are trained without large-scale robot pretraining. Code and checkpoints will be released.
item.dc:creator: Frank Tsu-Fang Lu, Karthik Sundar Senthilkumar, Christopher Thirgood, Oscar Mendez, Simon Hadfield

item.title: Learning from Recurrence: Internalizing Depth-Induced Preferences in Looped Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.33468v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A looped language model repeatedly applies the same block to its hidden state before predicting each token. The number of passes is its recurrent depth. Increasing this depth gives the model more computation per token with the same parameters. Can the shared block learn from the predictions it makes at greater depth? Following prior work, we retrofit pretrained OLMo-2-1B with a shared recurrent block and continue mid-training over varying recurrent depths. In the four-pass model, additional passes mainly redistribute probability among tokens that already rank highly after one pass. We use the continuations generated at greater depth to train only the shared block through a single pass, without reference answers or correctness filtering. We call this transfer preference write-back. Write-back further improves one-pass and multi-pass accuracy on most tasks. At their target depths, the updated models outperform a non-recurrent control matched for mid-training data and token budget on all six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with a mean relative gain in accuracy of up to 46.2% across tasks. At four-pass inference, one-pass training outperforms full-depth training on the same targets in the model with input injection. This advantage disappears in the matched model without injection. On GSM8K, using the updated block only on passes two through four recovers nearly the entire four-pass gain, showing that an update learned in one pass can improve later applications of the same block.
item.dc:creator: Hui Chen, Joshua Elsdon, Can Goksen

item.title: Memory as the Backbone: A Dual-Store Associative Memory Architecture for Visual Recognition
item.description: arXiv:2611.33475v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate whether explicit memory can serve as the organizing principle of a general-purpose visual backbone. Inspired by the interaction between working and long-term memory in human cognition, we introduce DuSAM (Dual-Store Associative Memory), a hierarchical memory-native visual backbone coupling image-local working memory (WM) with a fixed-capacity persistent semantic memory (PM). WM organizes local visual evidence into compact, spatially anchored states that are updated and transported across stages, then read back to refine dense features. PM consolidates semantic evidence from training images and annotated regions into prototypes, whose retrieved content enriches the same working states. With these memory operations in place of self-attention or state-space blocks, DuSAM achieves competitive performance relative to representative, similarly sized backbones on ImageNet-1K classification, ADE20K semantic segmentation, and COCO object detection and instance segmentation. Ablations show contributions from both stores, with PM particularly benefiting class groups with fewer annotated training pixels. At $2048\times2048$, the complete DuSAM-based UPerNet segmentor achieves $2.36\times$ the throughput of the evaluated DeiT-S/16 counterpart while using $59.5\%$ less GPU memory, and $1.24\times$ the throughput of the linear-complexity VMamba-T. Memory analyses reveal spatially selective WM access and semantic associations between retrieved prototypes and training regions. Class-targeted removal and restoration further demonstrate that category-specific experience can be replenished through state updates without changing network parameters. These results establish explicit memory as a viable organizing principle for visual backbones and provide a foundation for jointly designing contextual computation and addressable semantic memory.
item.dc:creator: Ruizhi Wang, Xiangtao Wang, Bayar Menzat, Jianfeng Wang, Thomas Lukasiewicz

item.title: On the Impact of Extra Information in Bandit Learning: More is Not Always Merrier
item.description: arXiv:2611.33479v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: More data is commonly assumed to improve learning performance, however, we show that this intuition can surprisngly fail in sequential decision-making. Considering a stochastic bandits setup with exogenous extra information, we ask if the free and unbiased extra reward samples are guaranteed to reduce the regret of the learner. We introduce a formal notion of `non-degradation under extra information' and demonstrate that the widely used Upper Confidence Bound algorithm (UCB) violates this property, i.e., there exist benign extra-information under which UCB incurs strictly higher regret than when run without extra information. We contrast this behaviour with Thompson Sampling and Explore-Then-Commit, which appear to benefit from the same extra information. Constructively, we propose a meta-algorithm that provably enforces non-degradation for a broad class of bandit algorithms. We also run empirical simulations to study our meta-algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Ramakrishnan Krishnamurthy

item.title: Data-free continuous-time physics-informed neural networks for vortex shedding: a consistent pressure across time windows
item.description: arXiv:2611.33489v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Without data, physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in continuous time have so far failed to develop vortex shedding past a circular cylinder in a domain symmetric about the wake centerline: the training converges to the steady symmetric solution. We obtain shedding at Re=100 with a continuous-time PINN trained over successive time windows, without any reference data and without temporal discretization, the symmetry being broken by an analytical, divergence-free initial condition. The Strouhal number and the mean drag coefficient agree with an OpenFOAM solution computed on the same domain to within 0.5%. The pressure, however, is discontinuous at the junctions between windows, and the lift coefficient is a staircase. We relate this discontinuity to the differential-algebraic structure of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, of index 2 after spatial discretization: a consistent initial condition of each window must satisfy the constraint $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{v}=0$ for the velocity, and the hidden constraint $\nabla\cdot\partial_t\mathbf{v}=0$, with $\partial_t\mathbf{v}$ given by the momentum equation, then determines the pressure. Imposing the pressure alone makes the solution continuous but not consistent; our remedy imposes the pressure at the junctions and adds this hidden constraint to the loss. Over five shedding periods, the jumps of the lift coefficient become 20 times smaller.
item.dc:creator: Micka\"el Delcey, Cyril Regan, Masaki Fuchiwaki, Yoann Cheny

item.title: Learning to Reason in Real-Time
item.description: arXiv:2611.33513v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI agents that operate in the real world must reason correctly and on-time, yet they currently do not account for how time should alter their reasoning. Modern agents learn to do tasks in environments that are entirely synchronous: where the world waits for the agent to act before changing. A real-time environment, by contrast, changes independent of the agent. Existing approaches try to bridge this gap by imposing a ratio of thinking to acting. However, for an agent to succeed in real-time it must learn to act quickly when delay is costly and to reason longer when the benefit outweighs the missed opportunities. To this end, we introduce real-time reasoning training (RRT) as the class of training techniques for real-time reasoning agents. We develop three standard RRT techniques: (1) using real-time data, (2) decoupling acting and observing, and (3) curriculum learning in time. Together, these simple techniques substantially outperform strong baselines. Across time pressures, we outperform the strongest non-RRT baseline by an average of 33% reward on in-distribution and 55% reward on out-of-distribution tasks in two real-time environments: Frogger and Snake. These results demonstrate that we can teach agents to balance reasoning and responsiveness under real-time constraints, and that RRT opens a broad, new set of capabilities for real-time agents.
item.dc:creator: Xavier Schneider, Benjamin Schneider, Sun Sun, Olga Vechtomova, Victor Zhong

item.title: Model Predictive Control of a Multirotor UAV with a Cable-Suspended Payload: A Comparison of Shifted and Transformer-Based Warm Starts
item.description: arXiv:2611.33514v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This study investigates model predictive control (MPC) of a multirotor drone (unmanned aerial vehicle, UAV) carrying a cable-suspended payload, comparing conventional shifted initialization with Transformer-based warm starting of a sequential convex programming (SCP) optimizer. The controller uses a coupled mechanical model with an elastic cable and a double-pendulum representation of the suspended load. Its formulation includes move-blocked control inputs, finite-difference sensitivities, constrained quadratic subproblems, and input-feasibility projection. A Transformer trained on expert SCP solutions predicts an initial control sequence, which is subsequently refined by the same optimizer used for the conventional methods. Numerical experiments compare zero, shifted, and Transformer initialization under identical controller settings. For independently solved MPC problems, Transformer initialization reduces computation time relative to zero initialization. In sequential closed-loop simulations, however, shifting the preceding optimized control sequence provides the lowest computation time, while all three methods produce similar tracking behavior. These findings emphasize the importance of comparing learned warm starts with conventional initialization methods that reuse previous MPC solutions. The measured optimization times exceed the control sampling period; consequently, real-time implementation is not demonstrated. Keywords: Model predictive control; sequential convex programming; Transformer; warm start; cable-suspended payload; multirotor drone.
item.dc:creator: Athanasios Zeris

item.title: Adversarial Bandit Convex Optimization with $d^{3/2}\sqrt{n}$ Regret
item.description: arXiv:2611.33531v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study adversarial bandit convex optimization, where in each of $n$ rounds a learner chooses a point $A_t$ in a convex body $\mathcal{K}\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ and observes only a noisy value of a convex loss $f_t:\mathcal{K}\to[0,1]$ at that point. The losses are chosen by an adversary, who may change them from round to round and adapt them to the learner's past actions. We improve the best known regret bound for this problem from $\widetilde O(d^{5/2}\sqrt n)$ (Lattimore, 2020, 2026) to $\widetilde O(d^{3/2}\sqrt n)$, which matches the rate conjectured by Bubeck et al. (2017). Together with the recent lower bound of $\Omega(d^{4/3}\sqrt n)$ due to Rajaraman and Han (2026), it determines the minimax regret up to a factor of $d^{1/6}$ and logarithmic factors. The algorithm is an online Newton step with Gaussian exploration. Unlike earlier methods of this kind, it uses unbiased estimates of the gradient and Hessian of the Gaussian smoothing of the loss, rather than of an optimistic surrogate.
item.dc:creator: Alireza Bakhtiari, Kevin Jamieson, Tor Lattimore, Lillian Ratliff

item.title: RankCast: Phase-Aware Rank Balancing in MoE Serving
item.description: arXiv:2611.33542v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern large language model (LLM) inference increasingly adopts disaggregated architectures that separate Prefill (P) and Decode (D) phases. Meanwhile, Expert Parallelism (EP) has been widely adopted in large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model serving. However, load imbalance still slows down MoE inference because each layer must wait for the busiest EP rank. The main source of latency differs between prefill and decode. Prefill is compute-bound, and its MoE layers' latency is determined by the maximum token count of the busiest rank. At the same time, under moderate batch sizes, Decode is memory-bound, so the latency is dominated by the maximum active-expert count across ranks. To solve both problems under a unified framework, we present RankCast, a system that reduces rank-level maximum token counts during prefill and active-expert counts during decode. For every token, RankCast preserves the predicted Top-p experts and chooses the remaining k-p from its Top-L candidates (L > k). In prefill, RankCast yields a price per rank that steers flexible assignments to less loaded ranks. In decode, RankCast closes experts on the busiest ranks while preserving the constraints for each token. Both paths are implemented and tested in the state-of-the-art inference frameworks SGLang and DeepEP. We overlap RankCast's kernels with model execution and reuse the existing DeepEP communication channel for metadata transmission. On Qwen3-235B-A22B with EP=8 and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B with EP=16, RankCast removes over 75% of the busiest rank's excess prefill load, improves prefill input throughput by up to 19%, and reduces decode time per output token by up to 10%. The quality cost is below one percentage point.
item.dc:creator: Kaidi Fu, Xu-Hao Lu, Pingwei Sun, Jianchao Tan, Yuchen Xie, Xunliang Cai

item.title: FokasNets: Completing missing boundary data in Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Operators via the Global Relation
item.description: arXiv:2611.33549v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce FokasNets, a framework that combines Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and operators (PINOs) with the Global Relation (GR) formulation of the Fokas method (also referred to as the Unified Transform), for mixed boundary problems. The general framework considers lifted representations of the neural network models, where the Dirichlet boundary conditions are imposed by construction and the neural network learns the interior correction. The Global Relation is used as an additional solve during training that provides the missing boundary conditions to the lifted neural network, making training more efficient and accurate in the interior and on the boundary. We develop the construction of FokasNets for elliptic and evolution PDEs (Fokas-PINNs), and the corresponding PDE solution operator problems (Fokas Operator Networks - FONets), using the Global Relation formulations for these PDE classes. Furthermore, we develop the necessary theoretical framework for FokasNets, including error and stability analysis and show that FokasNets are universal approximators. We provide comprehensive numerical experiments, using examples with manufactured solutions and literature benchmarks. Compared to standard PINNs and Physics-Informed DeepONets and their lifted versions, FokasNets achieve significant improvements in solution accuracy in the interior and boundaries, both for single PDEs and particularly for solution operators, where the improvement reaches multiple orders of magnitude and fixed threshold errors are reached faster during training.
