GDS agent allows users to ask any question that implicitly and intrinsically requires graph algorithmic reasoning about their data, and quickly obtain accurate and grounded answers. We introduce new benchmarks that evaluate intermediate tool calls as well as final responses, and the results indicate that the GDS agent solves a wide spectrum of graph tasks. We also demonstrate how the GDS agent can perform open-ended analyses at the level of domain experts, on tasks such as money laundering tracing and pattern mining in biology. Finally, we discuss the remaining challenges and the future roadmap.
item.dc:creator: Borun Shi, Lusine Adunts, Ioannis Panagiotas

item.title: Analysis of Variational Sparse Autoencoders
item.description: arXiv:2509.22994v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Variational sparse autoencoders (vSAEs) replace a sparse autoencoder's deterministic Top-K mechanism with a sampled Gaussian posterior hypothesized to produce a more robust feature dictionary. To test this, we build permutation comparisons over training seeds for custom analyses, and score two popular benchmarks on one pair of existing checkpoints. When fixing the unit variance and ablating sampling on the vSAE, we find that the gap between the non-sampled vSAE and a Top-K SAE with an L2 activation penalty can be decomposed completely into a set of five implementation details. When we enable sampling and allow the network to learn its own variance, we find that the discrete selection process of Top-K fails when in conjunction with stochastic sampling methods. At the noise scale these models are trained upon, vastly different Top-K feature sets (Jaccard 0.075-0.29, chance 0.067) are found on equal model activations due only to the sampling noise, in two forward passes of one trained model on the same token. Soft methods such as JumpReLU fail to hold their sparsity target as well due to sampling, though under different failure modes. Noise moves its achieved sparsity, and at matched sparsity reconstruction fails to track selection stability (r = -0.55). Ablating the KL loss term recovers only 3.9 percent of the lost reconstruction. The rest is due to sampling.
item.dc:creator: Zachary Baker, Yuxiao Li

item.title: Fixed Points and Envelope Dynamics on Credal Hyperspaces
item.description: arXiv:2510.04769v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Let $X$ be a compact metric space and consider the hyperspace $\mathscr C_X$ of nonempty weakly closed convex sets of Borel probability measures on $X$, called credal sets. These sets represent uncertainty about which probability law governs the phenomenon of interest. We equip $\mathscr C_X$ with the Hausdorff metric induced by a metric for weak convergence. Credal order intervals $[\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}] = \{ \mathcal{P}\in\mathscr C_X: \mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{P}\subseteq\mathcal{B} \}$ are complete lattices, and every inclusion-monotone, Hausdorff-continuous self map of such an interval has least and greatest fixed points obtained as limits of iteration from $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$. For families of inclusion-monotone updates that may vary with time, we construct lower and upper envelope maps that bound every admissible trajectory. When these envelope maps are Hausdorff-continuous, the distance of every trajectory from a limiting credal interval vanishes uniformly over all switching sequences and initial credal sets. Coalescence of the limiting interval endpoints yields convergence to a common credal limit. We then construct the credal evolution induced by a time consistent Nisio semigroup. Uniform $W_1$ contraction of the underlying Markov semigroups induces Hausdorff-Wasserstein contraction of the credal evolution, yielding a unique common invariant credal set, exponential convergence from every initial credal set, and a support functional equal to the robust ergodic limit. We also derive perturbation bounds from finite time Nisio discrepancies and one step kernel set discrepancies, and characterize the countable sequences of support coordinates that represent credal sets, providing an explicit reconstruction formula.
item.dc:creator: Michele Caprio, Mengqi Chen, Siu Lun Chau, Krikamol Muandet

item.title: ELBO$_{\mathrm{TDS}}$: Temporal Distribution Shift Generalization for Industry-Scale Recommender Systems
item.description: arXiv:2511.21032v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Temporal distribution shift (TDS) degrades the generalization of recommender systems: models trained on past interactions face systematically different user behavior in future time windows. While incremental training on recent data is widely used in industrial production, it can over-adapt to transient patterns and exacerbate instability. Existing approaches such as invariant learning and self-supervised learning offer partial solutions but often suffer from unstable temporal generalization, representation collapse, or inefficient data utilization. To address these limitations, we propose ELBO$_{\mathrm{TDS}}$, a probabilistic framework for temporally robust recommendation. First, we identify key shifting factors in real-world production data and design a simple yet effective data augmentation strategy that simulates realistic time-varying factors and expands the training support. Second, we derive a self-supervised variational objective, ELBO$_{\mathrm{TDS}}$, to harness the benefits of this extended distribution while preventing representation collapse. Extensive experiments on both a public benchmark and a large-scale industrial dataset demonstrate that ELBO$_{\mathrm{TDS}}$ consistently improves next-period ranking performance over strong baselines. It achieves a 2.33\% uplift in GMV per user in online experiments and has been successfully deployed in production. Code is available at https://github.com/FuCongResearchSquad/ELBO4TDS
item.dc:creator: Yuxuan Zhu, Cong Fu, Yabo Ni, Anxiang Zeng, Yuan Fang

item.title: ML-Tool-Bench: Tool-Augmented Planning for ML Tasks
item.description: arXiv:2512.00672v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The development of autonomous machine learning (ML) agents capable of end-to-end data science workflows represents a significant frontier in artificial intelligence. These agents must orchestrate complex sequences of data analysis, feature engineering, model selection, and hyperparameter optimization, tasks that require sophisticated planning and iteration. While recent work on building ML agents has explored using large language models (LLMs) for direct code generation, tool-augmented approaches offer greater modularity and reliability. However, existing tool-use benchmarks focus primarily on task-specific tool selection or argument extraction for tool invocation, failing to evaluate the sophisticated planning capabilities required for ML Agents. In this work, we introduce a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating tool-augmented ML agents using a curated set of 61 specialized tools and 15 tabular ML challenges from Kaggle. Our benchmark goes beyond traditional tool-use evaluation by incorporating an in-memory named object management, allowing agents to flexibly name, save, and retrieve intermediate results throughout the workflows. We demonstrate that standard ReAct-style approaches struggle to generate valid tool sequences for complex ML pipelines, and that tree search methods with LLM-based evaluation underperform due to inconsistent state scoring. To address these limitations, we propose two simple approaches: 1) using shaped deterministic rewards with structured textual feedback, and 2) decomposing the original problem into a sequence of sub-tasks, which significantly improves trajectory validity and task performance. Using GPT-4o, our approach improves over ReAct by 16.52 percentile positions, taking the median across all Kaggle challenges. We believe our work provides a foundation for developing more capable tool-augmented planning ML agents.
item.dc:creator: Yaswanth Chittepu, Raghavendra Addanki, Tung Mai, Anup Rao, Branislav Kveton

item.title: Network of Theseus (like the ship)
item.description: arXiv:2512.04198v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A standard assumption in deep learning is that the inductive bias introduced by a neural network architecture must persist from training through inference. The architecture you train with is the architecture you deploy. This assumption constrains the community from selecting architectures that may have desirable efficiency or design properties due to difficulties with optimization. We challenge this assumption with the Network of Theseus (NoT), a method for progressively converting a trained, or even untrained, guide network architecture part-by-part into an entirely different target network architecture while preserving the performance of the guide network. At each stage, components in the guide network architecture are incrementally replaced with the target architecture modules and aligned via representational similarity metrics. This procedure preserves most of the functionality of the guide network even under substantial architectural changes-for example, converting a convolutional network into a multilayer perceptron, or GPT-2 into a recurrent neural network. By decoupling optimization from deployment, NoT expands the space of viable inference-time architectures, opening opportunities for better accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs and enabling more directed exploration of the architectural design space.
item.dc:creator: Vighnesh Subramaniam, Colin Conwell, Boris Katz, Andrei Barbu, Brian Cheung

item.title: Learning with Limited Antigenic Labels: Semi-supervised Prediction of Influenza A Antigenic Relationships with Protein Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2512.05222v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Influenza A viruses (IAVs) undergo frequent antigenic changes that require regular vaccine updates. Because haemagglutination inhibition (HI) assays are labour-intensive, antigenic measurements remain limited relative to the available sequence data. We combined pre-trained protein representations with semi-supervised learning (SSL) to predict antigenic relationships when labelled data are scarce. HA1 sequences from H1N1, H3N2, H5N1, and H9N2 were encoded using ESM-2, ProtVec, ProtT5, and ProtBert. Using these embeddings, we compared self-training and label spreading with supervised baselines, including random forest (RF) and support vector machine (SVM) models. Nested cross-validation evaluated performance with 25%, 50%, 75%, or 100% of training labels retained. Self-training slightly improved RF performance in most settings but generally reduced SVM's ability to distinguish antigenically similar from antigenically different virus pairs. With 25% of training labels retained, self-training increased mean macro-F1 from 0.791 to 0.798 for ProtVec-RF and from 0.776 to 0.778 for ESM-2 RF. Label spreading performed best with ProtVec but remained below supervised RF across all protein representations and training-label proportions. In supervised and self-training RF models using ESM-2 or ProtBert, additional training labels improved classification of H3N2 antigenic relationships, whereas H9N2 remained the most difficult subtype. RF frequently misclassified antigenically similar H9N2 pairs as variants.
item.dc:creator: Yanhua Xu

item.title: CoDeQ: Compression with a Dead-Zone Quantizer for Differentiable Joint Pruning--Quantization
item.description: arXiv:2512.12981v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Joint pruning and quantization can reduce the inference cost of neural-networks, but determining layerwise sparsity and precision often requires auxiliary allocation procedures and considerable hyperparameter tuning. We introduce CoDeQ, a quantization-aware training method that unifies pruning and quantization through a learnable dead-zone quantizer. Its learned dead-zone width controls layerwise sparsity, while bit widths can be held fixed or learned in mixed-precision mode. A pruning-aware scale allocates all available nonzero reconstruction levels over the retained range. We derive the spacing that minimizes worst-case reconstruction error over this range for a fixed bit width and range endpoint. Model weights and compression parameters are optimized jointly under one global compression coefficient, with a shared learning rate for the compression parameters. On VGG7/CIFAR-10, CoDeQ with 2-bit activations achieves 0.05% relative BOPs, for an accuracy drop of 0.32 percentage points. On DeiT-Tiny/ImageNet-1K, mixed-precision CoDeQ preserves FP32-level accuracy at only 8.12% relative BOPs. Additional experiments across several architectures and datasets demonstrate competitive accuracy--BOP trade-offs against other joint compression methods.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Wensh{\o}j, Mikkel Dahl, Tong Chen, Bob Pepin, Raghavendra Selvan

item.title: Neural Isomorphic Fields: A Transformer-based Algebraic Numerical Embedding
item.description: arXiv:2601.12095v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neural network models often face challenges when processing very small or very large numbers due to issues such as overflow, underflow, and unstable output variations. To mitigate these problems, we propose using embedding vectors for numbers instead of directly using their raw values. These embeddings aim to retain essential algebraic properties while preventing numerical instabilities. We introduce Neural Isomorphic Fields (NIF), a digit-sequence Transformer autoencoder trained with two learned commutative operators and an antisymmetric neural comparator. At zero loss, the embeddings provably form an ordered integral domain isomorphic to the decimal fractions, whose field of fractions is isomorphic to the rationals. For the trained model, we bound errors of operations, chains and algebraic laws by decoding margins, defects and Lipschitz constants. Trained on up to 25 digits, NIF reaches at least 99.9% exact match on closure, identity, associativity and distributivity and 99.8% on ten-step chains and the order relation. With four channels per decimal place, reconstruction and both operations exceed 99.7% exact match on numbers of up to 200 digits whose parts stay within training lengths, so the dimension grows linearly. In a language model, frozen operators raise exact match on 14-20-digit word problems from 12.0% (operators off) to 39.7%.
item.dc:creator: Hamidreza Sadeghi, Saeedeh Momtazi, Reza Safabakhsh

item.title: Latent Diffusion for Internet of Things Attack Data Generation in Intrusion Detection
item.description: arXiv:2601.16976v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The growing deployment of IoT systems has increased the need for reliable intrusion detection under heterogeneous and imbalanced network traffic. However, representative malicious traffic, particularly for underrepresented attacks, remains difficult to obtain, while existing generative approaches do not consistently preserve distributional fidelity, multivariate dependencies, and coverage simultaneously. This work proposes LaDIS, an attack-specific framework that learns a mixed-type autoencoder representation and performs diffusion in an adaptive continuous latent space. LaDIS was compared with established adversarial, variational, and direct-space diffusion approaches across representative Flooding, Botnet, Recon, and Stealthy attacks using complementary measures of marginal and multivariate fidelity, dependency preservation, real--synthetic distinguishability, manifold structure, and computational efficiency. LaDIS provided a competitive balance across these dimensions, with particularly strong results for representative Botnet, Recon, and Stealthy attacks, while revealing an attack-dependent fidelity--coverage trade-off. Performing diffusion in latent space also reduced sampling time by approximately 3--5 times relative to direct-space diffusion, with negligible decoding overhead. Downstream utility was evaluated using TabNet and XGBoost, demonstrating that partial LaDIS augmentation consistently produced the best performance, increasing balanced accuracy from 0.86 to 0.94 for TabNet and from 0.92 to 0.96 for XGBoost, while improving the F1-score for low-volume attack families from 0.73 to 0.84 and from 0.82 to 0.88, respectively. These results show that attack-adaptive latent diffusion can generate structurally faithful attack traffic efficiently and, when used selectively, improve intrusion detection for underrepresented attacks.
item.dc:creator: Estela S\'anchez-Carballo, Francisco M. Melgarejo-Meseguer, Jos\'e Luis Rojo-\'Alvarez

item.title: TopoPrune: Robust Data Pruning via Unified Latent Space Topology
item.description: arXiv:2602.02739v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Geometric data pruning methods, while practical for leveraging pretrained models, are fundamentally unstable. Their reliance on extrinsic geometry renders them highly sensitive to latent space perturbations, causing performance to degrade during cross-architecture transfer or in the presence of feature noise. We introduce TopoPrune, a framework which resolves this challenge by leveraging topology to capture the stable, intrinsic structure of data. TopoPrune operates at two scales, (1) utilizing a topology-aware manifold approximation to establish a global low-dimensional embedding of the dataset. Subsequently, (2) it employs differentiable persistent homology to perform a local topological optimization on the manifold embeddings, ranking samples by their structural complexity. We demonstrate that our unified dual-scale topological approach ensures high accuracy and precision, particularly at significant dataset pruning rates (e.g., 90%). Furthermore, through the inherent stability properties of topology, TopoPrune is (a) exceptionally robust to noise perturbations of latent feature embeddings and (b) demonstrates superior transferability across diverse network architectures. This study demonstrates a promising avenue towards stable and principled topology-based frameworks for robust data-efficient learning.
item.dc:creator: Arjun Roy, Prajna G. Malettira, Manish Nagaraj, Kaushik Roy

item.title: Explainable Machine-Learning based Detection of Knee Injuries in Runners
item.description: arXiv:2602.11668v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Running is a widely practiced activity but shows a high incidence of knee injuries, especially Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome (PFPS) and Iliotibial Band Syndrome (ITBS). Identifying gait patterns linked to these injuries can improve clinical decision-making, which requires precise systems capable of capturing and analyzing temporal kinematic data. This study uses optical motion capture systems to enhance detection of injury-related running patterns. We analyze a public dataset of 839 treadmill recordings from healthy and injured runners to evaluate how effectively these systems capture dynamic parameters relevant to injury classification. The focus is on the stance phase, using joint and segment angle time series and discrete point values. Three classification tasks are addressed: healthy vs. injured, healthy vs. PFPS, and healthy vs. ITBS. We examine different feature spaces, from traditional point-based metrics to full stance-phase time series and hybrid representations. Multiple models are tested, including classical algorithms (K-Nearest Neighbors, Gaussian Processes, Decision Trees) and deep learning architectures (CNNs, LSTMs). Performance is evaluated with accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Explainability tools such as Shapley values, saliency maps, and Grad-CAM are used to interpret model behavior. Results show that combining time series with point values substantially improves detection. Deep learning models outperform classical ones, with CNNs achieving the highest accuracy: 77.9% for PFPS, 73.8% for ITBS, and 71.43% for the combined injury class. These findings highlight the potential of motion capture systems coupled with advanced machine learning to identify knee injury-related running patterns.
item.dc:creator: David Fuentes-Jim\'enez, Sara Garc\'ia-de-Villa, David Casillas-P\'erez, Pablo Flor\'ia, Francisco-Manuel Melgarejo-Meseguer

item.title: In- and Out-of-Distribution Generalization of Reasoning in Multimodal LLMs for Simple Visual Planning Tasks
item.description: arXiv:2602.15460v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Integrating reasoning in (multimodal) large language models has recently led to significant improvement of their capabilities. However, generalization in reasoning models is still vaguely defined and poorly understood. In this work, we present an evaluation framework to rigorously examine how well chain-of-thought (CoT) approaches generalize in simple visual planning, specifically on a grid-based navigation task. The versatility of the task and its data allows us to fine-tune model variants using different input representations (visual and textual) and CoT reasoning strategies, and systematically evaluate them under both in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) test conditions. Our experiments show that the out-of-distribution generalization (e.g., to larger maps) is largely impacted by the format used for input maps and CoT chains. Surprisingly, we find that coordinate-based reasoning traces which combine text descriptions yield the best OOD generalization. Moreover, CoT reproducing the steps of the A* algorithm yields the state-of-the-art ID accuracy, and simple augmentation of the map solutions seen during training greatly boosts OOD results. Repeating the experiments with maps represented by coordinates yields similar results for another model family. Tests on structurally complex maps reveal a sharp performance drop when shortest solutions require many movement directions or turns. Additional fine-tuning on examples of directionally complex maps substantially recovers this performance. Finally, purely text-based models consistently outperform those utilizing image-based inputs, including a recently proposed approach relying on latent space reasoning.
item.dc:creator: Yannic Neuhaus, Chanoknan Tanchotikul, Nicolas Flammarion, Matthias Hein, Francesco Croce

item.title: Localized Dynamics-Aware Domain Adaptation for Off-Dynamics Offline Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2602.21072v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Off-dynamics offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims to learn a policy for a target domain using limited target data and abundant source data collected under different transition dynamics. Existing methods typically address dynamics mismatch either globally over the state space or via pointwise data filtering; these approaches can miss localized cross-domain similarities or incur high computational cost. We propose Localized Dynamics-Aware Domain Adaptation (LoDADA), which exploits localized dynamics mismatch to better reuse source data. LoDADA clusters transitions from source and target datasets and estimates cluster-level dynamics discrepancy via domain discrimination. Source transitions from clusters with small discrepancy are more likely to be retained compared with those from clusters with large discrepancy. This yields a fine-grained and scalable data selection strategy that avoids overly coarse global assumptions and expensive per-sample filtering. We provide theoretical insights and extensive experiments across environments with diverse global and local dynamics shifts. Results show that LoDADA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art off-dynamics offline RL methods by better leveraging localized distribution mismatch.
item.dc:creator: Zhangjie Xia, Yu Yang, Pan Xu

item.title: SVDP: Training-Free Contextual Sparsity Predictors for Fast LLM Inference
item.description: arXiv:2603.14110v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Contextual sparsity is one of the approaches used to reduce computational complexity in the inference process of large language models (LLMs). Existing techniques for efficient LLM inference acceleration based on contextual sparsity with minimal accuracy degradation require training sparse pattern predictors. This paper presents a framework for accelerating inference of ReGLU-based feed-forward networks (FFNs) within LLMs. The proposed framework provides a fast, training-free method for building sparse pattern predictors using truncation-aware singular value decomposition (SVD) of the gate projection matrix, along with a threshold calibration algorithm, and inference executors supporting conditional computation on CUDA and CANN devices. Experiments on three sparse LLMs with an average activation sparsity level of 90% in the FFNs demonstrate up to a 1.8x reduction in end-to-end decoding time while maintaining less than 1% degradation in benchmark scores on tasks involving complex math and code generation. This work advances the deployment of LLMs on edge devices.
item.dc:creator: Georgii Serbin, Kirill Koshkin, Zhongao Sun, Anastasiya Bistrigova, C. C. Korikov

item.title: FairMed-XGB: A Bayesian-Optimised Multi-Metric Framework with Explainability for Demographic Equity in Critical Healthcare Data
item.description: arXiv:2603.14947v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Background:Machine learning models in emergency medicine often exhibit demographic biases, particularly gender disparities, which can compromise fairness, clinical trust, and decision-making reliability. Existing mitigation approaches typically optimise isolated fairness metrics, failing to address the multi-dimensional nature of bias while maintaining predictive performance and interpretability. Methods: We propose FairMed-XGB, a Bayesian-optimised, multi-metric fairness framework integrated into an XGBoost classifier. The model incorporates a composite fairness-aware loss function combining Statistical Parity Difference, Theil Index, and Wasserstein Distance. Bayesian optimisation is used to balance fairness and predictive accuracy. The framework is evaluated on seven cohorts derived from the MIMIC-IV-ED and eICU datasets. SHAP-based explainability is employed to analyse feature contributions and identify bias-related patterns. Results: FairMed-XGB significantly reduces gender-based disparities across all cohorts. Statistical Parity Difference decreases by 40-51% on MIMIC-IV-ED and 10-19% on eICU datasets. Theil Index values reduce by four to five orders of magnitude, approaching near-zero levels, while Wasserstein Distance decreases by 20-72%. These improvements are achieved with minimal impact on predictive performance (AUC-ROC reduction <0.02). SHAP analysis demonstrates reduced dependence on gender-proxy features and improved distributional fairness. Conclusions: FairMed-XGB provides a robust and interpretable framework for mitigating demographic bias in emergency medicine prediction models. By jointly optimising multiple fairness objectives and preserving model performance, it enables equitable and trustworthy AI deployment in high-stakes clinical settings. The integration of explainability further supports transparency and clinical adoption.
item.dc:creator: Mitul Goswami, Romit Chatterjee, Arif Ahmed Sekh

item.title: Manifold-Matching Autoencoders
item.description: arXiv:2603.16568v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Manipulating the structure of data in the latent space of an autoencoder is a long-standing goal of representation learning. We propose a simple regularization, Manifold Matching, that imposes an explicit geometric structure on that latent space. The idea is to take a reference representation R of the data, which need not be the raw input X fed to the network, and to minimize, batch-wise, the mean squared error between the pairwise distances in R and those in the latent space Z. Although the autoencoder still learns to reconstruct X, the shape of its latent space comes to mimic that of R. The objective requires no labels, only reference distances, and because those are scalars, the dimensionality of R is decoupled from that of Z: any reference can guide any bottleneck. Using this single instrument we study how different geometric structures can be imposed on a latent space, comparing against autoencoders built on geometric or topological regularizers. Across fifteen datasets under a shared protocol with statistical testing, the resulting Manifold-Matching Autoencoder (MMAE) matches the global-structure quality of persistence-based autoencoders, statistically tying RTD-AE on distance correlation and triplet accuracy, and stays competitive on the local and topological metrics that other methods lead, at the computational cost of a plain autoencoder: it uses only a batched distance loss, with no persistence computation. We frame MMAE not as a universal winner but as an efficient and controllable regularizer whose reference selects which structure the latent inherits, and which turns any fixed embedding into a reusable out-of-sample encoder. All experiments use a two-dimensional bottleneck.
item.dc:creator: Laurent Cheret, Vincent L\'etourneau, Isar Nejadgholi, Chris Drummond, Hussein Al Osman, Maia Fraser

item.title: Thinking Deeper, Not Longer: Memory-Efficient Latent Chain-of-Thought with Depth-Recurrent Transformers for Compositional Generalization
item.description: arXiv:2603.21676v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Standard Transformers have a fixed computational depth, limiting their ability to generalize to tasks that require variable-depth reasoning. The usual remedy, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), spends tokens to reason, inflating the key--value cache, so memory becomes the limiting cost when reasoning is served over large query batches. We study a depth-recurrent Transformer that decouples computational depth from parameter count by iterating a shared-weight block, so that adding reasoning steps leaves peak inference memory unchanged and grows latency only linearly, with no token generation. Three ingredients support the recurrence over 20+ thinking steps: a silent thinking objective that supervises only the final output, LayerScale initialization, and an identity-biased gate that opens a gradient highway across steps. We characterize it on three compositional domains with decreasing structural bias: graph reachability (adjacency masking), nested boolean logic (relative positioning), and unstructured relational text (no structural positional cue). We find a \emph{computational frontier}: accuracy climbs once the thinking-step count meets the task's complexity, reaching near-perfect performance on the two structured tasks and a lower plateau on unstructured text. How it climbs depends on the structural bias---abruptly from chance on the graph task, gradually on the other two. Depth recurrence extrapolates beyond the training range: it succeeds on the graph task where fixed-depth models barely extrapolate, and on the two sequence tasks comes within two points of fixed-depth Transformers that use $4$--$6.4\times$ more parameters. On the graph task, whose adjacency mask makes propagation depth verifiable, intermediate per-step supervision---a standard recipe for deep iterative models---consistently \emph{harms} this extrapolation at widths $d \geq 256$. We release the code for reproducibility.
item.dc:creator: Hung-Hsuan Chen

item.title: Benchmarking LLM-Based Investment Advisor Agents for Asset Allocation in the Chinese ETF Market: Overview of NLPCC 2026 Shared Task 4
item.description: arXiv:2603.22305v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) convert unstructured financial news into actionable trading strategies, yet standardized end-to-end benchmarks tailored for Chinese market remain scarce. We select common Chinese Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs) as the investment universe and introduce CN-Buzz2Portfolio, the official benchmark of NLPCC 2026 Shared Task 4. Investment agents take daily trending Chinese financial news and historical ETF price-volume series as inputs to complete news filtering, news-to-ETF mapping and risk-controlled portfolio construction. To facilitate fair comparison, we provide a reproducible Compression--Perception--Allocation baseline compatible with mainstream LLMs. The task contains two ETF allocation tracks: Macro-Asset Allocation and Sector-Rotation Allocation. We adopt chronological data split across 2024--2026 to alleviate overfitting, with final rankings determined by out-of-sample Sharpe ratios on unseen test data. 26 teams registered for the task, and 14 submitted self-designed agent systems. Three core findings emerge: (1) Native LLM reasoning capability cannot translate to superior investment returns, as models show highly differentiated risk-return characteristics; (2) Hybrid frameworks are widely adopted, where LLMs extract textual semantic signals and quantitative modules incorporate price-volume factors and risk constraints; (3) Systems based on identical base LLMs yield distinct results with different signal processing, memory and portfolio construction modules. The project is publicly released at https://github.com/splash-li/NLPCC2026-Shared-Task-4.
item.dc:creator: Liyuan Chen, Shilong Li, Jiangpeng Yan, Shuoling Liu, Xi Cheng, Haoran Zhang, Jianqiu Deng, Xiu Li, Jian Li, Wu Zhu, Yingzi Zhu, Li Yuan, Qianqian Xie, Nan Tang, Yang Veronica Liu, Qiang Yang

item.title: Biologically Inspired Coordination of Parameter Selection and Update Strength for Language Model Adaptation
item.description: arXiv:2604.00533v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Adapting a source-trained language model to a target task requires deciding which parameters to update and how strongly when learning signals are uncertain. We introduce Synapse Consolidation (SyCo), a biologically inspired framework that coordinates these two controls. Rac1-associated forgetting and memory-trace redistribution motivate retaining selected source-derived low-rank components while resetting others for target adaptation. MAPK-associated signal processing motivates combining multiple prediction-based indicators over time to regulate update strength. SyCo combines these controls with a structured consistency objective and a small, fixed buffer of labelled source examples. Target labels are not used during adaptation. We evaluate the framework in Multi-source Open-set Adaptation (MOA), using source-initialized target learners for tasks absent from source training and for perturbed held-out inputs from source tasks. Across 18 natural-language-processing datasets, SyCo reaches 78.01% average accuracy on unseen-task adaptation and 85.37% under unseen-data shifts, outperforming the strongest evaluated hybrid baselines. Ablations support complementary contributions from selective plasticity, evidence-guided update control and structured consistency. These results show how coordinated control of update location and strength can improve target adaptation under uncertain learning signals.
item.dc:creator: Xiao Zhang, Tianyu Hu, Juntao Lyu, Qianchuan Zhao, Huimin Ma

item.title: EEG Foundation Models Need Channel Adaptation, but Fixed Channel Mappings Often Suffice
item.description: arXiv:2604.23091v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scaling EEG foundation models requires pooling data across heterogeneous montages, so every model needs a channel-adaptation step mapping an arbitrary source montage onto its expected input. Whether this step must be learned, and whether it confounds cross-model comparison, is untested. We compare five channel-adaptation routes (a learned Conv1d projection, spherical spline interpolation, source-space decomposition, Riemannian re-centering, and each model's native handling) across five pretrained models (5M--157M parameters), five downstream tasks, two training regimes, and up to 15 random seeds. The answer is architecture-dependent rather than adapter-universal: fixed or native mappings are best in 18 of 25 model--task cells, but regime-specific wins are distributed across Native/Conv1d/SSI/OmnEEG/Riemannian. Rigid fixed-input BENDR is the main case where a learned bridge is needed; the strongest model, CBraMod, reaches its best results without adding a learned channel adapter. Because a learned adapter adds a montage-dependent task parameter budget, we recommend reporting frozen-probe benchmarks under a fixed/native route, and treating learned adapters in full fine-tuning as part of the model being evaluated. Source code is available at https://github.com/Kkuntal990/eeg-channel-adaptation.
item.dc:creator: Kuntal Kokate, Dung Truong, Pierre Guetschel, Bruno Aristimunha, Arnaud Delorme

item.title: Regret-Oracle Complexity Tradeoffs in Agnostic Online Learning
item.description: arXiv:2605.07155v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agnostic online learning is classically solved via a reduction to the realizable setting, utilizing Littlestone's Standard Optimal Algorithm (SOA) as a base learner. However, the SOA can be computationally intractable to implement even for a single round. To overcome this barrier, recent work in oracle-efficient online learning replaces the SOA with a realizable base learner that accesses the concept class exclusively through an offline empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle. While such agnostic learners achieve expected regret $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(\sqrt{T\cdot 2^{\mathcal{O}(d_{\mathrm{LD}})}}\big)$, which is near-optimal in the horizon $T$ for fixed Littlestone dimension $d_{\mathrm{LD}}$, they require $\mathcal{O}\big(T^{2^{\mathcal{O}(d_{\mathrm{LD}})}}\big)$ oracle calls. In this work, we significantly improve this oracle complexity while relying on an even weaker primitive: a weak-consistency oracle, which merely decides whether a given labeled dataset is realizable. At the core of our approach is an adaptive and dynamic agnostic-to-realizable reduction that actively prunes non-realizable label sequences on the fly. By using the VC dimension ($d_{\mathrm{VC}}$) to bound the number of dynamically maintained active paths, our algorithm reduces the total query complexity down to $\mathcal{O}(T^{d_{\mathrm{VC}}+1})$ while perfectly preserving near-optimal expected regret. Crucially, this dynamic pruning also yields a memory reduction over the standard reduction. Furthermore, we formally quantify the regret--oracle complexity tradeoff, providing upper bounds that smoothly interpolate between restricted query budgets and attainable expected regret. We complement these with lower bounds proving that any learner restricted to $Q = o(\sqrt{T})$ queries must suffer an expected regret of $\Omega(T/Q)$.
item.dc:creator: Idan Attias, Steve Hanneke, Arvind Ramaswami

item.title: The Transformer as a Polar State Estimator
item.description: arXiv:2605.11007v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that the core components of the Transformer---attention, residual connections, normalization, and rotary encodings---arise from a single state-estimation problem. We treat each token as a noisy reading of a rotating direction on the hypersphere, taken at its own magnitude. Estimating this direction unifies the architecture: rotational dynamics give rotary encodings, robust estimation gives attention, normalization enforces the spherical geometry, and the residual connection steps toward the estimate. This reconciles normalized queries and keys with unnormalized values as opposite assumptions on whether token magnitudes are independent or share a common scale. Finally, the \emph{Polar Transformer} restores three elements standard blocks drop: rotating values alongside keys, using key magnitudes as confidence, and stepping toward the estimate rather than adding it.
item.dc:creator: Peter Racioppo

item.title: Human-Centered Learning Mechanics: Observable Entropy Control under Protected-Risk Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2605.22940v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Human-Centered Learning Mechanics (HCLM) treats learning as an open, controlled process in which task progress, representation information, structural restrictions and externally specified risk limits jointly govern parameter updates. We characterise this mechanism through a normalised covariance-information force, metric observability and exact feasible rate constraints. The projected task rate depends on an observable cross-product that differs from the ordinary task information product when a probe set does not contain the training task. Error, finite-step and delay margins specify when admissible local requests can be implemented. A primary 288-run neural study separates information control from empirical risk protection and retains cases where extra compression worsens held-out loss. Follow-up experiments train the observable restriction in a declared 13-dimensional subspace, implement a frozen-public-encoder readout through an actual Gaussian sample channel, evaluate a fixed-coefficient sensitivity grid, and test targeted nuisance control with two-hidden-layer minibatch learning on Fashion-MNIST. The nuisance study improves shifted accuracy over ERM, while generic protected balancing accounts for most of the gain. Together, the theory and experiments identify attainable information actions, predictive costs and the separate assumptions required for population-risk certification.
item.dc:creator: Kim Phuc Tran

item.title: Scalable Heterogeneous Graph Foundation Models for Data-Driven Optimal Power Flow in Smart Grids
item.description: arXiv:2605.23194v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fast and reliable optimal power flow (OPF) approximation is important for power system operation, yet heterogeneous OPF graph models are often evaluated either with architecture-specific implementations or on limited training corpora. This paper presents a large-scale heterogeneous graph-learning workflow, built on HydraGNN, for data-driven OPF surrogate modeling and graph foundation-model (GFM) development. The workflow preserves buses, generators, loads, shunts, alternating-current (AC) lines, transformers, and device-to-bus relations and provides a common implementation for distributed preprocessing, multi-graphics-processing-unit (GPU) training, hyperparameter optimization (HPO), and downstream adaptation. Using approximately three million heterogeneous graphs from ten Power Grid Library for Benchmarking AC Optimal Power Flow Algorithms (PGLib-OPF) cases spanning 14 to 13,659 buses, we compare six heterogeneous graph neural network (GNN) families under a common HPO campaign on Frontier, resulting in two compact HeteroSAGE and HeteroHEAT models (~1.6-1.7 million parameters) that achieve the lowest observed validation MSE. Strong and weak scaling using up to 1,024 Frontier nodes show that 256 nodes (corresponding to 1,024 AMD MI250X GPUs) provides the best time-to-solution balance for the measured workload. Two downstream tasks evaluate task adaptation on the IEEE 118-bus case: a classification task to distinguish nominal operating conditions from artificially generated extreme-overload conditions and N-1 single-component-outage regression to predict bus voltage magnitude and phase angle. Partial fine-tuning provides the strongest balance between predictive performance and computational requirements.
item.dc:creator: Massimiliano Lupo Pasini, Yijiang Li, Kibaek Kim, Teja Kuruganti

item.title: Global linear convergence of entropy-regularized softmax policy gradient beyond tabular MDPs
item.description: arXiv:2605.24939v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the global convergence of policy gradient for infinite-horizon entropy-regularized Markov decision processes (MDPs) with continuous state and action spaces. We consider log-linear softmax policies with linear function approximation, which extend the tabular softmax parameterization while retaining a tractable policy class. Under $Q^\pi_\tau$-realizability up to a state-dependent baseline for the regularized state-action value function, we establish a non-uniform Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) inequality for two different feature regimes. The non-uniformity arises through degeneracy of the state-averaged Fisher information matrix in the first feature regime and the uncentered feature second-moment matrix in the second. In both regimes we prove that these non-uniform constants can be bounded uniformly from below along the gradient flow. For full-affine-span features, we prove radial unboundedness of the KL regularizer and show that the state averaged smallest eigenvalue of the Fisher information matrix remains bounded below by an initialization-dependent positive constant. For simplex-valued features, we prove an analogous radial unboundedness result in the subspace orthogonal to the one vector and obtain an initialization dependent lower bound for the state averaged smallest eigenvalue of the uncentered second-moment matrix. These results imply global linear convergence of the regularized objective along the gradient flow, i.e., suboptimality decaying as $\mathcal{O}(e^{-Ct})$ for some $C>0$. Our analysis complements the global convergence theory of entropy-regularized softmax policy gradient beyond the tabular setting of Agarwal et al. (2020); Bhandari and Russo (2024); Mei et al. (2020).
item.dc:creator: Ziyue Chen, David \v{S}i\v{s}ka, Lukasz Szpruch

item.title: A Geometric View for Understanding Concept Learning and Neuron Interpretation in Sparse Autoencoders
item.description: arXiv:2606.07007v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a unified mathematical framework for a geometric understanding of concept learning and neuron interpretation in sparse autoencoders (SAEs). While SAEs improve interpretability of neural networks by learning sparse feature representations, a principled definition of ''concept'' and ''learning'' remains unclear. We formalize concepts as sets of data points and cast concept learning as a set-alignment problem between human-defined and model-induced concepts. This formulation distinguishes three increasingly strong notions of learning -- detection, separation, and approximation -- and yields geometric conditions, error bounds, and capacity constraints for when concepts can be represented by individual neurons or multi-neuron units. It also provides a set-theoretic account for common SAE phenomena, including feature splitting, feature absorption, feature families, and hierarchical concepts. Finally, we connect concept learning and neuron interpretation through formal concept analysis, showing that the two directions need not agree and that their many-to-many structure can be organized by concept lattices. Experiments on synthetic data with ReLU and Top-$K$ SAEs illustrate the theory and reveal the effects of SAE size and sparsity on concept learning.
item.dc:creator: Chenhao Zhang, Chris Lin, Xiaojian Chen, Hanqi Feng, Su-In Lee

item.title: Sample Where You Struggle: Sharpening Base Model Reasoning via Entropy-Guided Power Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2606.09926v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sampling from the sequence-level power distribution elicits RL-level reasoning from base language models without any parameter updates, but the standard Metropolis--Hastings (MH), a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampler, is both expensive and slow-mixing. We trace both to a structural mismatch: the power distribution mainly departs from the base distribution at a sparse, spatially clustered set of high-entropy decision points, yet MH proposes resampling positions uniformly along the prefix---wasting compute on near-degenerate conditionals while under-mixing precisely where modes diverge. We propose Entropy-Guided Power Sampling (EGPS), a training-free and verifier-free approximate sampler that re-derives its proposal from token-level entropy already in the forward pass. EGPS skips deterministic blocks, localizes each MCMC move to a high-entropy neighborhood, and applies Multiple-Try Metropolis at decision points---making sampling cost scale with entropy mass rather than sequence length. EGPS targets significant speedup with accuracy that matches or improves on MH power sampling: across three base models and three benchmarks it attains best or tied-best accuracy on 5 of 9 settings; on Qwen2.5-Math-7B it is best or tied-best on all three (MATH500 $75.8\%$, HumanEval $62.2\%$, GPQA $42.4\%$), with wall-clock speedups over the MH baseline of up to $12.6\times$ across these benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/hongguo7/EGPS
item.dc:creator: Hong Guo, Nianhui Guo, Christoph Meinel, Haojin Yang

item.title: The Curse of Multiple Mediators: Hidden Interaction Effects in Activation Patching
item.description: arXiv:2606.27510v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Activation patching is a primary tool in mechanistic interpretability. It attributes causal responsibility for a model's behavior to each of its individual components by estimating its natural indirect effect (NIE). Re-deriving the activation patching estimand from causal mediation analysis, we find that the NIE does not solely capture the causal effect through the specific component. It also contains interaction effects (INT) that measure how much the component's causal effect itself depends on the states of other components in the model. A natural response may be to try to eliminate INT by adjusting the estimator or unit of analysis, but each of these potential remedies has predictable failure modes. We demonstrate these failure modes in the GPT-2 IOI circuit; components whose causal importance is conditional on the state of other components are either invisible or artificially inflated. We prove that INT scales with the distance between clean and patched component activations, is negligible when the model is nearly affine between them, and decomposes combinatorially into pairwise and higher-order group interactions. Despite its inevitability, INT is not a nuisance to be eliminated, but rather a diagnostic for interpretability studies. Its individual and group-level magnitude and sign signal when causal conclusions are prompt-dependent, and when greedy NIE-based component ranking will miss mechanisms only discoverable through combinatorial search.
item.dc:creator: Sankaran Vaidyanathan, David Arbour, Aaron Mueller, Scott Niekum, David Jensen

item.title: Anti-Collapse Dynamics and the Emergence of Multi-Time-Scale Learning in Recurrent Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2606.29519v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-range learning is hard for recurrent networks trained with stochastic gradient descent, because the influence of a past input fades with the lag $\ell$, and if it fades too fast the dependence cannot be learned from finite data. This fade is captured by an envelope $f(\ell)$. An exponential fade makes the data needed to learn a lag-$\ell$ dependence grow exponentially, putting long horizons out of reach; a power-law fade keeps the cost polynomial. We show that the asymptotic decay behavior of $f(\ell)$ is not fixed by the architecture. Instead, it emerges from the coupling between the state dynamics and parameter dynamics, settling into either a collapsed regime (fast, exponential forgetting) or an extended, anti-collapsed regime (slow, power-law forgetting). The intuition is a competition within these coupled dynamics. The systematic part of the training updates pulls long effective time scales back toward the network's typical range, while rare, heavy-tailed fluctuations can push a few far beyond it. When these pushes are strong enough to balance the pull, the extended regime survives. We make this mathematically precise with a coarse-grained stochastic process and derive the explicit threshold above which this balance holds. A single exponent, the spectral exponent~$\beta$, then governs both the spread of time scales and how slowly the network forgets. Realizing the regime in practice needs one more ingredient: the joint action of the architecture and the optimizer must be able to hold such a broad spread. A network whose capacity to generate broad time-scale spectra is severely constrained still collapses, even when supplied with strong heavy-tailed forcing. Heavy-tailed fluctuations thus act not as noise to be suppressed, but as the mechanism that sustains long-range learning.
item.dc:creator: Lorenzo Livi

item.title: Can Tabular In-Context Learners Generalize to Biomolecular Property Prediction?
item.description: arXiv:2606.31126v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Predicting biomolecular properties from limited labeled data is a central bottleneck in protein engineering and small-molecule design. As strong pretrained encoders now supply rich fixed-length representations, the difficulty has shifted from representation learning to building a data-efficient predictor for the few-shot regime. Tabular foundation models such as TabPFN and TabICL perform this prediction through in-context inference after pretraining on synthetic tables. We test whether they can act as flexible interpolators over informative fixed biomolecular representations. Treating each method as a predictor-representation pair, we evaluate across two domains. On ProteinGym, TabPFN3-ESMC600M is competitive with leading supervised-substitution entries and obtains the lowest MSE among the leaderboard-context rows considered, while Kermut remains stronger by Spearman. Performance is substantially lower under modulo and contiguous holdouts than under random splits. On the five-endpoint PpEST dataset, tabular models show favorable descriptive performance against matched supervised baselines, but the random split measures within-family interpolation and the small endpoint count precludes strong model-ordering claims. For small-molecule classification with ECFP/RDKit descriptors, no single predictor-representation pairing dominates across TDC ADMET, MoleculeNet, FS-Mol, and DrugOOD, but several pairings are competitive with strong descriptor and graph baselines. Crucially, on both protein and small-molecule few-shot tasks, these predictor-representation pairs offer strong performance. We conclude that tabular foundation models can be strong biomolecular predictors, but only when coupled with expressive representations.
item.dc:creator: Davy Guan, Lu Zhang, Asiri Wijesinghe, Allen Zhu, He Zhao, Helen Power, F. Hafna Ahmed, Andrew Warden, Cheng Soon Ong, Daniel M. Steinberg

item.title: Safe Inference-Time Alignment via Lagrangian Reward Augmentation
item.description: arXiv:2607.02781v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Inference-time alignment steers a frozen language model during decoding using auxiliary reward signals, avoiding the cost of repeated weight updates. However, existing inference-time alignment methods typically optimize a single scalar score, so explicit safety constraints must either be ignored or encoded through manually tuned penalties. We propose Lagrangian Reward Augmentation (LARA), a general inference-time alignment framework under safety constraints. Starting from a KL-regularized constrained objective with a reward model and a cost model, LARA dualizes the constraint and reduces the optimization problem to a one-dimensional convex problem over a nonnegative dual variable. Estimated on a small calibration set, this dual variable defines an augmented reward that can be used as a drop-in scoring signal within existing inference-time alignment methods. For sequence-level sampling methods, such as Best-of-N reranking, the calibrated dual variable corresponds to the solution of the expected-cost constrained problem. For token-level reward-guided decoding methods, the same construction yields a principled dual-calibrated heuristic rather than an exact constrained-policy guarantee. We evaluate LARA on both sequence-level and token-level inference-time alignment methods, and find that LARA improves the helpfulness-harmlessness tradeoff, with Best-of-N achieving the best performance among inference-time methods, approaching finetuning-based direct alignment baselines.
item.dc:creator: Yaswanth Chittepu, Ativ Joshi, Sohini Chintala, Scott Niekum

item.title: A Graph Signal Processing Perspective on Numerical Sequence Representations in LLM In-Context Learning
item.description: arXiv:2608.03015v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pretrained large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated in-context learning (ICL) capabilities for numerical inference over sequences serialized as text. Prior work has identified and characterized this form of numerical inference primarily through output-level evaluations such as prediction error. However, how numerical information is organized within LLM representations remains much less understood. To study this internal organization, we adopt a graph signal processing perspective in which attention induces a weighted graph over tokens, while token hidden states define signals on its nodes. Quantitative graph-spectral diagnostics and qualitative token-graph visualizations reveal that representations become more clearly differentiated by input dynamical complexity as context length increases. Simpler inputs produce attention-induced token graphs with stronger global connectivity and smoother, spectrally concentrated hidden-state signals, whereas more complex inputs produce more localized graphs and hidden-state signals with broader spectral support and greater high-frequency energy. These diagnostics and visualizations offer an interpretable view of the internal structure associated with numerical ICL, beyond what output-level prediction error alone reveals. Together, these findings point to systematic, context-dependent internal signatures associated with numerical ICL that are qualitatively conserved across model families.
item.dc:creator: Jiajun Bao, Zihao Qi, Toni J. B. Liu, Gurbir Arora, Rapha\"el Sarfati, Nicolas Boull\'e, Christopher J. Earls

item.title: ED-DiT: Physics-Guided Diffusion Pretraining for Transferable Molecular Representations from Electron Density
item.description: arXiv:2608.03260v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pretraining has shown strong potential for learning transferable representations, yet it remains underexplored for electron-density-based molecular learning. Electron density provides a continuous three-dimensional description of molecular electronic structure, capturing both local spatial patterns and global physical quantities. This raises a key question: can electron-density fields be used for self-supervised pretraining to learn a shared representation that transfers across diverse electronic-structure-related tasks? We propose ED-DiT, a physics-guided Diffusion Transformer for self-supervised pretraining on electron-density point clouds. ED-DiT learns reusable representations by reconstructing corrupted and partially masked log-density fields across diffusion noise levels. An electron-number consistency constraint is further introduced to preserve the total electronic mass. The pretrained encoder can be adapted to property prediction, open-/closed-shell classification, molecule-electron-density retrieval, and molecule-conditioned electron-density prediction. Experiments on six EDBench tasks show that ED-DiT consistently outperforms the same architecture trained from scratch, especially under limited supervision. For molecule-conditioned electron-density prediction, it reduces RMSE from 2.2474 to 1.3753 and surpasses the available baseline. With only 10% labels, it improves orbital energy prediction RMSE from 0.0293 to 0.0138. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of physics-guided electron-density pretraining for learning transferable molecular representations.
item.dc:creator: Shuang Liang, Haocheng Wang, Jiayi Song, Shuquan Ye, Ben Fei

item.title: CrevasseSeg: A Label-Efficient UAV Crevasse Segmentation Framework
item.description: arXiv:2608.15790v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Crevasse mapping from uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery supports glaciological research and field safety, but pixel-level annotation requires costly expert effort. We introduce CrevasseSeg, a binary segmentation evaluation framework from the terminus of Borebreen, Svalbard, comprising 2,244 unlabelled UAV orthomosaic tiles for self-supervised/unsupervised fine-tuning and 200 labelled tiles (24 validation, 176 test). We benchmark five self-supervised objectives (BYOL, Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD), Barlow Twins, VICReg and a combined BYOL-JSD) across O-Net, O-Net++ and a DINOv3-initialised O-Net. Frozen features are read out with a linear probe and an XGBoost classifier, both fit only on the 24 validation tiles. At the final decoder block, the two readouts invert. DINOv3 models are mostly the weakest under linear probing, often collapsing to a constant prediction, yet they are the strongest under XGBoost. This pattern does not hold at earlier decoder blocks. UMAP suggests why: DINOv3 fragments pixels into many small, locally interleaved clusters, whereas the convolutional models embed them on a single class-sorted manifold. Satellite-pretrained DINOv3 beats natural-image initialisation for every objective under XGBoost (+9.7 mDSC on average), but not consistently under linear probing. Our pipeline, DINOv3-ViT-L-Sat-O-Net-BYOL-JSD, reaches 74.75 mDSC / 61.16 mIoU (77.04 / 64.28 with a decoder-block ensemble), on par with BYOL alone, and outperforms RGB-pixel ML baselines. However, a frozen DINOv3-Sat encoder with an XGBoost readout alone reaches 77.18 / 64.17. It matches or exceeds every SSL variant and comes within 0.71 mDSC of a fully supervised DINOv3 U-Net, highlighting satellite foundation models as a strong baseline. We release CrevasseSeg as a benchmark for label-efficient segmentation in remote sensing.
item.dc:creator: Steven Wallace, William D. Harcourt, Richard Hann, Aiden Durrant, Somayajulu Sripada, Georgios Leontidis

item.title: Online Non-Monotone DR-Submodular Maximization Beyond $1/e$ with Feasible Gradient Queries
item.description: arXiv:2609.02145v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study adversarial online maximization of nonnegative, non-monotone DR-submodular functions over compact convex down-closed sets $K\subseteq[0,1]^d$ when gradients may be queried only at feasible points. The online approximation coefficients $4/9$ (Aggarwal and Lu) and $2\sqrt{3}-3\approx 0.4641$ (Aggarwal and Du) rely on queries along chains that start from the all-ones vector and leave $K$. With every query in $K$, the best known coefficient was $1/e$. We give an online algorithm with coefficient $0.4013$ that, in each round, plays a random action, queries one gradient at a point of $K$, and makes one projection. Its expected approximate regret is $O(RB(1+R)\sqrt{T})$, where $R\le\sqrt{d}$ bounds the norm of points of $K$ and $B$ bounds the gradient norm on $K$. For a budget $\sum_i x_i\le k$, the bound is $O(kB\sqrt{T})$. The algorithm keeps a state $x\in K$, and the analysis applies the coordinate-chain comparison of Aggarwal and Lu inside the box $[0,x]$, which keeps every query feasible. A second comparison, along a path from $0$ in the direction $x$, cancels the extra terms that the box creates. Because the queries are feasible, they can be played, which gives regret $O(T^{2/3})$ under semi-bandit feedback and $O(T^{4/5})$ under bandit feedback with bounded values. Unbiased stochastic gradients with bounded second moment keep the $\sqrt{T}$ rate, and on a fixed function the algorithm attains $0.4013\,\mathrm{OPT}-\varepsilon$ in expectation with $O(1+R^2(1+R)^2B^2/\varepsilon^2)$ feasible gradient queries.
item.dc:creator: Vaneet Aggarwal, Yiyang Lu

item.title: Reification as a Transferable Vocabulary: Zero-Shot Link Prediction with Vanilla GNNs
item.description: arXiv:2609.11347v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Knowledge graph foundation models such as ULTRA achieve zero-shot link prediction on unseen graphs through dedicated architectures that hard-code a transfer mechanism. In this work we move that mechanism out of the architecture and into the representation, by \emph{reifying} the input graph: every fact becomes a node, connected to its subject, object, and relation type through a fixed vocabulary of six meta-relations, with relation types as anonymous shared nodes rather than model parameters. On this representation, five textbook GNNs (GAT, GINE with sum and with mean+max aggregation, GraphSAGE, R-GCN), each trained on a single knowledge graph of 4,245 triples for 30 minutes on one NVIDIA A100, transfer zero-shot to 40 inductive link-prediction benchmarks. The best of them, an off-the-shelf GAT, matches ULTRA, a dedicated foundation model pretrained on three graphs, across ULTRA's own evaluation suite. The same fixed vocabulary extends to relational databases, a row becoming an entity and a foreign-key column a relation type; a preliminary probe on two unseen databases, with no cell values, schema text or in-context labels, shows a model of this family pretrained on three knowledge graphs ranking foreign-key targets far above random-initialization and degree controls. We release the code, the checkpoints, and the evaluation pipeline for all 40 benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Camille Pradel

item.title: Tabby: An Open Pretraining Recipe for Time Series Foundation Models
item.description: arXiv:2609.13956v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this report, we release Tabby, a long context probabilistic time series foundation model, together with a complete and open recipe of how it was built. Tabby adopts an encoder-only patch Transformer architecture and concentrates the contributions on the data and the training procedure. The pretraining corpus combines an extended real-world collection, GIFT-Eval-Pretrain+ and BLAST, with synthetic data from KernelSynth and CauKerV2, an online generator that composes temporal dynamics through randomly sampled structural causal models. Training couples a progressive convergence schedule, which yields reusable intermediate checkpoints, with a deep quantile supervision objective for intermediate layers. The resulting 145M parameter backbone supports contexts of up to 8,192 observations and serves forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection, while a prompt-tuning module further improves in-distribution forecasting performance with the pretrained weights frozen. Tabby achieves competitive zero-shot forecasting performance on GIFT-Eval and the out-of-distribution TIME benchmark, while the same pretrained backbone also supports classification on the UCR Archive and zero-shot anomaly detection on TSB-AD-U. We release training pipeline and model as open source at huawei-noah/trustworthyAI.
item.dc:creator: Shifeng Xie, Bahaeddine Abdessalem, Zehao Xiao, Youssef Attia El Hili, Ambroise Odonnat, Zhiwei Dong, Lei Zan, Themis Palpanas, Jianfeng Zhang, Lujia Pan, Keli Zhang, Malik Tiomoko

item.title: LSTM-UT and Bounded Gated Memory for Looped Transformers
item.description: arXiv:2609.19521v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Can the loop of a looped Transformer serve as a rollout, with one application of the shared block per step of a dynamical system? We started with two existing designs, one that carries only its residual stream and one, CoTFormer, that also caches every earlier state. On Rule 30, a chaotic cellular automaton, both lose the computation shortly after their trained depth. LSTM-UT, which adds an LSTM-style gated cell, does not, and it recalls earlier states better. Taking it apart shows that each ability has a simpler source. For rollouts it is decay: a fixed decay on the plain model's stream is sufficient. For recall it is an input-dependent gate: at the longest horizon a gated stream with no cell recalls as well as LSTM-UT, and no fixed decay helps. The two do not simply add, since a gated stream with a fixed decay does neither reliably. Storing every earlier state hurts extrapolation, where CoTFormer fits and rolls out further with its cache cut to the most recent repeat; in recall, the stored copy is looked up at the shortest horizon and not at the next. LSTM-UT, whose forget gate makes the decay itself input-dependent, is the only model in the leading group on both. The forget gate was added to the LSTM so that a state carried at weight one could be reset instead of accumulating; we find the same need over depth. In language modelling LSTM-UT is competitive with CoTFormer at lower training cost. Code is available at https://github.com/arskvnc22/lstm-ut
item.dc:creator: Aras Kavuncu, Muhammad Burhan Hafez

item.title: Relative Discharge Stage Classification from Battery Sensor Measurements in Laboratory Discharge Tests
item.description: arXiv:2609.27986v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Relative discharge stage (RDS) is an ordinal target obtained by dividing the realized remaining discharge time by the total duration of the same discharge episode and assigning the ratio to a bin. We investigate whether these bins can be predicted from measurements available up to the present sample. The framework combines an electrothermal equivalent-circuit model and adaptive extended Kalman filter to estimate state of charge (SOC), then classifies discharge stage using the estimated SOC, current, terminal voltage, and surface temperature. With the evaluated two-layer convolutional network, the final-time prediction directly uses the three most recent observations. Earlier measurements can influence the output through the recursive SOC estimate. On complete discharge tests, the five-stage classifier achieved accuracies of 95.38% and 81.23% for FTP-75 and PDMHC and 76.41% and 73.87% for LCO_5 and LCO_6, respectively. These results characterize classification within the laboratory protocols. Incremental value over SOC alone, reference-based SOC accuracy, and utility in vehicle operation remain to be established.
item.dc:creator: Khoa Tran, Tri Le, Hung-Cuong Trinh, Hung Tran-Nam

item.title: Even Sharper Bounds for Transductive Learning and Its Applications
item.description: arXiv:2609.28459v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce Sharper Transductive Local Complexity (STLC) as a new tool for improving current transductive bounds. Although Local Rademacher Complexity (LRC) has been used to obtain sharp inductive generalization bounds and local-complexity-based transductive bounds, it has remained open whether a localized Rademacher-complexity framework can achieve the same fixed-point and confidence structure as its inductive counterpart. STLC provides an affirmative answer to this question. STLC is constructed by first deriving a new Bernstein-type concentration inequality for the test-train process, under uniform sampling without replacement. The proof uses a new two-parameter entropy argument based on the modified log-Sobolev inequality for the swap walk. A subsequent peeling strategy with a surrogate localization functional yields transductive excess-risk bounds that match the fixed-point and confidence structure of the classical LRC-based inductive bounds without the additional logarithmic confidence gap in existing works. We further advance transductive learning through two applications. First, for realizable transductive learning over a binary-valued class of VC dimension $2\le d <\infty$ with $u\ge m\ge d$, where $u$ and $m$ are the test and training sizes, STLC gives the upper bound $O(d\log(me/d)/m}$. This rate matches the classical LRC-based, standard ERM-style inductive upper bound. It remains a logarithmic factor $\log(me/d)$ above both the optimal realizable inductive PAC rate and the transductive minimax lower bound, which are of order $d/m$. Our prior work achieves the excess risk of $O(d/m)$ in a transductive setup by randomized learning. Second, STLC gives a sharper, spectrum-adaptive excess-risk bound for transductive kernel learning than the prior local-complexity-based result.
item.dc:creator: Yingzhen Yang

item.title: Policy Iteration Is Not Polynomial for Deterministic Markov Decision Processes: The Price of Algorithmic Anarchy
item.description: arXiv:2609.40147v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We establish exponential iteration lower bounds in the number of states for Howard's policy iteration on deterministic discounted and average-reward Markov decision processes (MDPs), with a constant number of actions per state. This rules out polynomial-time complexity of Howard's policy iteration in both settings. We further prove that a Dantzig counterpart of Howard's policy iteration runs in strongly polynomial time on deterministic average-reward MDPs. Together with the known strongly polynomial bound for Dantzig's rule on deterministic discounted MDPs, these results establish an exponential separation between the two algorithms in both settings. This separation between Howard's decentralized and simultaneous selfish improvements and Dantzig's coordinated selection of a single action with the largest improvement across all states reveals a "price" of algorithmic anarchy.
item.dc:creator: Han Zhong, Yinyu Ye

item.title: SLIM: Simplex-Lattice Interpolation Merging
item.description: arXiv:2610.01037v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Optimizing merging coefficients for large language models can require many costly benchmark evaluations. We propose Simplex-Lattice Interpolation Merging (SLIM), which constructs a quadratic surrogate of aggregate performance on the coefficient simplex using a classical mixture design. Evaluations of individual experts and equal-weight pairs determine the surrogate with the minimum number of measurements needed to identify a general quadratic on this domain. SLIM then optimizes the surrogate without further target-metric evaluations. Experiments on two model architectures demonstrate accurate prediction of unseen multi-expert mixtures and competitive merge performance under limited evaluation budgets. Matched-budget comparisons show that structured evaluation points improve prediction fidelity over random designs, including those using regularized fitting.
item.dc:creator: Seongcheol Jeong, Masahiro Suzuki, Yutaka Matsuo

item.title: Frozen Factor or Spectral Band? In LoRA, the Factor Matters More at Low Rank
item.description: arXiv:2610.06621v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: On two main task-model pairs, at ranks 1 to 8 with few optimiser steps, the factor a LoRA variant freezes matters more than its band of singular directions. MiCA and PiCa are compared by band, minor against dominant, yet MiCA freezes the output factor B and PiCa, in our notation, the input factor A. We cross factor and band in a 2 x 2 design on models from 1B to 8B parameters. Freezing A beats freezing B on both bands, by +12 to +20 points at rank 2 on a format task, our primary evidence, and still by about +7 points at rank 8 on OpenBookQA. A Holm correction over 258 primary tests, added post hoc, keeps this advantage in 15 of 16 tests and the lead of factor over band at ranks 1, 2 and 4, rank 1 of the format task being itself post hoc. At rank 8 that lead passes its own test but not the correction. The advantage repeats at rank 2 with two 7B models, by +11 to +13 points. Outside the correction, it repeats on GSM8K with a 1B model and, in a post hoc experiment, with an 8B model at ranks 8 and 16. It holds when B frozen gets as many parameters or more, with a random frozen A, and with sixteen times the format-task budget. It narrows above rank 8 on most pairs, at rank 8 with the 8B model on the two main tasks, on ARC and in a task mixture, and it closes at the last step of longer training on OpenBookQA. At MiCA's and PiCa's own settings, it is smaller or not detected.
item.dc:creator: Adnan Slimane Ali, David Ngwe Pouth

item.title: Amortized Counterfactual Prediction with Graph Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.13724v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Counterfactual inference asks how an observed outcome might have differed under different circumstances, such as whether a patient would have recovered had they received a different treatment. Such questions arise whenever decisions depend on the outcomes of alternatives that were not observed. Answering counterfactual queries generally requires knowledge of the underlying causal structure, which is often unavailable in practice. A common approach is therefore to first estimate the causal graph from observational data and then perform counterfactual inference. However, errors in the estimated causal graph can propagate to downstream counterfactual predictions. To address this challenge, we introduce the Counterfactual Graph Neural Process (CFGNP), an end-to-end approach that answers counterfactual queries directly from observational data without first estimating a causal graph. CFGNP uses Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to exploit the dual-graph structure by restricting cross-world message passing to corresponding factual--counterfactual variables. CFGNP both offers an approach that does not require knowledge of the causal graph and achieves stronger predictive performance than existing approaches. When trained on counterfactual pairs from the same structural causal model used for testing, CFGNP achieves $1.6-7 \times$ lower MSE than baselines that receive the true causal graph and the same counterfactual supervision, across seven benchmark variants. Furthermore, on synthetic causal graphs, a model trained only on 10-node graphs maintains strong predictive performance on graphs with up to 30 nodes, without retraining.
item.dc:creator: Hendrik Stumpf, Francesco Quinzan

item.title: A Geometric Perspective on Reward Function Updates in Inverse Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.14041v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) is classically solved using Lagrangian optimisation, by jointly optimising a primal-dual problem with gradient descent to obtain the optimal reward function parameters and corresponding optimal policy. While this algorithmic view of IRL has been highly influential, gradient-based reward updates only paint a partial picture, largely ignoring the geometry of the problem in occupancy space. In this paper, we present an occupancy-space view of reward updates in IRL. We leverage the insight that both the optimal solution and its geometry in occupancy space are known, and show that the geometry along the e-geodesic (straight line in occupancy space) toward the optimal occupancy directly affects the gradient of the IRL dual problem in reward parameter space. This perspective naturally suggests preconditioning the dual gradient with the average Fisher information along the occupancy trajectory. We show that this preconditioned gradient is just a convex interpolation of the old reward and a new target reward, yielding efficient natural-gradient-style updates with little additional computational overhead. We then analyse these occupancy-space reward updates from a Mirror Descent (MD) perspective, and show that policy search over the resulting rewards induces approximate entropic MD on the policy. Finally, we conclude with convergence results of such geometry-aware IRL algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Anish Diwan, Jan Peters, Oleg Arenz

item.title: Recurrent In-Context Learning for Tabular Foundation Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.14998v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tabular foundation models predict unlabelled rows from labelled rows in a single forward pass via in-context learning (ICL). Like language models, these architectures have scaled by stacking transformer blocks, each with its own parameters. However, this approach couples compute with model size: increasing computation requires increasing the parameter count. In this work, we investigate whether tabular ICL requires distinct parameters at every block, or simply sufficient depth. We introduce Tab-Loop, a looped tabular foundation model built on the TabICLv2 architecture. Instead of stacking unique blocks, Tab-Loop takes a small set of blocks with shared parameters and applies them repeatedly in a loop during its ICL stage.
