We evaluate this design against standard architectures under equal training and inference compute budgets. Our experiments show that depth, rather than unique parameters, drives performance. Across classification and regression tasks on held-out synthetic tables, the TabArena and TALENT benchmarks, Tab-Loop matches the accuracy of a standard model with three times as many ICL blocks while using roughly 60% fewer parameters. Conversely, a non-looped baseline of the same size as Tab-Loop underperforms it, even when trained on 32% more tables. This pattern holds consistently whether we vary the number of distinct blocks from one to twelve or the effective depth. Furthermore, running additional loops at inference improves predictive accuracy without retraining. Training the model with deeper loops extends the range over which these extra inference steps remain beneficial, eventually matching the released TabICLv2 on TabArena at 2.7 times the ICL compute. These results show that tabular foundation models can scale their compute independently of parameter count, pointing to test-time compute scaling as a practical path toward efficient tabular models.
item.dc:creator: Tejas Vaidhya, Gaurav Sahu, Ishita Sanjay Hiremath, Irina Rish

item.title: Not All Change Is Damage: Update-Matched Unlearning for Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.21230v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Unlearning aims to remove selected knowledge from large language models to mitigate privacy and safety risks while preserving useful capabilities. For models that continue to be fine-tuned after release, this goal is insufficient: they must also resist relearning the deleted knowledge while preserving plasticity, the ability to learn new tasks. Existing defenses train against simulated relearning while trying to preserve useful capabilities, but low relearning alone cannot distinguish selective resistance from a general loss of plasticity. Evaluating preservation after an update requires deciding what the updated model should remain close to. A pre-update reference penalizes useful changes induced by the update simply because they depart from earlier outputs. We therefore formulate the reference-timing hypothesis that, at comparable target suppression, an update-matched reference better preserves plasticity than a pre-update one. To test and address this hypothesis, we propose Update-Matched Unlearning (UMU), which applies the same simulated relearning update to the defended model and to an undefended reference initialized from the same unlearned model, and uses new-task learning to guide model selection. Extensive experiments on TOFU and FaithUn with Llama and Qwen models show that UMU improves both relearning resistance and plasticity across all four base unlearning methods, lowering harmful and benign relearning by 30.4 and 9.9 points on average while raising new-task accuracy by 3.5 points. When the reference does not receive the update, relearning remains similarly low but new-task accuracy falls below the base method, supporting the reference-timing hypothesis and showing that robust unlearning should prevent recovery selectively without suppressing learning itself.
item.dc:creator: Jie Li, Youming Tao, Bowei He, Meng Ding

item.title: Representation Redistribution in Sparse Autoencoders
item.description: arXiv:2610.21240v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Presenting the same request with different context or formatting can change which sparse autoencoder (SAE) features respond inside a language model. Understanding these changes raises two questions. Which feature responses recur across related inputs, and which of them contribute to downstream computation? We study this phenomenon as representation redistribution and introduce the redistribution sensitivity score (RSS) to identify large feature changes that recur in a consistent direction. We select features on one set of prompt variants and evaluate them on separate variants. Across 27 pretrained SAEs spanning eight language models, RSS reveals a consistent pattern of redistribution. Context and wrapper transformations produce stronger recurring responses than local edits. We then use two frozen safety readouts to measure how these changes contribute to downstream computation. RSS identifies features with approximately twice the mean held out contribution of features selected by the largest readout coefficients, using activation responses alone. An exact decomposition explains how feature changes and readout coefficients determine their effects on the decision margin. Combining RSS contributions with the clean margin improves recurrent failure AUROC from 0.863 to 0.935 and from 0.901 to 0.958, approaching the full readout results of 0.965 and 0.964. These findings show that recurring changes in sparse representations provide a way to identify features with meaningful downstream contributions. Code is available at https://github.com/OpenSAE/Redistribution-Sensitivity-Score.
item.dc:creator: Ziye Mei, Haotian Ma

item.title: Behavioral Compositionality of Sparse Autoencoder Representations
item.description: arXiv:2610.21261v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide features that can be combined to explain and steer language model behavior. Understanding these combinations requires knowing how reliably individual feature effects predict their joint impact on the model. We study this relationship by retaining or removing subsets of SAE feature contributions and measuring the resulting behavioral responses. We introduce SAE Additivity Residuals (SAR) to quantify how much behavioral variation is explained by feature interactions beyond a chosen order. We prove that, under independent feature subset sampling, SAR measures the normalized energy of these interactions and bounds errors in ranking feature combinations. Across 18 model and behavior settings, learned SAE coordinates have lower first order residuals than matched rotations of the same activation subspace. This shows that SAE coordinates support comparatively simple descriptions of joint feature effects. Pairwise modeling further improves the ranking of held out feature combinations in all 18 settings. We also demonstrate the practical value of modeling these interactions. Across five challenging benchmarks, pairwise models select feature combinations that give higher probability to the correct answer and preserve the original behavioral response more closely than first order models. In MMLU-Pro steering, pairwise modeling improves rank fidelity from 0.5874 to 0.7790 and reduces ordering error from 0.1444 to 0.0606. These results establish behavioral compositionality as a measurable property of SAE representations and show how modeling feature interactions improves the analysis and selection of feature combinations.
item.dc:creator: Haotian Ma, Ziye Mei, Frederic Sala

item.title: STAR-XPC: Set Transformer for Estimating X-ray Transmission in Polymer Composites
item.description: arXiv:2610.28709v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Evaluating the energy transmission ratio of an X-ray beam through a polymer composite is a challenging task in radiation shielding studies. The reference solution with Monte Carlo transport simulation is highly accurate but computationally expensive: each of our reference simulations is capped at $4\times10^9$ photon histories and a 20,000 s (over 5 hours) time limit, while closed-form analytical methods fail to represent such complex scenarios. We present an artificial neural network model that maps the unordered multi-set of molecular constituents, their mass fractions, and four bulk physical descriptors directly to the transmission ratio $I(t)/I_0$ in 1-3 milliseconds. The model is a Set Transformer, which makes it permutation invariant by construction and accepts mixtures of different sizes up to 11 constituents within a fixed-size padded set. Each constituent is embedded with a chemistry-pretrained transformer language model, ChemBERTa. In our proposed method, training data are produced by an automated PENELOPE/penEasy pipeline using the radiation source at 30, 80, 100, and 120 kV tube voltages over polyethylene-based shielding composite slabs of thicknesses spanning 0.15-2.5 mm. After preprocessing, the dataset contains $n = 4697$ simulated configurations on which a leakage-free, jointly stratified 10-fold cross-validation is performed, attaining mean squared error MSE = $(1.12 \pm 0.56)\times10^{-4}$, normalized-MSE percentage NMSE% = 0.0294% $\pm$ 0.0147%, and $R^2 = 0.9988$. The corresponding per-sample percentage errors give an alpha-trimmed ($\alpha = 0.10$) absolute percentage error (APE) of 1.66% and a median APE of 1.15%. Our model's inference is several orders of magnitude faster than the underlying Monte Carlo simulation (sub-millisecond per query vs. several hours for the reference run) with effective accuracy in predicting $I(t)/I_0$.
item.dc:creator: Can Erer, H. Birkan Yilmaz, Nebahat Aral

item.title: Conditional Flow Models Convert Epistemic Uncertainty into Apparent Aleatoric Variance
item.description: arXiv:2610.29172v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Conditional Flow Models (CFMs) are increasingly being used in place of deterministic predictors across machine learning, including for tasks that were classically formulated as regression. Given their success in such tasks, we ask the question: what useful information do the conditional distributions produced by CFMs carry beyond what a point predictor would provide? We identify a systematic phenomenon: in many natural regimes, CFM samples routinely have larger variance than the true conditional distribution, even in nearly deterministic regression problems. This effect is most pronounced where the model has not resolved the dependence on the conditioning variable, and thus the additional variance can be viewed as converting \emph{epistemic uncertainty} in fitting the ground truth conditional distribution into apparent \emph{aleatoric variance} in the generated samples. Through controlled synthetic and real-data experiments, and comparisons with explicit smoothing estimators, we show that the induced variance tracks model underfitting of complex or hard-to-fit targets, and decreases with additional training or data. We uncover surprising structure in this excess conditional variance that seems unique to CFMs and absent in the other standard probabilistic models that we test. We provide a theoretical account of the phenomenon in a simplified setting and demonstrate a consequent practical use-case of conditional flow-matching: designing high-coverage predictive sets that cover the ground-truth regression target.
item.dc:creator: Navodita Sharma, Abhishek Shetty, Max Simchowitz, Pulkit Agrawal

item.title: Compatible Likelihoods for Flow Matching on Manifolds
item.description: arXiv:2610.31981v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: On the simplest non-Euclidean manifold, the 1D flat torus, we exhibit a distribution where a recent extension of Riemannian flow matching is globally optimized by a velocity field that pushes samples away from the data distribution. We trace this failure mode to a property we call compatibility; a likelihood-based flow matching objective is compatible if its population minimizer recovers the marginal velocity field induced by the data and coupling. We derive a general condition for compatibility, apply it to existing methods, and bound the worst-case error by a residual term that vanishes under compatibility. On compact manifolds, we show that existing compatible objectives put density on infeasible velocities. To tackle both issues, we propose an exponential family over endpoints with the conditional velocity as sufficient statistic, which is both compatible and supported only on feasible velocities. In practice, and with low overhead, this reduces to a reweighting of the flow matching loss. On spaces of constant curvature, this treats errors in flow speed and direction differently. Compared to prior art, our method finds the correct velocities on the test case, outperforms in general on high-dimensional product tori, and, for two of four standard geospatial benchmarks on the sphere, achieves substantial NLL improvements. When evaluated on a large dataset of human poses, our method surpasses prior work according to sample-based metrics.
item.dc:creator: Lucas Ng, Georgios Batzolis, Mark Girolami

item.title: Gaussian Approximation for Composition and Subsampling of Differentially Private Algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2610.33333v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The privacy analysis of differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) relies on bounds for composition of subsampled mechanisms. Its privacy is bounded by that of a pair of product distributions, whose privacy loss is a sum of independent terms and has been analyzed via a variety of concentration results. Yet, existing closed-form bounds either lose a logarithmic factor or require restrictive conditions on the noise scale. Further, while sums of independent random variables are approximately Gaussian, existing CLT-based techniques give an approximation with a large error in $\delta$. We show that the privacy loss of any composition is close to a Gaussian random variable with the same mean and variance as long as each step has a small privacy loss except with small probability. Specifically, the privacy profile is bounded from above and from below by that of the Gaussian, up to an additive error $\beta$ in $\delta$ and a shift of $\varepsilon$ that grows only as $\ln(1/\beta)$. This shift does not depend on the number of steps, and thus the composition typically satisfies Gaussian differential privacy up to lower-order shifts. For $t$ steps of a mechanism with Poisson subsampling at rate $\lambda$, the variance of the Gaussian is essentially $t\lambda^2$ times the $\chi^2$ divergence of its dominating pair. This gives a new simple analysis of subsampled composition. We extend it to random allocation (balls-and-bins sampling). For the Gaussian mechanism with either sampling method at rate $1/t$, we obtain the central limit rate for $\sigma\gtrsim\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}/\ln(t)$, whereas the standard R\'enyi-divergence analyses of Poisson subsampling need $\sigma\gtrsim\sqrt{t\ln(1/\delta)}/\ln(t)$. We also show that for bounded privacy losses the approximation explains the high accuracy of the connect-the-dots discretization of privacy loss distributions.
item.dc:creator: Vitaly Feldman, Moshe Shenfeld

item.title: Best Policy Tracking in Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.34501v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning commonly exhibits non-monotonic performance dynamics in single-task settings. During learning, a sequence of policies is generated whose true performance is unknown and may oscillate significantly across iterations. Despite this well-known phenomenon, standard experimental practice typically reports either the final visited policy or the best among periodically evaluated ones, implicitly assuming that these selection criteria reliably approximate the best-performing policy visited throughout the entire sequence. In this work, we present an empirical study on the implications of non-monotonicity for policy selection in single-task policy-based reinforcement learning. We introduce post-hoc diagnostic metrics to characterize performance degradation and assess the accuracy and efficiency of different selection criteria. These metrics allow us to evaluate commonly used selection strategies across standard continuous-control benchmarks using a well-established on-policy actor-critic method. Our results show that, in this representative experimental setting, widely adopted selection practices can deviate considerably from the best policy encountered during learning, leading to underperforming estimates and suboptimal use of computational resources. As an alternative, we recommend a validation-based policy selection strategy constrained by computational cost, which provides a more consistent and accurate approximation of the best visited policy while improving selection efficiency. Overall, our findings highlight policy selection as an underexplored factor in the evaluation protocols of reinforcement learning and motivate further study on explicit and standardized validation-based selection procedures.
item.dc:creator: Judith Echevarrieta, Etor Arza, Aritz P\'erez, Josu Ceberio

item.title: InterQ-RL: Interaction-Aware Correction of Execution Mismatch in Quantized Agentic RL
item.description: arXiv:2610.35303v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-turn agent reinforcement learning (RL) relies on long closed-loop rollouts, making generation and KV-cache costs a major bottleneck. Quantized rollout reduces these costs, but its low-precision executor also serves as the behavior policy and can induce execution mismatch with the learner. Existing quantized-RL methods are designed primarily for single-turn generation. They align the learner forward with quantized rollout or correct the current-token rollout-learner ratio, without modeling the policy history that produces each agent state. Even after quantization alignment, residual rollout-learner mismatch accumulates along the state-reaching policy history, so a current action may look locally aligned despite a mismatched history. We introduce InterQ-RL (Interaction-aware Quantized Reinforcement Learning) to correct this post-alignment mismatch. It applies bounded execution-prefix correction over the state-reaching policy history, allocates correction strength across action segments by effective support under a fixed displacement budget, and requires no additional model forward pass. We evaluate dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) backbones from 4B to 30B on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, with all quantized arms sharing the same rollout with 8-bit weights, activations, and KV cache (W8A8-KV8). Across four environment-backbone settings, InterQ-RL achieves the strongest quantized endpoint result, matching BF16 to within 0.7 points and exceeding it in two settings. It matches or exceeds the learning speed of alignment alone while avoiding its late performance regression.
item.dc:creator: Yingbo Hao, Song Liu, Guanghua Yu, Zhaojing Zhou, Jianchen Zhu, Yi Zou

item.title: When does off-block Hessian curvature help an optimization step?
item.description: arXiv:2611.01335v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Testing an off-block Hessian correction alone can discard a step that lowers minibatch loss. We measure both the missed improvement and the gain from rescaling the remaining correction. A reference based on diagonal-block norms distinguishes changes in the diagonal profile during training from changes in relative off-block mass. This reference sharply bounds the off-block fraction for positive semidefinite matrices. Regrouping fixed ResNet-18 weights from stages to layers takes the estimated fraction from below to above its partition-specific bound in all six CIFAR-100 comparisons under a conditional probe screen. At nine ResNet-50 checkpoints on Stanford Cars, we measure the off-block contribution to the linearized gradient change along a K-FAC step. At four base-step endpoints, predicted and measured slopes along the original correction have opposite signs. Each subspace draw (two per checkpoint) supplies one Hessian-informed map for the off-block residual, the remainder and their sum. At unit scale before acceptance, the off-block correction alone worsens the base in 17/18 comparisons; the combination beats the remainder in ten, including nine of those 17. At one checkpoint only the combination improves on the base in both draws. Matching correction norms reverses seven of the ten preferences, including both at that checkpoint.
item.dc:creator: Maxim Bolshim (ITMO University, Saint Petersburg, Russia), Alexander Kugaevskikh (ITMO University, Saint Petersburg, Russia)

item.title: Same behavior, different mechanism: what finite experiments can certify about how a network computes
item.description: arXiv:2611.08469v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Interpretability research, AI audits and assessments of machine consciousness make claims about how a system computes, not what it outputs. We give such claims a measurement theory. A claim is certifiable from finite interventions exactly when the mechanism lies at positive information distance from those that falsify it; it then costs at least log(1/alpha) over that distance, and an adaptive experiment attains this price asymptotically. Access, geometry and the logical form of the claim set the distance. In solvable networks, behavior carries no evidence about integrated information, and quantities that select one thing and report another have cliffs beside which cost grows as the inverse square of distance, whatever the margin. Equally accurate networks implement different circuits. In language models of up to 7.6 billion parameters, 220 of 223 audited claims about circuits, and a refusal mechanism, were certified on live interventions, 89% within the cost range registered beforehand.
item.dc:creator: Diaoxuan He, Linqian Wu, Chang Kong, Haoming Peng

item.title: Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery
item.description: arXiv:2611.12491v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bayesian optimization is widely used in active learning loops for materials science. Gaussian processes serve as the de-facto surrogate model family, but require task-dependent kernel choices and can lack the modeling capacity for complex relationships. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have recently emerged as the state-of-the-art for predictive tasks on structured data, without requiring bespoke kernels or hyperparameter tuning. We evaluate two TFMs, TabPFN and TabICL, as out-of-the-box surrogate models on two standard materials science benchmarks, comparing against a large field of baselines encompassing Gaussian processes, random forests, and CatBoost. Our findings indicate that TFMs are highly competitive surrogate models across the two benchmarks, without task-specific training for active learning or GP kernel selection. Our results motivate developing TFMs further as surrogates for active learning in materials discovery.
item.dc:creator: Klemens Fl\"oge, Simon Bing, Leo Grinsztajn, Eliott Kalfon, Lennart Purucker, Noah Hollmann, Frank Hutter

item.title: A Cardiorespiratory Foundation Model Pretrained on Ten Physiological Signals for Perioperative and Critical Care
item.description: arXiv:2611.15004v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Arterial, venous, pulmonary artery, and intracranial pressures and ventilator waveforms guide decisions in operating rooms and intensive care units, yet foundation models for physiological waveforms rely almost entirely on the electrocardiogram and photoplethysmogram. We present the CArdio-Respiratory Multi-modal ENcoder (CARMEN), a single encoder pretrained without labels on ten cardiorespiratory waveforms (2.27 million modality-hours). CARMEN accepts any combination of co-recorded signals at variable lengths. A conditioning mechanism, LSCNorm, restores the absolute signal level removed by normalization; in a matched ablation, replacing it with standard normalization lowered the AUROC for intraoperative hypotension by 0.11. Across 19 tasks from Korean and US cohorts, the frozen encoder significantly outperformed both supervised models in 12 of the 15 tasks on which they were evaluated. It outperformed three pretrained foundation models on 14--17 of 19 tasks, and none of them exceeded it on any task. Given the electrocardiogram or photoplethysmogram alone, it matched or exceeded the signal-specific foundation models in most comparisons, and the performance was largely preserved even after removing the secondary channels.
item.dc:creator: Cheol-Hui Lee, Wookyung Kim, Hyeonhoon Lee, Garam Lee, Da-in Eun, Hyung-Chul Lee

item.title: Enrichment-Oriented Virtual Screening of Perovskite Solar Cells through Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.18043v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Experimental optimization of perovskite solar cells is constrained by combinatorial diversity in absorber compositions, device layers, and processing, which makes virtual screening attractive for prioritizing recipes before fabrication. We develop a surrogate-guided reinforcement-learning framework that casts recipe generation as virtual screening, enriching candidate shortlists near high-performing experimental neighbors. A frozen Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network (TabPFN) guides recipe generation, while a reference pool of 890 measured devices enables neighborhood-based assessment. Five-fold evaluation on 1,846 devices shows top-ten selection raises mean power conversion efficiency (PCE) from 19.68\% to 23.74\%. Three learned policies are compared with six baselines under 3,000 surrogate evaluations per run. In top-100 shortlists, Proximal policy optimization (PPO) and recurrent PPO (RPPO) achieve neighborhood-supported hit rates of 23\% and 24\% (7.9- and 8.3-fold Pure Random's 2.9\%), versus 10\% (3.4-fold) for the baselines with the highest supported hit rate (L-SHADE and Ax BO, tied) at $K = 100$. Gains coexist with weak-support fractions. Of 9,000 recipes, 65.4\% match a composition family at similarity 0.80, falling to 11.7\% at 0.90. Results support enrichment-oriented prioritization but not experimental performance, seed robustness, or matched-budget advantage.
item.dc:creator: Yezeyuan Zheng, Ziyang Hu, Maojun Sun, Ruijian Han, Jian Huang, Guanhua Chen, Jie Liu

item.title: Improving fine-grained expressivity of graph neural networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.20020v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This thesis investigates the expressive power of neural networks for structured data, focusing on graph neural networks and symmetry-aware architectures. We present four main contributions. First, we characterize the generic expressive power of geometric message-passing neural networks on sparse graphs and introduce EGenNet, an architecture achieving the corresponding guarantees. Second, we use representation theory to characterize linear layers equivariant to multiple permutations, including wreath-product symmetries. Third, we study permutation-invariant set representations that preserve containment, establish dimensional bounds and impossibility results, and introduce MASNet. Finally, we propose FSW-GNN, a message-passing architecture combining strong expressivity and bi-Lipschitz stability guarantees with strong empirical performance on long-range graph-learning tasks. Together, these results provide a broader understanding of how neural architectures can preserve the geometric, algebraic, order-theoretic, and metric structure of their inputs.
item.dc:creator: Yonatan Sverdlov

item.title: Escaping Latent Traps by Remembering: Training-Free Episodic Kernel Repulsion for World-Model Planning
item.description: arXiv:2611.22470v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Latent world models plan towards a goal image by minimising the distance between predicted and goal latents. Because this distance is not geodesic, it creates latent traps---local minima or flat basins behind walls, at corners and in dead ends---where memoryless receding-horizon replanning keeps revisiting states far from the goal. We propose Episodic Kernel Repulsion (EKR), a training-free, test-time cost term that penalises candidate plans via a top-$k$ Gaussian kernel to a novelty-gated memory of the latents the agent has actually visited, normalised by the current batch base cost so a single strength transfers across models. Across two JEPA world models and four benchmarks, EKR improves success in all eight settings without changing the model, planner or search budget, matching or exceeding $4\times$ samples at $0.8$--$1.5\times$ compute in seven of eight settings while adding $\sim 25$ ms ($<1\%$) per replan. Controlled trap-fork interventions confirm that the memory causes escape, and an untuned configuration transfers directly to DINO-WM with CEM (e.g. $44.7\%\to 100.0\%$ on long PointMaze, $+19.3$ points on long Wall) and to JEPA-WM on Metaworld mw-reach-wall ($25.3\%\to 40.7\%$).
item.dc:creator: Yican Zhao, Bolin Yang, Ruizhe Wang, Haiyang Guo, Fuji Yang, Bingo Wing-Kuen Ling, Zelin Zang

item.title: Replay, Don't Resample: Off-Policy Consolidation of Long-Horizon RL Experts
item.description: arXiv:2611.24059v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Frontier post-training follows a common recipe: train one expert per domain with reinforcement learning (RL), then consolidate the experts into one model via multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). Such consolidation is expensive: the student samples in every environment again, an expert scores every sampled token, and the student inherits the drift of the final experts. Yet we argue that the experts' RL runs have already produced what consolidation needs: rollouts with their sampling probabilities and rewards, in the order the experts learned from them. We propose multi-expert replay policy distillation (MRPD), which replays these training logs through the student in the experts' order. At each step, the policy gradient is recomputed on these scored trajectories, and the final experts' distributions are distilled at the logged prefixes. Following the experts' own trajectory reduces the training-inference mismatch and keeps the student within the clip range, so the replay is off-policy in origin but quasi-on-policy throughout consolidation. MRPD samples nothing and calls no environment or reward model: the trainer is the sole process, and consolidating the experts costs only about a seventh of the compute used to train them. On three long-horizon agentic domains (reasoning, search and SQL), MRPD yields the best student model, substantially outperforming online RL baselines, and surpassing MOPD from the same experts at a fraction of MOPD's cost. Our analysis on the same logs shows that the replayed trajectories carry most of the gain, and that both the policy gradient and the distillation term add to it. Most interestingly, the order of the logs matters more than their amount or rewards, suggesting that expert training logs are a curriculum, not a data mixture.
item.dc:creator: Zhenrui Yue, Gongxiaohui Chen, Huimin Zeng, Honglei Zhuang, Jiashuo Sun, Zhen Han, Dong Wang

item.title: TWICE: Toward a digital twin of ICU patients with a generative event model for forecasting trajectories and simulating treatment response
item.description: arXiv:2611.27028v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A digital twin of a patient in intensive care would forecast the patient's course and what a treatment would change. Generative event models, trained to continue a patient's electronic health record (EHR), have been proposed as a path toward such twins. We trained TWICE, a 79M-parameter decoder-only transformer, on the ICU records of one academic health system (127,332 training patients and 1.57 billion tokens). We evaluated it on clinical prediction tasks, generation fidelity, individual trajectories and counterfactual validation. Reading 19 clinical outcomes off 50 simulated futures, with no task-specific training, TWICE matched the best of 144 supervised configurations on held-out patients (mean AUROC 0.836 vs. 0.834). It led on events that change care within a day and trailed on death. With the training data fixed, more and longer simulated futures were worth more than a 6.8-fold larger model. Its generated records matched real ones closely and were as specific to each patient as its own variability allowed. Its predicted risk rose as events approached. Pre-specified controls showed that it reproduced the side effects of drugs and was barely moved by an inert drug. On the values that treatments are given to correct, however, an opposite treatment moved its forecasts like the right one. TWICE forecasts ICU events about as well as task-specific models, and we see it as a step toward a digital twin of the ICU patient.
item.dc:creator: Zhuoyang Lyu, Yiming Li, Peter C. Hou, Pengyu Hong, Li Zhou

item.title: Physics-Constrained Neural ODEs for Learning Traffic Dynamics and Trajectories from Road Entry/Exit Times
item.description: arXiv:2611.30577v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider the problem of learning microscopic traffic dynamics and reconstructing vehicle trajectories from section entry/exit timestamps (EET) recorded by cameras and from the positions of a probe vehicle leading the platoon. The dynamics are difficult to recover as each vehicle's position is measured only at two points, and its trajectory between them is unknown. By combining Neural ODEs with a local density approximation, we learn a follow-the-leader model whose speed--density relation is a neural network. With such sparse data, an unconstrained network may learn physically unrealistic relations, such as negative speeds or non-zero speeds on a fully congested road. We therefore introduce a normalization that, applied to a monotone neural network with a learned regime change, enforces the endpoint conditions, guaranteeing an admissible speed--density relation while provably retaining the ability to approximate any admissible one. We validate the method on first- and second-order simulations, recovering the speed--density relation of the first-order model and reconstructing the trajectories of both models, with mean maximum position errors of 2.50~m and 2.51~m, respectively, on a 125~m road segment. On real-world ring-road data, the proposed model still yields an admissible relation, whereas both baselines violate the constraints; the large spread in the data, however, highlights the limitations of a first-order model with homogeneous driver behaviors.
item.dc:creator: Dennis Bogatov Wilkman, Karl Henrik Johansson, Matthieu Barreau

item.title: Lowering the Bar for Everyone: Hidden Validation-Seeking Goals in Empathetic RL
item.description: arXiv:2611.30702v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When RL learns from the reactions of many users, the policy usually cannot see what each user wants. We ask what it learns from users who privately want validation: to validate them alone (targeting), or to lower its bar for endorsing everyone (a threshold shift). We answer this in one setting, empathetic RL against LLM-simulated users (RLVER, GRPO, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct): we vary only the share of validation-seeking users (0--50%; RLVER's default: 24.6%) and evaluate on 1,000 Reddit AITA posts with community fault verdicts. The policy shifts its threshold. Endorsement of at-fault posters rises by 3--4 percentage points per 10 points of share; without such users the Qwen model stays at base, and the effect persists at matched KL and under a goal-blind reward. Signal-detection analysis shows that the criterion for endorsing falls while discrimination between at-fault and not-at-fault posters does not decline. An explicit request to be told if one is wrong gives no measurable protection: at-fault posters who make it receive nearly the same rise as those who do not (+0.11 vs. +0.13). When the goal is stated during training, the policy instead largely targets, endorsing seekers regardless of fault. Standard sycophancy and empathy benchmarks miss the shift; five of six usable released empathetic-RL checkpoints also endorse at-fault posters who ask for honesty more than their base models, though a pre-registered prediction for two held for only one. The user mix is a training hyperparameter to audit and report.
item.dc:creator: Xinche Zhang, Shanghong Xie, Zhiyuan Ma, Jinhao Li, Sen Song

item.title: Actionwave: A Systematic Benchmark for Waveform-Centric Clinical Prediction Across Care Scenarios
item.description: arXiv:2611.31249v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Continuous bedside waveforms record rapid physiological changes that can inform clinical decisions. Existing benchmarks examine selected prediction conditions, but it remains unclear how model advantages depend on signal duration, warning time, and available inputs across care settings. We introduce Actionwave, a benchmark for waveform-centric clinical prediction across intensive-care, operating-room, and emergency-department settings. Actionwave uses a common decision-time prediction interface and groups clinically grounded tasks by what is inferred and when. It varies conditions relevant to clinical use, including the warning required before an intervention. We compare diverse architectures and pretrained biosignal encoders under specified model-size and compute budgets. The protocol requires patient-level splits, strict information cutoffs, and comparisons that isolate individual modeling factors. Across 20 tasks and 1.4M task-labelled windows from source datasets, the experimental grids account for over 87,000 model fits. These comparisons identify task-specific choices and show why matched cohorts, unimodal controls, and explicit timing are necessary when interpreting waveform model performance.
item.dc:creator: Jie Peng, Davis Hobley, Song Wang, Zachary Plotkin, Tianlong Chen

item.title: A Fused Gaussian Process Bandit Framework for Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.32092v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is widely used to maximize expensive black-box functions when direct evaluation is costly. In many real-world applications, the high-fidelity objective can be approximated by a series of lower-fidelity models that provide partial but informative signals at substantially reduced cost. Multi-fidelity BO (MFBO) algorithms aim to strategically combine these information sources to achieve an optimal trade-off between accuracy and evaluation cost. However, existing MFBO methods often oversimplify the complex dependencies between fidelity levels or rely on heuristic acquisition functions that lack theoretical performance guarantees. To address these limitations, we introduce a new formulation of the MFBO problem as a fused Gaussian Process bandit and develop a corresponding Fused Gaussian Process Upper Confidence Bound (FGP-UCB) algorithm. Our approach accurately predicts the high-fidelity function by fusing multi-fidelity observations through an autoregressive Gaussian Process model and explicitly quantifies the uncertainty arising from parameter estimation across fidelity levels. The proposed method also provides theoretical simple-regret guarantees, overcoming a key limitation of existing MFBO algorithms that lack provable performance bounds. Effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated via both theoretical analysis and empirical studies.
item.dc:creator: Muyun Lu, Jose E Aguilar Escamilla, Huazheng Wang, Ying Lin

item.title: LEGOSpec: A Composable and Efficient Framework for Speculative Draft Design and Training
item.description: arXiv:2611.33004v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) generation using a lightweight draft. Existing methods evaluate complete recipes under different training configurations, leaving component effects, interactions, and composition benefits unclear. Therefore, we present LEGOSpec, a composable framework for speculative draft design and training. LEGOSpec decomposes draft models into Context, Backbone, Proposal, and Objective components that share a unified training infrastructure. Using LEGOSpec, we systematically vary components and evaluate selected combinations under matched training conditions to isolate their effects and interactions. These experiments reveal three findings: (1) Different workloads favor different backbones, depending on context length and memory budget, with within-block dependency modeling particularly important for long contexts. (2) Proposal design must balance acceptance and latency. (3) The training objective should match token distributions locally and optimize acceptance length across the block. These findings guide workload-aware configurations and DFlux, a balanced general-purpose draft combining a convolution-equipped SWA--GQA hybrid backbone, Residual Corrector, and hierarchical supervision. Across Qwen and Gemma models, DFlux improves acceptance length over the strongest baseline by up to 13.7% on regular benchmarks and 34.7% on long-context workloads. To support efficient training, LEGOSpec integrates metadata-aware scheduling and asynchronous execution, increasing training throughput by up to 79% and accelerating offline supervision preparation by up to $3.11\times$ over SpecForge.
item.dc:creator: Hanzhen Wang, Jiaming Xu, Guohao Dai

item.title: Shifter Quantization: Compact Representations for Native Integer Computation
item.description: arXiv:2611.33080v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Groupwise quantization is used in LLM quantization to improve accuracy at low bit widths, but grouping weights keeps standard integer MMA from spanning the full dot product for efficient GPU inference. We develop a new quantization method, Shifter Quantization (SQ), that reconstructs native-width integer operands by appending and shifting shared bits. To further extend the efficiency, we develop a special variant of SQ, Shifter Integer (SHI), to use INT4 kernels. We show that SQ and SHI formats perform better than standard groupwise quantization in quality, as measured by projection error and KL divergence, and in inference speed, as measured during decoding and prefill. For low precision like 2-bit quantization, SQ2 and SHI2 achieve 2.71-3.77x the 4,096-token prefill throughput of llama.cpp on a Q2_K checkpoint and reduce WikiText-2 KL by 6.6-7.8%. For mid precision like 4-bit quantization, SQ4 achieves 1.43-2.47x the prefill throughput of NInfer's groupwise-integer baselines across the tested models and prompt lengths, with 24-40% lower KL than the NInfer baselines. For high precision like 8-bit quantization, SQ8 achieves 27.4% higher batch-one prefill throughput and 72.7% lower KL than vLLM's online FP8.
item.dc:creator: Yufeng Huang

item.title: Reinforcement Learning Can Be Recovered From Its Own Rollouts
item.description: arXiv:2611.33102v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Broadly speaking, reinforcement learning (RL) post-training converts compute into model capabilities by training on model-generated data. Typically, the rollouts are discarded after each update, and the knowledge acquired during RL resides in the model weights. In this work, we investigate how much of this knowledge is retained in the rollouts themselves. A natural first attempt is to replay the original RL algorithm on archived (rather than freshly generated) rollouts, but this generally leads to catastrophic collapse. We provide a simple explanation for this phenomenon, which in turn suggests a remedy we call maximum likelihood replay: fitting the model to its archived rollouts. Surprisingly, starting from the same base model and replaying the rollouts in the order in which they were generated, without any distinction between correct and incorrect responses, is sufficient to recover the performance of online RL. In fact, a single maximum likelihood update per rollout batch closely tracks the entire learning curve of online RL. Furthermore, maximum likelihood replay on the rollouts of the last few RL steps often suffices to recover the final model's performance. This suggests that much of the compute invested in RL goes into discovering an improved sampling distribution rather than learning it from samples.
item.dc:creator: Jiayi Sheng, Jingwen Gu, Guanning Zeng, Zhaoyi Zhou, Stefano Viel, Qianqian Wang, Fahim Tajwar, Andrea Zanette

item.title: Dynamic Tensor Product Regression
item.description: arXiv:2210.03961v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this work, we initiate the study of Dynamic Tensor Product Regression. One has matrices $A_1\in \mathbb{R}^{n_1\times d_1},\ldots,A_q\in \mathbb{R}^{n_q\times d_q}$ and a label vector $b\in \mathbb{R}^{n_1\ldots n_q}$, and the goal is to solve the regression problem with the design matrix $A$ being the tensor product of the matrices $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_q$ i.e. $\min_{x\in \mathbb{R}^{d_1\ldots d_q}} \|(A_1\otimes \ldots\otimes A_q)x-b\|_2$. At each time step, one matrix $A_i$ receives a sparse change, and the goal is to maintain a sketch of the tensor product $A_1\otimes\ldots \otimes A_q$ so that the regression solution can be updated quickly. Recomputing the solution from scratch for each round is very slow and so it is important to develop algorithms which can quickly update the solution with the new design matrix. Our main result is a dynamic tree data structure where any update to a single matrix can be propagated quickly throughout the tree. We show that our data structure can be used to solve dynamic versions of not only Tensor Product Regression, but also Tensor Product Spline regression (which is a generalization of ridge regression) and for maintaining Low Rank Approximations for the tensor product.
item.dc:creator: Aravind Reddy, Zhao Song, Lichen Zhang

item.title: Local structural transfer learning of non-Gaussian DAG and its application to multi-source cancer gene regulatory networks
item.description: arXiv:2310.10239v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Directed acyclic graph (DAG) is pivotal for modeling gene regulatory networks in cancer pathogenesis, yet single-study genomic data is often limited for accurate DAG reconstruction. Although multi-source datasets provide augmented sample sizes, substantial heterogeneity persists across real-world cohorts. It remains an open question how to pool the heterogeneous data with only local similarity together for better DAG structure reconstruction in the target study. In this paper, we introduce a novel set of structural similarity measures for DAGs and then present a transfer DAG learning framework by effectively leveraging information from auxiliary DAGs with node-level local similarities. Our theoretical analysis shows substantial improvement in terms of DAG reconstruction in the target study, which is in sharp contrast to most existing transfer learning methods requiring global similarity. The advantage of the proposed transfer DAG learning is also supported by extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic data and multi-source cancer genomics data.
item.dc:creator: Mingyang Ren, Xin He, Junhui Wang

item.title: Neur2BiLO: Neural Bilevel Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2402.02552v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Bilevel optimization deals with nested problems in which a leader takes the first decision to minimize their objective function while accounting for a follower's best-response reaction. Constrained bilevel problems with integer variables are particularly notorious for their hardness. While exact solvers have been proposed for mixed-integer linear bilevel optimization, they tend to scale poorly with problem size and are hard to generalize to the non-linear case. On the other hand, problem-specific algorithms (exact and heuristic) are limited in scope. Under a data-driven setting in which similar instances of a bilevel problem are solved routinely, our proposed framework, Neur2BiLO, embeds a neural network approximation of the leader's or follower's value function, trained via supervised regression, into an easy-to-solve mixed-integer program. Neur2BiLO serves as a heuristic that produces high-quality solutions extremely fast for four applications with linear and non-linear objectives and pure and mixed-integer variables.
item.dc:creator: Justin Dumouchelle, Esther Julien, Jannis Kurtz, Elias B. Khalil

item.title: Point2SSM++: Self-Supervised Learning of Anatomical Shape Models from Point Clouds
item.description: arXiv:2405.09707v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Correspondence-based statistical shape modeling (SSM) stands as a powerful technology for morphometric analysis in clinical research. SSM facilitates population-level characterization and quantification of anatomical shapes such as bones and organs, aiding in pathology and disease diagnostics and treatment planning. Despite its potential, SSM remains under-utilized in medical research due to the significant overhead associated with automatic construction methods, which demand complete, aligned shape surface representations. Additionally, optimization-based techniques rely on bias-inducing assumptions or templates and have prolonged inference times as the entire cohort is simultaneously optimized. To overcome these challenges, we introduce Point2SSM++, a principled, self-supervised deep learning approach that directly learns correspondence points from point cloud representations of anatomical shapes. Point2SSM++ is robust to misaligned and inconsistent input, providing SSM that accurately samples individual shape surfaces while effectively capturing population-level statistics. Furthermore, we present extensions of Point2SSM++ tailored for dynamic spatiotemporal and multi-anatomy scenarios, showcasing the broad versatility of the framework. Through extensive validation across diverse anatomies, evaluation metrics, and clinically relevant downstream tasks, we demonstrate Point2SSM++'s superiority over existing state-of-the-art deep learning models and the traditional approach. Point2SSM++ substantially enhances the feasibility of SSM generation and significantly broadens its array of potential clinical applications.
item.dc:creator: Jadie Adams, Mokshagna Sai Teja Karanam, Shireen Elhabian

item.title: ADformer: A Multi-Granularity Spatial-Temporal Transformer for EEG-Based Alzheimer Detection
item.description: arXiv:2409.00032v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Electroencephalography has emerged as a cost-effective, efficient tool to help neurologists detect Alzheimer's Disease. However, most existing approaches rely heavily on manual feature engineering or data transformation. While these techniques may help with small-scale datasets, they often cause information loss and distortion when applied to large-scale data, ultimately limiting model performance. Moreover, the limited subject scale and demographic diversity of datasets used in prior studies hinder comprehensive evaluation of model robustness and generalizability, thus restricting their applicability in real-world clinical settings. To address these challenges, we propose ADformer, a novel multi-granularity spatial-temporal transformer that captures both temporal and spatial features from raw EEG signals, enabling effective end-to-end representation learning. Our model introduces multi-granularity embedding strategies across both spatial and temporal dimensions, leveraging a two-stage intra-inter-granularity self-attention mechanism to learn local patterns within each granularity and global dependencies across granularities. We evaluate ADformer on 4 large-scale datasets totaling 1,713 subjects, one of the largest corpora for EEG-based AD detection to date, under a cross-validated, subject-independent setting. Experimental results demonstrate that ADformer consistently outperforms existing methods, achieving subject-level F1 scores of 87.11%, 89.83%, 67.99%, and 84.42% on the 4 datasets, respectively, in distinguishing Alzheimer's Disease patients from healthy control subjects.
item.dc:creator: Yihe Wang, Nadia Mammone, Darina Petrovsky, Alexandros T. Tzallas, Francesco C. Morabito, Xiang Zhang

item.title: Protecting Confidentiality, Privacy and Integrity in Collaborative Learning
item.description: arXiv:2412.08534v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A collaboration between dataset owners and model owners is needed for effective machine learning (ML) training. During this collaboration, however, dataset owners and model owners want to protect the confidentiality of their respective assets (i.e., datasets, models and training code), with the dataset owners also caring about the privacy of individual users whose data is in the datasets. Existing solutions provide limited confidentiality for models and training code, suffer from data privacy issues, or incur unacceptable performance. We present Citadel++, a collaborative ML training system to simultaneously protect the confidentiality of datasets, models and training code as well as the privacy of individual user data. Specifically, Citadel++ takes a chained approach. First, we employ the Virtual Machine-level Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) as the training runtime to provide confidentiality protections for datasets, model and training code. Second, we create a privacy barrier that improves upon differential privacy techniques to safeguard the privacy of individual user data while maintaining model utility. Third, we construct and optimize a Virtual Machine Privilege Level (VMPL)-enforced fine-grained sandbox to regulate the dataflow in the system to ensure that our privacy barrier is always applied even when the model and training code maybe maliciously designed. Finally, we employ specific TEE capabilities to ensure the integrity of our privacy barrier and sandboxing mechanisms for their correct execution. To our knowledge, Citadel++ is the first collaborative training system providing strong confidentiality and privacy protections for dataset owners and model owners simultaneously. We analyze Citadel++ security properties and implement a full prototype. Our evaluation shows that Citadel++ provides strong guarantees with modest overheads.
item.dc:creator: Dong Chen, Alice Dethise, Istemi Ekin Akkus, Ivica Rimac, Antti Koskela, Marco Canini, Wei Wang, Ruichuan Chen

item.title: DRAFT-ing Architectural Design Decisions using LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2504.08207v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Architectural Knowledge Management (AKM) is crucial for software development and Architectural Decision Records (ADR), an important artifact of AKM, provide a structured approach to capture Architectural Design Decisions (ADD). However, their adoption is limited due to the manual effort involved and insufficient tool support. Prior work shows that LLMs can support ADD generation, though basic prompting yields suboptimal results. This paper explores how LLMs can support architects in two complementary tasks: generating ADDs from Decision Contexts, and generating complete ADRs from titles. We propose Domain-specific Retrieval Augmented Few-shot Tuning (DRAFT), a novel approach that integrates Retrieval Augmented Few-shot Generation with Fine-tuning to generate. DRAFT operates in two phases: an offline phase that fine-tunes a model using retrieval-augmented prompts derived from historical ADRs, and an online phase that generates decisions or complete ADRs by combining retrieved examples with the fine-tuned model. Evaluated on 4344 ADRs across multiple LLMs using standard NLP metrics, DRAFT consistently produces outputs better aligned with real-world ADRs. A human evaluation with the authors and external architects, however, shows no uniformly preferred approach. DRAFT also maintains practical efficiency, reduces dependence- dence on proprietary models, and addresses organizational concerns around privacy, resource constraints, and inference costs.
item.dc:creator: Rudra Dhar, Adyansh Kakran, Amey Karan, Vasudeva Varma, Karthik Vaidhyanathan

item.title: Neural Fidelity Calibration for Informative Sim-to-Real Adaptation
item.description: arXiv:2504.08604v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Deep reinforcement learning can seamlessly transfer agile locomotion and navigation skills from the simulator to real world. However, bridging the sim-to-real gap with domain randomization or adversarial methods often demands expert physics knowledge to ensure policy robustness. Even so, cutting-edge simulators may fall short of capturing every real-world detail, and the reconstructed environment may introduce errors due to various perception uncertainties. To address these challenges, we propose Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), a novel framework that employs conditional score-based diffusion models to calibrate simulator physical coefficients and residual fidelity domains online during robot execution. Specifically, the residual fidelity reflects the simulation model shift relative to the real-world dynamics and captures the uncertainty of the perceived environment, enabling us to sample realistic environments under the inferred distribution for policy fine-tuning. Our framework is informative and adaptive in three key ways: (a) we fine-tune the pretrained policy only under anomalous scenarios, (b) we build sequential NFC online with the pretrained NFC's proposal prior, reducing the diffusion model's training burden, and (c) when NFC uncertainty is high and may degrade policy improvement, we leverage optimistic exploration to enable hallucinated policy optimization. Our framework achieves superior simulator calibration precision compared to state-of-the-art methods across diverse robots with high-dimensional parametric spaces. We study the critical contribution of residual fidelity to policy improvement in simulation and real-world experiments. Notably, our approach demonstrates robust robot navigation under challenging real-world conditions, such as a broken wheel axle on snowy surfaces.
item.dc:creator: Youwei Yu, Lantao Liu

item.title: A Unifying Framework for Robust and Efficient Inference with Unstructured Data
item.description: arXiv:2505.00282v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI can cheaply extract structured variables from unstructured data, with alternative implementation choices potentially yielding different measures of the same concept. This creates a credibility challenge, effectively moving specification search upstream. We confront this challenge with MAR-S (Missing At Random Structured Data), a framework which adapts semiparametric missing data theory to deliver valid, efficient, robust inference with AI predictions. MAR-S anchors measurement in a transparent validation sample design, while AI scales measurement. We provide general recipes for MAR-S estimation and extend the framework to aggregated and transformed AI predictions, a common setting not addressed by existing frameworks.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Carlson, Melissa Dell

item.title: Stability Regularized Cross-Validation
item.description: arXiv:2505.06927v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study hyperparameter selection via cross-validation, motivated by settings in which the selected $k$-fold cross-validation error underestimates the selected model's test error. We propose a nested $k$-fold cross-validation scheme that minimizes a weighted sum of the standard cross-validation error and empirical hypothesis stability, with the stability weight selected by an outer cross-validation loop. We derive a generalization bound that controls test error using the cross-validation error and empirical hypothesis stability, together with correction terms common to every candidate. In a stylized ridge regression setting, we then show that whether the stability weight improves expected test-set performance depends on the signal-to-noise ratio, with the greatest improvement when the signal-to-noise ratio is small. On $13$ real-world regression datasets, the procedure reduces the average out-of-sample MSE relative to $k$-fold cross-validation by $5.6\%$ for sparse regression and by $6.8\%$ for CART. A side benefit of an outer cross-validation loop is that the selected error estimates are better calibrated than those from ordinary $k$-fold cross-validation: the error estimate moves from 12.3\% below the selected test-set MSE to 5.8\% above it for sparse regression and from 10.3\% below to 0.2\% above it for CART.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Cory-Wright, Andr\'es G\'omez

item.title: Statistical Inference for Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent
item.description: arXiv:2507.20560v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Privacy preservation in machine learning, particularly through Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD), is crucial for analyzing sensitive data. However, existing statistical inference methods for SGD predominantly focus on cyclic subsampling, while DP-SGD requires randomized subsampling. This paper first bridges this gap by establishing the asymptotic properties of SGD under the randomized rule and extending these results to DP-SGD. For DP-SGD, we show that the asymptotic variance decomposes into statistical, sampling, and privacy-induced components. We propose two methods for constructing valid confidence intervals: the plug-in method and the random scaling method. We also perform extensive numerical analysis showing that the proposed confidence intervals achieve nominal coverage rates while maintaining privacy.
item.dc:creator: Xintao Xia, Linjun Zhang, Zhanrui Cai

item.title: StochEP: Stochastic Equilibrium Propagation for Spiking Convergent Recurrent Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2511.11320v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient, sparse, biologically inspired computation. Training them with Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) and surrogate gradients achieves strong performance but remains biologically implausible. Equilibrium Propagation (EP) provides a more local and biologically grounded alternative. However, existing EP frameworks for SNNs largely rely on deterministic neurons, which require complex mechanisms to handle spiking discontinuities and do not scale beyond simple benchmarks such as MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. Inspired by the stochastic nature of biological spiking mechanism and recent hardware trends, we propose a stochastic EP framework that integrates probabilistic spiking neurons into the EP paradigm. This formulation smoothens the optimization landscape, stabilizes training, and enables efficient and scalable learning in SNNs. We provide theoretical guarantees showing that the proposed stochastic EP dynamics approximate deterministic EP under mean-field theory, thereby inheriting its underlying theoretical guarantees. The proposed framework narrows the performance gap with both BPTT-trained SNNs and EP-trained non-spiking convergent recurrent neural networks (CRNNs) on CIFAR-10, DVS Gesture, and IMDB datasets, while preserving temporal and spatial locality. Our results highlight stochastic EP as a promising approach for neuromorphic and on-chip learning.
item.dc:creator: Jiaqi Lin, Yi Jiang, Abhronil Sengupta

item.title: db-SP: Accelerating Sparse Attention for Visual Generative Models with Dual-Balanced Sequence Parallelism
item.description: arXiv:2511.23113v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Scaling Diffusion Transformer (DiT) inference via sequence parallelism is critical for reducing latency in visual generation, but is severely hampered by workload imbalance when applied to models employing block-wise sparse attention. The imbalance stems from the inherent variation in sparsity across attention heads and the irregular distribution of dense blocks within the sparse mask, when sequence parallelism is applied along the head dimension (as in Ulysses) or the block dimension (as in Ring Attention). In this paper, we formalize a sparse imbalance ratio to quantify the imbalance, and propose db-SP, a sparsity-aware sequence parallelism technique that tackles the challenge. db-SP contains a dual-level partitioning approach that achieves near-perfect workload balance at both the head and block levels with negligible overhead. Furthermore, to handle the evolving sparsity patterns across denoising steps and layers, db-SP dynamically determines the parallel degrees for the head and block dimensions at runtime. Experimental results demonstrate that db-SP delivers an end-to-end speedup of 1.25x and an attention-specific speedup of 1.40x over state-of-the-art sequence parallel methods on average. Code is available at https://github.com/thu-nics/db-SP.
item.dc:creator: Siqi Chen, Ke Hong, Tianchen Zhao, Ruiqi Xie, Zhenhua Zhu, Xudong Zhang, Yu Wang

item.title: Luxical: High-Speed Lexical-Dense Text Embeddings
item.description: arXiv:2512.09015v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Frontier language model quality increasingly hinges on our ability to organize web-scale text corpora for training. Today's dominant tools trade off speed and flexibility: lexical classifiers (e.g., FastText) are fast but limited to producing classification output scores, while the vector-valued outputs of transformer text embedding models flexibly support numerous workflows (e.g., clustering, classification, and retrieval) but are computationally expensive to produce. We introduce Luxical, a library for high-speed "lexical-dense" text embeddings that aims to recover the best properties of both approaches for web-scale text organization. Luxical combines sparse TF--IDF features, a small ReLU network, and a knowledge distillation training regimen to approximate large transformer embedding models at a fraction of their operational cost. In this technical report, we describe the Luxical architecture and training objective and evaluate a concrete Luxical model in two disparate applications: a targeted webcrawl document retrieval test and an end-to-end language model data curation task grounded in text classification. In these tasks we demonstrate speedups ranging from 3x to 100x over varying-sized neural baselines, and comparable to FastText model inference during the data curation task. On these evaluations, the tested Luxical model illustrates favorable compute/quality trade-offs for large-scale text organization, matching the quality of neural baselines. Luxical is available as open-source software at https://github.com/datologyai/luxical.
item.dc:creator: DatologyAI, :, Luke Merrick, Alex Fang, Aldo Carranza, Alvin Deng, Amro Abbas, Brett Larsen, Cody Blakeney, Darren Teh, David Schwab, Fan Pan, Haakon Mongstad, Haoli Yin, Jack Urbanek, Jason Lee, Jason Telanoff, Josh Wills, Kaleigh Mentzer, Parth Doshi, Paul Burstein, Pratyush Maini, Ricardo Monti, Rishabh Adiga, Scott Loftin, Siddharth Joshi, Spandan Das, Tony Jiang, Vineeth Dorna, Zhengping Wang, Bogdan Gaza, Ari Morcos, Matthew Leavitt

item.title: Mechanism-Based Intelligence: Differentiable Incentives for Rational Coordination and Equilibrium Alignment in Multi-Agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2512.20688v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Autonomous multi-agent systems struggle with the Hayekian Information problem (using dispersed private knowledge) and the Hurwiczian Incentive problem (aligning local actions with global objectives). I introduce Mechanism-Based Intelligence (MBI), an architecture that treats intelligence as emergent from the coordination of specialized modules rather than a single monolithic model. At its core, the Differentiable Price Mechanism computes the exact gradient of the system loss as a price; subtracting its own marginal cost, each agent obtains the incentive signal $$\mathbf{G}_i = - \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{global}}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_i},$$ and the transfers take the Groves form. Each agent's best response minimizes the global loss given the actions of others, so the negative global loss is an exact potential for the resulting game, with a unique equilibrium at the global optimum. Gradient-based play converges to it under a step-size condition when effort is costless, and stops near it otherwise: a satisficing rule halts each agent's search when its marginal gain no longer exceeds its marginal computational cost. The equilibrium requires no knowledge of agents' private costs, so asymmetric information causes no welfare loss; simultaneous gradient dynamics require only a public bound on cost curvature. Each iteration scales linearly ($\mathcal{O}(N)$) with the number of agents, though for losses summed over agents the iteration count also grows with $N$. For known, differentiable losses, MBI avoids the combinatorial search of Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes. Under convexity and smoothness conditions, MBI aligns agent self-interest with the Planner's objective, offering an auditable approach to multi-agent coordination.
item.dc:creator: Stefano Grassi

item.title: BayesFlow 2: Multi-Backend Amortized Bayesian Inference in Python
item.description: arXiv:2602.07098v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern Bayesian inference involves a mixture of computational methods for estimating, validating, and drawing conclusions from probabilistic models as part of principled workflows. An overarching motif of many Bayesian methods is that they are relatively slow, which often becomes prohibitive when fitting complex models to large data sets. Amortized Bayesian inference (ABI) offers a path to solving the computational challenges of Bayes. ABI trains neural networks on model simulations, rewarding users with rapid inference of any model-implied quantity, such as point estimates, likelihoods, or full posterior distributions. In this work, we present the Python library BayesFlow, Version 2, for general-purpose ABI. Along with direct posterior, likelihood, and ratio estimation, the software includes support for multiple popular deep learning backends, a rich collection of generative networks for sampling and density estimation, complete customization and high-level interfaces, as well as new capabilities for hyperparameter optimization, design optimization, and multilevel modeling. Using a case study on dynamical system parameter estimation, combined with comparisons to similar software, we show that our streamlined, user-friendly workflow has strong potential to support broad adoption.
item.dc:creator: Lars K\"uhmichel, Jerry M. Huang, Valentin Pratz, Jonas Arruda, Hans Olischl\"ager, Daniel Habermann, Simon Kucharsky, Lasse Elsem\"uller, Aayush Mishra, Niels Bracher, Svenja Jedhoff, Marvin Schmitt, Paul-Christian B\"urkner, Stefan T. Radev

item.title: Learned Finite Element-based Regularization of the Inverse Problem in Electrocardiographic Imaging
item.description: arXiv:2602.07466v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Electrocardiographic imaging (ECGI) seeks to reconstruct cardiac electrical activity from body-surface potentials noninvasively. However, the associated inverse problem is severely ill-posed and requires robust regularization. While classical approaches primarily employ spatial smoothing, the temporal structure of cardiac dynamics remains underexploited despite its physiological relevance. We introduce a space-time regularization framework that couples spatial regularization with a learned temporal Fields-of-Experts (FoE) prior to capture complex spatiotemporal activation patterns. We derive a finite element discretization on unstructured cardiac surface meshes, prove Mosco-convergence, and develop a scalable optimization algorithm capable of handling the FoE term. Numerical experiments on synthetic epicardial data demonstrate improved denoising and inverse reconstructions compared to handcrafted spatiotemporal methods, yielding solutions that are both robust to noise and physiologically plausible.
item.dc:creator: Manuel Haas, Thomas Grandits, Thomas Pinetz, Thomas Beiert, Simone Pezzuto, Alexander Effland

item.title: Predictive Coding Implemented as a Hardware Substrate Computes Gradients faster than Backpropagation
item.description: arXiv:2603.18066v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Backpropagation has enabled modern deep learning but is difficult to realize as an online, fully distributed hardware system due to global error propagation, separate phases, and centralized memory. Predictive coding is an alternative learning algorithm with similar dynamics to backpropagation that arises from local prediction error dynamics. This paper shows that predictive coding can be instantiated as a discrete time digital hardware substrate, with local memory and computation, no instruction set architecture, and one physical core for each predictive-coding neuron. Each core stores its own activity and weights, communicates with the cores that it's connected to, and performs local gradient updates. By updating neuron cores concurrently, the architecture computes a network update in O(J+K) clock cycles. For dense layers of width n, this is O(n) cycles per update, compared with O(n^2) connection operations processed serially. This result is retained with scaling to larger predictive coding networks, demonstrating a decisive theoretical advantage for predictive coding instantiated in hardware.
item.dc:creator: Timothy Oh

item.title: Cross-Lingual Gaps in Visual STEM Reasoning: Auditing VLMs Across Six Indian Languages
item.description: arXiv:2603.26742v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are benchmarked on diagram-grounded science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) reasoning mostly in English, so it is unclear how much their accuracy changes when the same problem is posed in another language. We audit this for six Indian languages: 980 questions from MathVista, ScienceQA, and MMMU are machine-translated into Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Tamil, Telugu, and Kannada with IndicTrans2 while the images stay unchanged. We evaluate seven open-weight VLMs (Qwen2.5-VL-7B/32B, Qwen3-VL-30B, InternVL2.5-8B, Aya-Vision-8B, Gemma 3-27B, Llama-4-Maverick) and GPT-4o, plus no-image and chain-of-thought (CoT) ablations on Qwen2.5-VL-7B (68,600 inference records). Accuracy falls 9.8-24.9 percentage points (pp) from English to the Indian-language mean, and every model loses more on the Dravidian than on the Indo-Aryan languages (by 0.1-13.2 pp). For Qwen2.5-VL-7B with our prompt, CoT lowers Bengali (-14.4 pp) and Kannada (-11.4 pp) accuracy while barely changing English, but these losses coincide with more answer-extraction failures. Neither Aya-Vision-8B, trained for 23 languages of which only Hindi is among ours, nor scaling Qwen2.5-VL from 7B to 32B closes the gap, and response-level diagnostics show that fluent target-language output and correct answers can come apart. We quantify how machine translation, answer extraction, and English text in the images bound these measurements. Data and code are publicly available.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 6th Workshop on Multilingual Representation Learning (MRL 2026), pages 167-182, Association for Computational Linguistics, 2026
item.dc:creator: Swastik R

item.title: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: A Statistical Perspective
item.description: arXiv:2604.02507v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has emerged as a central framework for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences. Despite its practical success, RLHF raises fundamental statistical questions because it relies on noisy, subjective, and heterogeneous feedback to learn reward models and optimize policies. This survey provides a statistical perspective on RLHF, focusing primarily on LLM alignment. We introduce the main components of RLHF, including supervised fine-tuning, reward modeling, and policy optimization, and relate them to familiar statistical concepts such as the Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) model, latent utility estimation, active learning, experimental design, and uncertainty quantification. We review methods for learning reward functions from pairwise preference data and for optimizing policies through both two-stage RLHF pipelines and emerging one-stage approaches such as direct preference optimization. We further discuss recent extensions including reinforcement learning from AI feedback, inference-time algorithms, and reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, as well as benchmark datasets, evaluation protocols, and open-source frameworks that support RLHF research. We conclude by highlighting open challenges in RLHF.
item.dc:creator: Pangpang Liu, Chengchun Shi, Will Wei Sun

item.title: NSFL: A Post-Training Neuro-Symbolic Fuzzy Logic Framework for Boolean Operators in Neural Embeddings
item.description: arXiv:2604.10604v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Standard dense retrievers have no native mechanism for multi-atom logical constraints. We introduce Neuro-Symbolic Fuzzy Logic (NSFL), a training-free framework that brings fuzzy-logical structure to neural embedding spaces through a first-order finite-difference treatment of similarity. NSFL anchors logical operations on zero-order atomic scores while steering with Neuro-Symbolic Deltas (NS-Delta) -- the marginal semantic contributions induced by contextual fusion -- preserving atomic meaning while capturing contextual dependence, and avoiding the representation collapse and manifold escape endemic to geometric baselines. For latency-constrained deployment, Spherical Query Optimization (SQO) uses Riemannian optimization to project logical formulas into manifold-stable query vectors. Across six encoder configurations and two modalities, NSFL yields mAP@100 improvements up to +81% on QUEST and +70% on a COCO-derived text-to-image benchmark, and provides an additive +19% average gain on an encoder already fine-tuned for logical retrieval. On NevIR, where absolute accuracies are directly interpretable, NSFL doubles pairwise accuracy -- NevIR's both-correct criterion -- from 0.256 to 0.508. The decomposition is exact and general; the operators built on it are engineering realizations rather than a closed algebra, and we state that boundary precisely. Code is available at https://github.com/vladiaidev-lab/NSFL
item.dc:creator: Vladi Vexler, Ofer Idan, Gil Lederman, Dima Sivov

item.title: When the Prior Is Wrong: Probing Misspecified Diffusion Priors in Inverse Problems
item.description: arXiv:2604.21066v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While diffusion priors generate high-quality posterior samples across many scientific inverse problems, they are often trained on purely simulated data, thus inheriting the errors and biases of these underlying sources. Many approaches to adapting diffusion priors from a single observation require sufficient conflict between the data and the prior to successfully adapt and do not allow specific misspecification hypotheses to be tested. On the other hand, existing out-of-distribution (OOD) detection methods determine whether the observation is compatible with a fixed prior, rather than specifying which assumptions to relax or by how much. To address these issues, we propose PIVOT: Prior Inference Via Observation-driven Transformations, which formulates diffusion prior misspecification as inference over an underlying latent variable representing a scientifically plausible discrepancy. By expanding the prior along these plausible directions of misspecification, PIVOT infers a posterior over the strength of each proposed discrepancy given the observation. This process can be efficiently amortized with just one posterior sampling pass using a conditional diffusion model. We also demonstrate how to determine if a proposed discrepancy is inconclusive because the measurement is too noisy or ill-posed. We validate PIVOT on seismic imaging and real-world black hole imaging problems, where we find that OOD observations generally lead to larger perturbation strengths when the proposed discrepancy family captures relevant components of the mismatch, as long as the discrepancy is visible to the measurement. PIVOT thereby provides an interpretable probe into how real-world priors could be misspecified.
item.dc:creator: Frederic Wang, Katherine L. Bouman

item.title: Coreset-Induced Conditional Velocity Flow Matching
