item.description: arXiv:2605.12951v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose Coreset-Induced Conditional Velocity Flow Matching (CCVFM), a generative model that augments hierarchical rectified flow with a data-informed source distribution. Standard flow matching regresses only the conditional mean of the velocity; hierarchical flow matching instead models the full conditional velocity law with a second, inner flow in velocity space, but this inner flow is asked to transport isotropic Gaussian noise to a multimodal target velocity distribution from scratch. Our key observation is that this inner source can be replaced by a closed-form surrogate built from a coreset of the target. CCVFM first compresses the target into weighted atoms using an entropic Sinkhorn coreset and lifts them to a Gaussian mixture. The induced conditional velocity law is then a closed-form Gaussian mixture that can be sampled without a learned neural sampler. A lightweight correction flow, trained from this surrogate source, then refines the remaining surrogate-to-target residual rather than learning an entire noise-to-data map. We prove that the surrogate transport cost equals the target-surrogate Wasserstein gap under an explicit compression assumption, whereas the noise-source analogue has a dimension-scale lower bound. We further characterize the conditional second moment of the training target when the source velocity is drawn from the surrogate law independently of the target velocity, and show that the part of it that depends on the source is small when the surrogate conditional law is close to the true conditional velocity law in mean and covariance. Empirically, on MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet-32, and CelebA-HQ, the proposed method reaches competitive few-step generation under matched architectures. Code is available at https://github.com/ziwaa-se/CCVFM.
item.dc:creator: Zihua She, Jianxi Su, Xiao Wang

item.title: Hierarchical Two-Stage Framework for Environment-Aware Long-Horizon Vessel Trajectory Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2605.16442v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Long-horizon vessel trajectory forecasting under real ocean conditions is critical for collision avoidance, traffic management, and route planning. However, achieving accurate predictions is challenging due to long-range temporal dependencies and dynamic environmental factors such as currents, wind, and waves. To address these issues, we propose a hierarchical two-stage framework that combines a coarse long-term predictor with a grid-aware short-term predictor through a hierarchical fusion mechanism. The short-term branch leverages a Spatio-Temporal Graph Transformer on discretized maritime cells to capture localized dynamics, while the long-term branch encodes overarching navigational intent. An integrated environmental module incorporates oceanographic parameters, including surface currents, wind vectors, and significant wave height, using cross-modal attention and feature-wise modulation for adaptive response to varying sea conditions. Additionally, a learnable Savitzky-Golay smoothing layer enhances temporal coherence in fused trajectories. We evaluate our approach on Australian Craft Tracking System (CTS) data from the North West region, aligned with Copernicus Marine Service products, using a 3-hour input and a 10-hour prediction horizon. Experimental results show that our framework outperforms the state-of-the-art by 25% in Average Displacement Error (ADE) and 17% in Final Displacement Error (FDE). Ablation studies further validate the contribution of each component.
item.dc:creator: Ganeshaaraj Gnanavel, Sridha Sridharan, Clinton Fookes, Tharindu Fernando

item.title: SynVA: A Modular Toolkit for Vessel Generation and Aneurysm Editing
item.description: arXiv:2605.17620v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Intracranial aneurysms (IAs), characterized by unpredictable growth and risk of rupture, are a major cause of stroke and can lead to life-threatening hemorrhages with high mortality and long-term disability. With aging populations, the incidence and overall burden of cerebrovascular diseases are expected to increase, highlighting the need for scalable approaches to analyze complex medical data and improve population-level understanding of these conditions. While digital twins and deep learning offer promising avenues for improving diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment, their effectiveness is limited by the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality medical data and corresponding labels. We present Synthetic VAsculature (SynVA), a modular toolkit for vascular mesh generation and anatomically consistent aneurysm synthesis. SynVA combines novel flow-matching-based methods for generating healthy vessel meshes with learning-based approaches for anatomy-conditioned aneurysm mesh generation; it computes aneurysms from pre-existing vascular geometries rather than generating them in isolation. In addition, we introduce the SynVA procedural model for vascular and aneurysm synthesis based solely on physiological principles and statistical priors, which enables the generation of large-scale datasets. To this end, we release a dataset of 50,000 fully labeled mesh samples for a variety of downstream vision tasks. Extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations show that SynVA generates realistic vessel geometries and anatomically plausible aneurysms, with only minor trade-offs between expert-perceived realism and similarity to real aneurysms. Moreover, pretraining on SynVA data improves point-cloud segmentation and morphological parameter estimation on real data. Code will be released upon acceptance.
item.dc:creator: Marten J. Finck, Niklas C. Koser, Sarker M. Mahfuz, Tameem Jahangir, Jon E. Wilhelm, Daniel Behme, Naomi Larsen, Wojtek Palubicki, Sylvia Saalfeld, S\"oren Pirk

item.title: Hyrax: An Extensible Framework for Rapid ML Experimentation and Unsupervised Discovery in the Era of Rubin, Roman, and Euclid
item.description: arXiv:2605.18959v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory, Roman Space Telescope, Euclid, and other next-generation surveys will deliver imaging, spectroscopic, and time-domain data at scales that increasingly shift the bottleneck in astronomical machine learning (ML) projects from model design to infrastructure. We present Hyrax, an open-source, modular, GPU-enabled Python framework that supports the full ML lifecycle in astronomy: from data acquisition and training to inference and experiment comparison, with capabilities including multimodal dataset support, integrated vector databases for similarity search, and interactive two- and three-dimensional latent-space exploration for unsupervised discovery. We demonstrate Hyrax's versatility through five representative applications on real survey data: (i) unsupervised representation learning on $\sim 4\times10^5$ Rubin Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) Data Preview 1 (DP1) galaxies, surfacing new merger and low-surface-brightness candidates missing from reference Euclid and Dark Energy Survey catalogs, while also isolating imaging artifacts -- all without labeled training data; (ii) hybrid density-based clustering for identifying cluster-scale gravitational lens candidates in DP1 data; (iii) multimodal early-time transient classification in the Zwicky Transient Facility leveraging light curves, spectra, images, and metadata; (iv) supervised false-positive filtering in shift-and-stack searches for distant solar system objects in the Dark Energy Camera Ecliptic Exploration Project survey; and (v) supervised detection of semi-resolved dwarf galaxies in Hyper Suprime-Cam and LSST-like imaging using synthetic source injection. Together, these results demonstrate that Hyrax provides astronomy-specific ML infrastructure that enables systematic discovery and rapid methodological iteration across next-generation astronomical surveys.
item.dc:creator: Aritra Ghosh, Drew Oldag, Michael Tauraso, Andrew J. Connolly, Peter Ferguson, Derek Jones, Gourav Khullar, Argyro Sasli, Samarth Venkatesh, Gracia Wang, Maxine West, Dylan Berry, Neven Caplar, Colin Orion Chandler, Tanawan Chatchadanoraset, Michael W. Coughlin, Melissa DeLucchi, Alexandra Junell, Diego Miura, Naomi Morato, Felipe Fontinele Nunes, Hurum Maksora Tohfa, Wilson Beebe, Doug Branton, Sandro Campos, Liam Cunningham, Mi Dai, Jeremy Kubica, Konstantin Malanchev, Rachel Mandelbaum, Sean McGuire, Imad Pasha, Dan S. Taranu, Tianqing Zhang

item.title: Resolution-free neural surrogates for geometric parameterization and mapping with spatially varying fields
item.description: arXiv:2605.28551v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Many imaging problems require computing spatial transformations induced by spatially varying intensity, feature, or density fields. Canonical examples include distortion correction, deformable image registration, atlas-based segmentation, and deformation-driven image analysis. These tasks can be formulated as geometric mapping problems in which the transformation is constrained to preserve local structure, control boundary behavior, or regulate angular distortion. Such formulations typically lead to variational models, diffusion processes, or elliptic partial differential equations. However, repeatedly solving high-resolution systems becomes computationally expensive when the underlying parameter fields vary across instances. In this work, we propose a resolution-free neural surrogate for geometric parameterization and mapping problems. Given a spatially varying parameter field $p:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^m$ and grid nodes $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^N\subset\Omega$, the model predicts mapped locations $\{u(x_i)\}_{i=1}^N$ on structured grids of different sizes without retraining. To avoid dependence on a fixed grid, we use a multi-resolution geometric encoding strategy that conditions the network on coordinate-augmented samples of the parameter field. The model is trained without labeled solution data by enforcing geometry-aware constraints derived from variational energies, diffusion-based density equalization, and quasi-conformal theory. Experimental results on quasi-conformal mapping and density-equalizing mapping problems are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.
item.dc:creator: Yanwen Huang, Lok Ming Lui, Gary P. T. Choi

item.title: SparDA: Sparse Decoupled Attention for Efficient Long-Context LLM Inference
item.description: arXiv:2606.04511v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sparse attention reduces compute and memory bandwidth for long-context LLM inference. However, two key challenges remain: (1) KV cache capacity still grows with sequence length, and offloading to CPU memory introduces a PCIe transfer bottleneck; (2) sparse selection during prefill retains $O(T^2)$ complexity and can dominate attention cost at long contexts. We propose SparDA, a decoupled sparse attention architecture that introduces a fourth per-layer projection, the Forecast, alongside Query, Key, and Value. The Forecast predicts the KV blocks needed by the next layer, enabling lookahead selection that overlaps CPU-to-GPU prefetch with current-layer execution. Because Forecast is decoupled from the attention query, our GQA implementation uses one Forecast head per GQA group, reducing selection overhead versus the original multi-head selector. On the evaluated 8B models, SparDA adds <0.5% parameters and trains only the Forecast projections using attention-derived supervision from the frozen backbone. On two sparse-pretrained 8B models, SparDA maintains accuracy comparable to the full-query sparse-attention baseline while delivering up to 1.25$\times$ prefill speedup and 1.7$\times$ decode speedup over the sparse-attention offload baseline. By enabling larger feasible batch sizes on a single GPU, SparDA further reaches up to 5.3$\times$ higher decode throughput than the non-offload sparse baseline on MiniCPM4.1-8B. Our adaptation to GLM-5.1 (754B MoE) also achieves accuracy comparable to native token-level DSA, extending the accuracy evaluation beyond block-sparse 8B models. Our source code is available at https://github.com/NVlabs/SparDA.
item.dc:creator: Yaosheng Fu, Guangxuan Xiao, Xin Dong, Song Han, Oreste Villa

item.title: AlloGen: Conformation-Selective Binder Generation with Differential State Scoring
item.description: arXiv:2606.05474v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Protein binder design commonly optimizes compatibility with a single receptor conformation, leaving preference over alternative functional states unresolved. To address this gap, we introduce AlloGen, a modular method that decouples backbone generation from state-selectivity scoring. We train its SE(3)-invariant interface graph transformer, $Q_\theta$, through interface-quality regression followed by paired conformational discrimination. By comparing scores across states, we rerank candidates and guide frozen backbone generators without retraining. On a benchmark of 65 targets spanning 15 protein families, $Q_\theta$ achieved a mean Spearman correlation of $0.520$ on eight held-out targets. All 15 evaluated generator-guidance combinations achieved positive predicted selectivity averaged over these targets, and RFdiffusion with Langevin refinement reached $\bar{S}_{\mathrm{cons}}=0.677$ on calmodulin (CaM). To test the predicted preference experimentally, we measured binding by bio-layer interferometry. Five designed peptides bound holo CaM, with the strongest measured $K_D$ of 46.6 nM, and none showed detectable apo CaM binding under the tested conditions. Together, these results support computational prioritization of conformation-selective binders.
item.dc:creator: Hanqun Cao, Aastha Pal, Sumi Kimura, Yesol Kim, Jingjie Zhang, Pheng Ann Heng, Pranam Chatterjee

item.title: Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting with a Multi-GPU PyTorch Backend
item.description: arXiv:2606.11390v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Gaussian splatting methods have become increasingly popular for neural reconstruction of the real world. However, they are often limited in scale and resolution due to compute and memory constraints. We present a multi-GPU Gaussian splatting approach that scales reconstruction to higher resolutions and larger scenes while abstracting away the code complexity typically associated with distributing a model. We demonstrate city-scale reconstructions with street-level detail consisting of over 1 billion Gaussian splats. To accomplish this, we propose a PyTorch backend that distributes parameters and operators across GPUs via CUDA unified memory, with optional NVLink support. Because distribution occurs at the operator level, the model code requires no explicit cross-device communication. More broadly, the backend exposes multiple GPUs as an aggregate asynchronous PyTorch device and supports a broad set of PyTorch operators enabling the distribution of general PyTorch workloads.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Cong, Francis Williams, Jonathan Swartz, Mark Harris, Sanja Fidler, Ken Museth

item.title: Unsupervised Detection of Underground Tunnels in Ground-Penetrating Radar Using Depth-Restricted Reconstruction Scoring
item.description: arXiv:2607.04882v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hand-dug tunnels that reach buried pipelines from below are hard to find before they are used, and too rare to train a supervised detector. The engineering application of this work is detecting such tunnels in ground-penetrating radar surveys of a monitored site. The contribution in artificial intelligence is a detection scheme that needs no tunnel examples: a convolutional autoencoder learns the site's normal ground from surveys recorded before any tunnel exists, later survey windows are scored by their largest reconstruction errors within the travel-time band where a tunnel can lie, and evaluation holds out whole survey lines. On field data from a tunnel hand-dug for this study (0.6 m wide, 1 m high, roof 0.9-1.4 m deep) and surveyed repeatedly with a 250-megahertz radar in dry and wet conditions, the detector reaches an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.994 and an F1 score of 0.972 on 1,600 test windows and flags all 29 tunnel crossings. Restricting the score to the depth band improves all six detectors tested and, with a quarter of the training data, outperforms whole-window scoring trained on all of it; the best rule for the same band without learning misses 9 of the 29 crossings. On two unseen plots, false alarms stay at 1.6% on comparable ground but reach 9.3% on irrigated soil; recalibrating the threshold on a fifth of that plot's lines lowers them to 4.2%, retraining brings no significant further reduction, and models trained there alone still detect the original tunnel.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Junaid, Shoab A. Khan, Nisar Ahmed

item.title: How Much is Left? LLMs Linearly Encode Their Remaining Output Length
item.description: arXiv:2607.05316v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large Language models generate tokens, without explicitly keeping track of the length of the generated text. This paper asks the question: can we estimate the number of tokens remaining in a generated response, using just a linear probe on the model's hidden states? Previous work on inference scheduling established that length is statistically predictable, using nonlinear methods. This paper contributes a linear representation method, using frozen hidden states of 7-8B instruction-tuned models, across seven datasets. We show that total completion length can be estimated, with performance stronger than statistical baselines, and stronger than the fair comparison to the prediction at the last token of the prompt. On the natural-language datasets, the probe's error lies between 0.57 and 0.88 of the statistical baseline's. Interestingly, when a retraction token occurs ("Wait"), the probe predicted length jumps upward by over 70 tokens, on average, compared to the baseline, where it drops by 0.7, on average. Moreover, the direction found can be used for length steering: adding to the probe direction increases completion length and vice-versa, on Llama-3.1-8B / GSM8K. These results indicate that LLMs have a linearly decodable internal representation of output length.
item.dc:creator: Mohamed Amine Merzouk, Dmitri Carpov, Mirko Bronzi, Damiano Fornasiere, Adam Oberman

item.title: Near-Optimal Learning of Gaussian Sobolev Operators
item.description: arXiv:2607.11921v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A key question in operator learning is how to design surrogate operators with provable approximation guarantees in reasonable computational time. Whereas holomorphic operators can be approximated efficiently, i.e., with at least algebraic convergence in the number of training samples, learning finitely regular operators is known to be less efficient. The reason is an intrinsic curse of sample complexity, which allows only subalgebraic convergence rates. This fact makes it all the more important to develop algorithms which provably achieve these rates. In this work, we present a fully data-driven algorithm, termed Hermite-PCA approximation, for learning Gaussian Sobolev operators with near-optimal sample complexity. It employs principal component analysis and weighted least-squares methods and is therefore computationally efficient. Moreover, it is spectral, in the sense that it achieves faster (and near-optimal) convergence as the Sobolev regularity increases. We provide a full error analysis of this algorithm along with numerical experiments that match our theoretical results and empirically confirm the efficacy of Hermite-PCA approximation for learning Sobolev operators.
item.dc:creator: Ben Adcock, Michael Griebel, Gregor Maier

item.title: Toward Energy-Efficient and Low-Power Arrhythmia Detection for Wearable Devices
item.description: arXiv:2607.14747v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of death worldwide, and conditions such as arrhythmia often require long-term monitoring for effective detection and diagnosis. However, current wearable monitoring devices are bulky, uncomfortable, and typically rely on clinicians to manually evaluate electrocardiograms (ECGs). While Deep Learning (DL) algorithms have shown superior performance in arrhythmia detection and classification, their computational complexity coupled with high power consumption limit deployment in wearable devices. To address this challenge, this paper investigates the use of approximation techniques to reduce the power and energy consumption of DL architectures while maintaining acceptable classification performance. Specifically, techniques such as data precision reduction and approximate multiplication are investigated in a state-of-the-art DL model and its corresponding hardware architecture. The model is trained and validated using the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, and hardware implementations employing various approximate multipliers are synthesized and evaluated. Compared with the state-of-the-art 8.75 {\mu}W (and 2.08 {\mu}J) reference architecture, our proposed architecture consumes 3.07 {\mu}W (and 2.17 {\mu}J) at 12 kHz, showing 64.9% reduction in power consumption while providing an acceptable output quality, i.e., 93.7% classification accuracy and 92.1% sensitivity. At 100 MHz, our proposed architecture consumes 9.45 mW (and 0.8 {\mu}J), showing 61.5% reduction in energy consumption as compared to the state-of-the-art architecture. These results demonstrate that our proposed approximations significantly extend wearable device battery life while preserving the required arrhythmia classification performance.
item.dc:creator: Floriaan Bulten, Yawar Rasheed, Arlene John, Vincenzo Stoico, Ghayoor Gillani

item.title: A zero-one law for one-shot system identification
item.description: arXiv:2607.15832v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Can a model be identified from one experiment? We study analytic systems that are linearly parameterized by a combination of prescribed dictionary terms, such as partial differential operators and dynamical systems. For a single input-response pair, recovery is possible exactly when the evaluated dictionary terms are linearly independent. We prove a sharp zero-one law: either no input uniquely determines the coefficients, or almost every random input sampled from a nondegenerate Gaussian measure does. This dichotomy reduces one-shot system identification to a question about degenerate inputs and provides an a posteriori certificate in the noiseless setting. Numerical examples recover dynamical systems, nonlinear partial differential equations, and structured matrix families from single trajectory data, while also detecting when an extra probe is necessary.
item.dc:creator: Nicolas Boull\'e, Diana Halikias, Samuel E. Otto, Alex Townsend

item.title: QSTAR: Quantum Selective Transfer with Adaptive Routing
item.description: arXiv:2607.21411v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantum transfer learning (QTL) is commonly evaluated by replacing a classical classifier with a fixed variational quantum head, leaving unclear when quantum inference provides measurable benefit. We propose QSTAR: Quantum Selective Transfer with Adaptive Routing, which retains high-confidence classical predictions and routes low-confidence samples to a quantum fallback. Using a frozen ResNet18 backbone, we compare manually designed QTL heads, architecture-searched KetGPT heads, and parameter-matched classical baselines under consistent experimental settings. On Fashion-MNIST, standard QTL heads reach at most 59.7% accuracy and 0.564 F1-score, whereas compact KetGPT Candidate #160 reaches 80.2% accuracy and 0.800 F1-score. On the routed low-confidence subset, Candidate #160 improves accuracy over the matched MLP by 6.31, 5.38, and 3.73 percentage points at \tau=0.70, 0.80, and 0.90, respectively. At the selected operating point \tau=0.70, the adaptive system reaches 81.78% accuracy and 0.816 F1-score while routing only 36.12% of test samples to the quantum branch. Candidate #160 uses 10 quantum parameters and 9 gates, while experiments on CIFAR-10, KMNIST, and SVHN show consistent accuracy gains over the corresponding adaptive classical baselines. These results show that selective quantum invocation can reduce quantum execution while improving inference on low-confidence samples.
item.dc:creator: Saim Rehman, Nouhaila Innan, Muhammad Shafique

item.title: Improved Quantum Algorithms for Reinforcement Learning Under a Generative Model
item.description: arXiv:2608.02826v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning is a subfield of machine learning that studies how an agent interacts with an environment in order to extract as large a reward as possible. A standard approach to study such interaction is through Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) and the task of choosing an optimal policy---a function that tells the agent which action to take. In this work, we study two types of time-dependent MDP---finite-horizon and infinite-horizon discounted---and propose new quantum algorithms for computing approximate optimal policies. Our quantum algorithms are based on a new combination of standard value iteration and quantum subroutines like quantum mean estimation and quantum maximum finding, overall enhanced with techniques from sample-optimal classical algorithms. Our resulting query complexities improve upon previous works, thus approaching already established quantum lower bounds.
item.dc:creator: Joao F. Doriguello

item.title: LAION-BVD: A 13-Million-Hour Open Video Dataset for Multimodal Pre-training
item.description: arXiv:2608.24845v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present LAION-BVD (LAION - Big Video Dataset), a large-scale open video dataset for multimodal learning, which contains 1.3B platform-specific video URLs collected from CommonCrawl. From these, we download 80M videos with a total duration of 13.5 million hours. The dataset is designed for multimodal pre-training across the video, audio, and image modalities. Using content-aware scene detection, we extract clips for which we synthetically generate video and audio captions. Models trained on these data achieve competitive performance on standard video-text and audio-text benchmarks, with consistent improvements as training or model scale increases. Additionally, we explore video frames as an alternative source of image-text data by extracting scene-changing frames. These frames exhibit a visual distribution distinct from standard web image corpora, and models trained on this dataset achieve strong image-text retrieval performance. We release LAION-BVD to the research community. It significantly expands open access to multimodal videos at an unprecedented scale.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Hochlehnert, Marianna Nezhurina, Mehdi Cherti, Andrej Radonjic, Thadd\"aus Wiedemer, Christoph Schuhmann, Romain Beaumont, Wieland Brendel, Bernhard Sch\"olkopf, A. Sophia Koepke, Jenia Jitsev, Matthias Bethge

item.title: Attention Routing Stabilizes Early: Working-Set Inference for Recurrent Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2609.27373v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recurrent-depth language models, such as looped Transformers, repeatedly apply shared network blocks to refine latent representations, enabling additional test-time computation without generating explicit intermediate reasoning tokens. However, recurrent inference repeatedly accesses long contexts: full attention incurs quadratic computation during prefill, while autoregressive decoding repeatedly reads large key-value (KV) caches, introducing substantial memory traffic and capacity pressure. We study how attention routing evolves across recurrent depth and uncover a consistent separation in convergence timescales: routing-related quantities, including the attention support and the attention distribution, stabilize substantially earlier than representation-related quantities such as hidden states and attention outputs. This suggests a two-stage structure in which the model discovers a sparse working set and then refines representations over largely the same routing support. Motivated by this structure, we introduce WISE (Working-set Inference with Support Exploitation), a training-free method that uses unrestricted global attention during early recurrent steps to discover a block-structured working set, and then reuses it as the routing support in later steps while keeping recurrent refinement and within-support attention computation dynamic. By combining sparse recurrent attention with compact KV-cache management, WISE reduces both redundant attention computation and memory movement during inference. Across reasoning and long-context benchmarks, WISE closely approaches full-attention accuracy on key evaluated workloads while outperforming early-static support baselines. At 64K context, our implementation achieves up to a 6.46x decode throughput improvement under GPU memory pressure. Our code is available at https://github.com/tbn5pj/WISE_code.
item.dc:creator: Ke Wan, Chen Chen

item.title: Reducing Fixed-Batch Client Idleness in Many-Client Edge Split Learning
item.description: arXiv:2609.29395v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Parallel Split Learning with Global Sampling (GPSL) trains a split model on a fixed-size batch drawn from the data of all clients. When the client population is much larger than the batch, most clients contribute no data in a round, and additional server capacity does not change this. We propose Global Clustered Parallel Split Learning (GCPSL), which assigns clients to stable clusters, runs one GPSL workload per cluster concurrently, and periodically fuses the split-model replicas. We derive the expected direct data participation under the batch sampler, which separates repeated sampling of the same clients from idling at the fusion barrier. With 256 clients, more clusters raise participation but reduce the client diversity seen by each workload. In three paired runs on four H100 GPUs, GCPSL raises direct data participation from 22% to 57-60%. With random or size-balanced clusters, it reaches 85% CIFAR-10 validation accuracy in 5.7 minutes, 1.6 times faster than GPSL with its batch sharded across the same GPUs. It matches per-step synchronized data-parallel GPSL at 85% and reaches 88% in about 10 instead of 19.5 minutes, without per-step global gradient or BatchNorm synchronization. Concurrent execution is 3.11 times faster than sequential execution of the same workloads.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Kohankhaki, Valentin Rentschler, Carsten Kamp, Sigrid Brell-Cokcan, Anke Schmeink

item.title: Conformal Prediction and Conditional Coverage for Tabular Foundation Models
item.description: arXiv:2609.34887v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) provide predictive distributions for regression, but their prediction regions can exhibit undercoverage or overcoverage even when point predictions are accurate. We introduce C-USIM (Conditionally-Uniformized Score Integration Method), a lightweight application of highest predictive density split conformal prediction that accommodates multimodal predictions. Given calibration and test outputs, it requires no additional training or model inference. It provides finite-sample marginal validity under our assumptions. We bound conditional-marginal coverage gaps using distribution-estimation error and score discreteness, and examine coverage heterogeneity through percentile rank-score plots. Experiments with TabPFN and TabICL show improved marginal coverage accuracy and lower average conditional and group coverage errors. Under a fixed data budget, allocating more observations to calibration can reduce marginal coverage error despite less accurate point predictions.
item.dc:creator: Sungwoo Park, Sunghee Park, Won Chang

item.title: RNA Design via Conditioned Flow Matching and Finite-Policy Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2609.36885v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: RNA design aims to identify sequences that fold into specified secondary structures. Existing methods formulate the task as target-specific search or conditional generation. However, natural RNA evolution proceeds through sequence variation and selection, with compensatory substitutions, whereas these methods do not explicitly model this process. To address this limitation, we propose a two-stage framework comprising RNA Inverse-Folding Flow (RNA-IFlow) and RNA-IFlow-RL. RNA-IFlow uses structure-conditioned Dirichlet Flow Matching to model coordinated variation across the sequence, while RNA-IFlow-RL maps the learned flow to a pairing-preserving finite policy and refines it with thermodynamic feedback. Our framework achieves leading performance on multiple benchmarks, reaching 85.19% Pass@1 on Rfam-27. Further analyses reveal thermodynamic gains, policy dynamics, and robustness across settings. Our work couples coordinated variation with thermodynamic selection, offering a novel paradigm for RNA design.
item.dc:creator: Zefeng Lin, Xianyong Fang, Tianfan Fu, Xiaohua Xu

item.title: VirusCascade: Hijacking Collaborative Reflection in LLM-Powered Recommender Agents
item.description: arXiv:2609.38270v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Advancing beyond traditional static scoring models, LLM-powered agentic recommender systems (LLM-ARS) instantiate users and items as autonomous agents, whose semantic states are dynamically refined through a recurrent process known as collaborative reflection. While this mechanism improves recommendation quality, it simultaneously introduces a systemic vulnerability: adversarial evidence injected into a single agent can be rationalised into a legitimate preference narrative, written back into memory, and propagated to other agents through interaction contexts. We term the local rationalisation process reflection laundering, and its system-wide escalation through collaborative reflection collaborative-reflection hijacking. Existing attacks on recommender systems, whether based on interaction-level data poisoning or text-level adversarial perturbations, assume static pipelines and thus cannot exploit this recurrent, multi-agent amplification pathway. To bridge this gap, we first conduct a controlled vulnerability analysis that establishes two exploitable properties underlying collaborative-reflection hijacking: reflective persistence and cross-agent propagation. Then building on these findings, we propose VirusCascade, the first black-box targeted promotion attack that jointly shapes semantic and structural attack surfaces: the former ensures the target item is naturally rationalised as satisfying broad user preferences, the latter positions it for system-wide propagation. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets across diverse LLM-ARS architectures demonstrate that VirusCascade consistently achieves state-of-the-art targeted exposure under evaluated stealth constraints, reaching a mean E@20 of 0.384 and surpassing the strongest baseline by an absolute margin of +0.185.
item.dc:creator: Yurong Hao, Wen Zhou, Guowei Guan, Tiantong Wu, Fuyao Zhang, Wei Yang Bryan Lim

item.title: GazeFlow: From Human Gaze Behavior to Generative Egocentric Gaze Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2609.38519v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Egocentric gaze prediction enables many downstream applications but remains challenging, as human gaze is inherently stochastic. This stochasticity is constrained by structured temporal dynamics alternating between fixations and saccades, top-down influences from tasks, and bottom-up visual saliency. Based on this observation, we introduce GazeFlow, a framework that directly models gaze as a joint distribution of temporal gaze positions conditioned upon both top-down and bottom-up information. In particular, GazeFlow uses conditional flow matching (CFM): a learned velocity field iteratively transports a Gaussian noise sample into a plausible gaze trajectory drawn from this joint distribution. The velocity field is conditioned on bottom-up visual features extracted by a video encoder and on top-down task information obtained by globally querying these features. On standard datasets, GazeFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance on per-frame metrics, and the generated trajectories align better with human gaze temporal dynamics. The project page and source code are at: https://horizon-lab.org/gazeflow/
item.dc:creator: Sheng Zhao, Weikai Lin, Yuhao Zhu

item.title: CompMat-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Computational Materials Science
item.description: arXiv:2610.00636v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Evaluating AI agents on scientific research tasks is constrained by the time and resources required for the underlying experiments or calculations. In computational materials research, repeating the same expensive simulations across agents and trials can make evaluation impractical. We introduce CompMat-Bench, a benchmark of 94 tasks derived from recently published computational materials studies, each asking agents to complete a step toward achieving the study's scientific goal. We reproduce the research steps in advance and assess agents on preparing inputs and analyzing outputs for expensive simulations, so expensive simulations can be avoided during evaluation. The reproduced inputs and results serve as ground truth for grading agents with fixed rules, without an LLM judge. We extend the benchmark to four evaluation conditions: single tasks and workflows composed of related tasks, each with full or reduced methodological guidance. In a workflow, the agent runs all simulations itself. With full guidance on single tasks, agents based on nine LLMs demonstrate the ability to complete individual materials research steps, with pass rates of 62.8-97.9% across 94 tasks. Both longer workflows and reduced guidance can limit agent performance, but in different ways for different agents: they lower the pass rates of the weaker agents, whereas the stronger agents fall only when a long workflow is combined with reduced guidance. Failure analysis attributes more failures to scientific errors than to errors in software usage. CompMat-Bench provides a basis for comparing agents on the steps of real materials research and for analyzing agent failure modes.
item.dc:creator: Chenmu Zhang, Levi Felix, Jun-Jie Zhang, Xingfu Li, Xuelian Jiang, Tao Jiang, Subhendu Mishra, Xixi Qin, Boris Yakobson

item.title: SearchWorld: Spatial Value-Grounded Imagination for UAV Object Search via World Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.09335v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Autonomous unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) object search involves a closed loop of perception, decision-making, and action under partial observability. Urban environments pose several challenges: large search areas and narrow egocentric views limit coverage, dense 3D geometry constrains safe motion, and open-world instructions require identifying a specific target among distractors. Many existing methods mitigate partial observability through explicit maps or memory representations, yet remain largely reactive, reasoning over past observations without explicitly predicting future states. World models enable prospective reasoning through imagined rollouts. However, image-generating world models can incur high inference latency, while spatially grounded planning remains challenging for latent world models. We propose SearchWorld, a recurrent state-space world model that connects explicit spatial memory with value-guided imagination. The model maintains BEV exploration and obstacle memory and decodes a task-aware spatial value layer to guide search. A cognition-action network uses this learned spatial value prior to improve the policy through imagined rollouts, without training a separate scalar critic. Training progresses from world-model learning to expert imitation and imagination-based exploration refinement. On UAV-ON, SearchWorld improves the success rate to 23.8% (19.5% for the strongest published agent) and raises oracle success to 35.5%, while remaining robust on unseen scenes (19.9% success rate). By grounding imagination in explicit spatial representations, SearchWorld enables UAV agents to plan prospectively rather than react.
item.dc:creator: Yatai Ji, Zhengqiu Zhu, Yong Zhao, Yue Hu, Fanglong Yao, Chen Gao, Pengfei Zhu, Quanjun Yin

item.title: Extreme Binary Classification: Extreme Value Theory for Extreme Constraint on False Negative
item.description: arXiv:2610.09984v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While binary classification is one of the most extensively studied problems in machine learning, the regime in which the goal is to learn a classifier with an almost zero false negative rate remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce the Extreme Binary Classification problem, where the objective is to learn a classifier whose false negative rate $\alpha$ is constrained by $\epsilon_{N_1}=o_{N_1\to\infty}(1/N_1)$, with $N_1$ denoting the number of positive examples in the training set. To address this problem, we propose a threshold adaptation method theoretically grounded in guarantees derived from Extreme Value Theory, together with a feature selection procedure based on a permutation test applied to sample maxima. Experimental results on four real-world datasets of varying sizes demonstrate that our approach compares favorably with state-of-the-art methods. In addition, we illustrate its interpretability through an application to a cancer screening dataset.
item.dc:creator: Samuel Gruffaz, Muhammad Fawad, Jaakko Nevalainen

item.title: Minimax estimation of the pseudo-spectral gap of continuous Markov chains, with applications to empirical concentration bounds
item.description: arXiv:2610.20007v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the minimax estimation of the pseudo-spectral gap $\gamma_{ps}$ of a Markov chain from the observation of a single trajectory. Extending earlier works on finite-state space chains by Wolfer and Kontorovich (2024), we provide an estimator in the case of a compact, continuous state-space. Our estimator appears to be minimax-optimal on the class of chains with a transition operator with Lipschitz density, up to logarithmic terms. Our estimator, combined with Paulin's version of Bernstein inequality, allows to derive empirical concentration inequalities for Markov chains. This unlocks many applications, from confidence intervals, to active learning and generalization bounds. In particular, for rested bandits with Markov rewards, we provide a version of UCB with a regret bound similar to the one in the iid case, without assuming any knowledge on the pseudo-spectral gap of the chains.
item.dc:creator: Vahe Karagulyan, Miko{\l}aj Kasprzak, Pierre Alquier

item.title: L2GSSL: Label-Efficient Local-to-Global Self-Supervised Learning for Volumetric Healthcare Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.21356v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Healthcare institutions routinely accumulate high-dimensional computed tomography (CT) volumes, but only a fraction can be annotated by experts. We present L2GSSL, a local-to-global self-supervised learning framework that leverages unlabeled volumes by decomposing pretraining into intra-slice and inter-slice representation spaces. A slice encoder learns view-invariant local features, and a global encoder aggregates the resulting tokens to model volumetric context. The stop-gradient isolates the local space from the global objective, while slice-wise execution and a three-phase schedule support training under constrained GPU memory. On LIDC-IDRI lung nodule malignancy classification, L2GSSL reaches $0.9229$ AUROC with only $10\%$ of the labels and $0.9377$ with $25\%$, exceeding the volume-level VICReg by $0.0229$ and $0.0294$, respectively. With all labels, the strongest supervised baseline exceeds L2GSSL by only $0.0044$ AUROC, consistent with self-supervised pretraining providing its greatest value when annotations are limited. A model fine-tuned on $25\%$ of LIDC-IDRI and evaluated on the external LNDb cohort without further training obtains $0.8138$ AUROC and $0.7589$ AUPRC, improving over the strongest evaluated self-supervised baseline by $0.1130$ and $0.0954$. Experiments across data sources, thoracic and abdominal anatomy, downstream tasks, and two backbones examine healthcare-data variety, while masking malignant lesion-bearing slices at inference sharply reduces performance, indicating that predictions rely substantially on lesion content.
item.dc:creator: Po-Cheng Cheng, Hung-Hsuan Chen

item.title: Explaining Chess and Go with Discovered Motifs
item.description: arXiv:2610.23166v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern chess engines play far beyond human ability, often choosing moves whose underlying ideas are difficult for humans to understand. We propose an automatic metric for chess explanations based on how well the motifs they describe generalize to new positions. Evaluating state-of-the-art language models using this metric, we find that they perform surprisingly poorly, often relying on surface-level board observations rather than robust, transferable chess concepts. We then introduce BinProp, a training-free method that enables these same models to discover reusable chess concepts and use them to explain moves in natural language. BinProp improves motif generalization for every model tested, nearly tripling the average score compared with direct prompting. Beyond chess, the same method discovers useful concepts in Go, draughts, and shogi without additional tuning.
item.dc:creator: Ori Press, Alexander Golubev

item.title: Federated Community Detection in Bipartite Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.25997v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study federated spectral estimation when a large matrix is horizontally partitioned across servers that cannot share raw data. We propose FLICKER, a target-specific gradient-based power iteration that recovers a singular direction associated with a prescribed spectral target using only matrix-vector products on local blocks. Different target directions can be recovered independently and in parallel. We establish non-asymptotic convergence guarantees and provide a recursive grid-search procedure for spectral target selection. Building on FLICKER, we develop BiFLICKER for federated community detection in bipartite networks, together with a sequential projected variant for nearby or repeated singular directions. Under a sparse bipartite stochastic block model, we show that properly rescaled leading singular values from a reference server provide valid global targets, and that Sequential BiFLICKER achieves a vanishing misclustering rate and exact recovery under stronger sparsity conditions. Simulations show that BiFLICKER remains close to centralized spectral clustering and is more robust than existing federated spectral baselines when local sample sizes are small. On a LastFM user-artist network naturally partitioned by country, Sequential BiFLICKER attains an overall ARI of 0.96 against centralized clustering while revealing cross-country communities with distinct listening profiles.
item.dc:creator: Wanjie Wang

item.title: High-Order Gaussian Approximation of Besov Functions on Manifolds
item.description: arXiv:2610.27022v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study high-order Gaussian approximation for Besov functions $f\in B^\alpha_{2,\infty}(X)$ with $\alpha>0$ on a compact smooth embedded manifold $X$ without boundary. For $r<\alpha$, a suitable signed combination of Gaussian integral operators at different bandwidths gives an $H^r(X)$ error bounded by $C\gamma^{\alpha-r}\|f\|_{B^\alpha_{2,\infty}(X)}$. The squared Gaussian RKHS norm of the approximant is bounded by $C\gamma^{-\varrho}\|f\|_{L_2(X)}^2$, where $\varrho$ is the intrinsic dimension of $X$. We apply these approximation results to two statistical learning problems. For regularized Gaussian logistic classification, we combine the approximation bounds with a localized oracle inequality. For a potentially unbounded Bayes function in $B^\alpha_{2,\infty}(X)$ and a marginal density in $L_p(X)$, the excess logistic risk has upper bounds of order $((\log n)^{\varrho+1}/n)^{2\beta/(2\beta+3\varrho)}$ for the unclipped predictor and $((\log n)^{\varrho+2}/n)^{\beta/(\beta+\varrho)}$ for clipped predictions with suitably selected parameters, where $\beta=2\alpha(1-1/p)$. Under bounded marginal densities, our excess misclassification risk bound matches, up to logarithmic factors, the classical H\"older-class exponent. For elliptic operator learning, we assemble a Gaussian Galerkin solution operator from random manifold samples. Its error in the operator norm from $B^\alpha_{2,\infty}(X)$ to $H^1(X)$ is bounded with high probability by two terms. The trial-space term has a decay exponent in the number of Gaussian centers that can approach $(\alpha+1)/\varrho$. The bias and sampling term is of order $n^{-2N/(4N+\varrho)}$ for a fixed trial space, where $n$ is the number of sample pairs and $N$ is the number of Gaussian scales used for matrix assembly. The convergence rates for both problems depend on the intrinsic dimension $\varrho$ and are independent of the ambient dimension $d$.
item.dc:creator: Guanhang Lei, Lei Shi, Xiaoming Yuan

item.title: ConceptARC at Scale: Studying Conceptual Understanding in Reasoning Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.06732v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) perform well on challenging benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether they form generalizable abstractions across conceptually related reasoning tasks. The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) provides a controlled testbed for studying abstraction, requiring solvers to infer transformation rules over two-dimensional grids from a small set of examples. While ARC evaluates rule abstraction within individual tasks, different tasks may share higher-level structure despite requiring different transformations$\unicode{x2014}$for example, several tasks may involve reasoning about objects contained within other objects. Benchmarks such as ConceptARC capture this structure by grouping ARC-style tasks into recurring spatial and semantic concepts, but they often contain only a few manually constructed tasks per concept. We introduce ConceptARC at Scale, a generator for creating thousands of ARC-style tasks targeting a specific concept. Using this generator, we construct ConceptARC-100, a dataset of 1,600 new, manually reviewed tasks, with 100 tasks for each of the 16 concepts defined by ConceptARC$\unicode{x2014}$ten times the size of the original benchmark. We evaluate a range of recent LRMs and models trained from scratch on ConceptARC-100 to characterize which concepts they solve reliably and where they struggle. We further analyze the models' internal representations and find clear semantic structure: task representations cluster according to the operations applied to objects, such as recoloring, removal, or translation, even when realized through substantially different rules and scenarios. Together, our results suggest that models form stable abstractions of transformation operations that generalize across diverse tasks.
item.dc:creator: Philipp Mondorf, Adrien Deli\`ege, Solim LeGris, Claas Beger, Ryan Yi, Barbara Plank, Brenden M. Lake, Todd M. Gureckis

item.title: Ostinato: Low-Latency CPU-GPU MoE Inference for Local Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.11533v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Language-model agents increasingly run on local workstations with consumer GPUs, where quantized mixture-of-experts (MoE) models split routed experts between GPU and host memory. Prefix-cached agent sessions alternate single-token decode with short tool-return prefills, typically up to a few hundred tokens. Short tool turns touch more experts than consumer GPUs can hold, yet direct roughly 85% of DeepSeek-V4-Flash's routes to a static GPU pool while leaving 3.3-5.5 tokens per cold expert. Widely used local engines such as llama.cpp and KTransformers either copy tens of gigabytes over PCIe per turn, compute every route on the CPU while idling resident GPU experts, or budget GPU memory by whole layers and uniform per-layer quotas. We present Ostinato, a CPU-GPU MoE engine that reuses one static cross-layer GPU pool in place across every forward pass. During decode and short tool turns, Ostinato computes resident routes on the GPUs and sparse cold routes on the CPU, so short turns copy no expert weights; on long prefills, it deduplicates cold uploads; and for multi-GPU decode, all-zero expert slots with device-side synchronization capture each GPU's decode step in one CUDA graph. Across held-out SWE and -bench sessions on three MoE models, Ostinato cuts median tool-turn waits by 2.5-6.6x and finishes sessions 1.36-3.83x faster than default baselines, staying 1.30-1.94x faster when baselines align their upload threshold and weight loading. It finishes sessions fastest across seven agent workloads, one to four GPUs, and up to eight concurrent sessions, while its cross-layer pool speeds up 335 GB DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash by 1.81-2.19x over llama.cpp's expert cache.
item.dc:creator: Junning Zhu, Jianxiong Guo

item.title: Whether untrained networks beat trained ones at V1 depends on a normalisation convention: evidence from two fMRI datasets
item.description: arXiv:2611.15533v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Untrained convolutional networks have been reported to rival or beat trained networks as models of primary visual cortex (V1), and we had reported such an advantage in THINGS fMRI. Under a pre-specified ridge readout, the trained network was ahead at every pooling grid in THINGS and in NSD (8 of 8 subjects), also when voxel responses were centred within runs. Representational similarity analysis (RSA) in THINGS depended on analysis choices (28 analyses: intervals above 0 in 5, below 0 in 9, including 0 in 14); in NSD with its standard normalisation, none of 28 analyses favoured the untrained network. The untrained advantage appears when a response profile common to all trials is left in the voxel patterns and model units are not centred, under correlation distance: removing the session-mean profile in THINGS reduced it from +0.030 to +0.005; with raw betas it reached +0.100 in THINGS, appeared in the THINGS test images, and appeared in NSD (+0.116, 8 of 8 subjects, a pre-specified prediction), where it was confined to this one of 28 analyses. With the profile left in, both representational dissimilarity matrices are dominated by per-image response amplitude, which in V1 tracks contrast energy, and the untrained network's matrix is more amplitude-dominated; the amplitude itself is matched equally by both networks; removing the amplitude structure from both matrices removes the advantage in NSD (+0.116 to -0.009, 8 of 8 subjects). A luminance-and-contrast baseline outperformed every network under ridge in both datasets (point estimates); the networks reached 10-15% of the NSD noise-ceiling lower bound. 24 of 88 pre-specified predictions were not met. We recommend centring or normalising voxel responses within session, reporting the sensitivity of RSA rankings to this choice and to model-unit centring, and replicating on a second dataset.
item.dc:creator: Nils Leutenegger

item.title: Where Is Uncertainty Observed? A Mechanistic Understanding of Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2611.15735v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Knowing when a large language model's (LLM's) response can be trusted is critical for its safe use. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) can help LLMs recognize if their responses may be unreliable. Existing taxonomies organize UQ methods by uncertainty source or estimation mechanism. They leave unresolved the question of where uncertainty is observed in the model's computation. The answer matters because the observation point determines whether an estimator has access to enough information to recover a given target, and how well it can recover it. Drawing on mechanistic interpretability, we define four mechanistic observation lenses: the structural lens observes component updates, the representational lens observes hidden states, the distributional lens observes token probabilities, and the semantical lens observes distributions over meanings. We relate these lenses through the residual stream and order them by the information they carry, which gives a principle for selecting UQ methods for different targets. We survey existing methods through the four lenses. Furthermore, we distinguish evaluation targets, criteria, and metrics to clarify different UQ evaluation protocols. Finally, we identify open problems and research directions to connect uncertainty estimation to the internal computation and downstream use of LLMs.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyu Liang, Virginia Ceccatelli, Aliai Eusebi, Tobias Braun, Nils Loose, Carlo Malagnino, Lorenzo Cavallaro

item.title: Imitation Policies Learn a Proprioceptive Anchor: A Predictive Law for Perception Noise and Its Closed-Loop Cost
item.description: arXiv:2611.17658v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Imitation policies for robot manipulation are often trained on noisy object positions, and they learn to discount the noisy reading. We show how much they discount it, and why. Because demonstrators steer toward the object, the robot's own state carries information about where the object is. A trained policy combines this proprioceptive anchor with the reading and weights the reading by $\alpha = V/(V + s^2)$, where $s^2$ is the reading noise and $V$ the anchor's error variance. $V$ belongs to the learner and is far smaller than a linear model of the demonstrations implies, which is why classical errors-in-variables (EIV) regression overestimates $\alpha$. Measured once, $V$ predicted ten held-out sensitivities across two robomimic tasks, two learners and four new noise levels, with mean absolute error 0.025 against 0.37 for classical EIV, and a parameter-free bias test rules out the simpler explanation that the policies just overestimate the noise. The discount does not carry over to deployment, where the policy produces its own state: closed-loop sensitivity to a persistent reading offset exceeded $\alpha$ in all 15 policies that passed the registered gates, although the stricter registered prediction, that all would follow the offset fully, held for 8 of them. Post hoc, lower $\alpha$ went with lower success, steeply for diffusion, and a registered prospective test confirmed this for diffusion on Can at two new noise levels: the measured $\alpha$ predicted success before any rollout, within 0.03 (95% intervals $\pm 0.08$), although training noise predicts it equally well. Every test was registered before its data, including the classical benchmark that failed, and all other analyses are labelled post hoc; all results are in simulation with synthetic Gaussian noise.
item.dc:creator: Christopher Malili

item.title: Distributional Deep Hedging
item.description: arXiv:2611.26652v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Deep hedging learns a hedging strategy by optimising a risk preference over a neural-network policy. The preference is fixed before training, so each new preference requires a new policy and, in actor-critic methods, a new critic. We propose distributional deep hedging, in which the distribution of the hedging profit and loss is learned through its quantiles and the risk preference is applied afterwards, as a weight on those quantiles. We characterise the preferences that admit this representation, which include expected shortfall and its mixtures, and show that the entropic utility is computed from the same quantiles. At the current policy, each of these preferences is bounded below by an expected utility with the same gradient. This bound reduces risk-sensitive hedging to a sequence of risk-neutral problems, from which we derive policy-search and actor-critic algorithms. In numerical experiments, the learned hedges approach references computed by dynamic programming, and a single distributional critic trained without a preference can serve preferences chosen after training.
item.dc:creator: El-Amine Cherrat, Skander Kazdaghli, Iordanis Kerenidis

item.title: SparseHPS: A Unified Model for Human Pose and Shape Estimation across Depth Cameras and LiDARs
item.description: arXiv:2611.26730v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recovering 3D human pose and shape from point clouds is central to motion capture, robotics and self-driving vehicles, because depth cameras and LiDARs sense a person directly in metric 3D and work under any lighting. However, current approaches are each tailored to one sensor type: point density differs by more than ten times between devices, public datasets are labeled with incompatible body models, and LiDAR approaches need long input sequences to offset sparse scans. In this work, we present SparseHPS, a novel sensor-agnostic network that recovers SMPL-X pose, shape and global translation from a human point cloud with one set of weights, for single frames and streams alike. Specifically, SparseHPS encodes the cloud with a LitePT backbone over sparse voxels, represents every joint by a learnable query decoded with one common head, localizes the body by voting over voxels, and draws temporal context from a causal memory of tokens from the seven preceding frames. A single model is trained on ten datasets that mix rendered clouds with real depth-camera and LiDAR captures, all converted to one body model. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art results on the SLOPER4D and FreeMotion LiDAR benchmarks, where SparseHPS lowers the root-relative joint error by 22% and 11%, respectively, compared with the strongest prior method, which needs 32 frames. On real Azure Kinect captures of held-out HuMMan subjects, SparseHPS attains a joint error of 34.7 mm. Moreover, the current frame alone already yields the bulk of this accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Ilya Zaychuk

item.title: Search From the Start: Search-Native Pretraining for Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.26809v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed with access to search tools at inference. Yet pretraining remains predominantly focused on predicting static text, with search capabilities typically introduced during post-training. We propose Search-Native Pretraining as a practical route to teach search capability during pretraining from ordinary text corpora. Specifically, we augment pretraining corpus at scale with web-search queries and retrieve web response using a local index. Training on this augmented corpus teaches models to generate search calls and incorporate retrieved evidence during language modeling. Across Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu corpora and 360M to 3.3B parameter scales, search-pretrained models ("QueryLM") show improved performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and higher steerability toward the retrieved evidence. Crucially, their advantage persists after supervised fine-tuning of both search-pretrained and conventionally pretrained models, indicating that the tested post-training procedures do not fully recover the capabilities developed during pretraining. Throughout our experiments, we find that a 1.4B QueryLM consistently beats or matches the performance of a FLOP-matched 3.3B baseline model across all knowledge intensive tasks. These results establish search-pretraining as a practical way to develop foundational search capabilities during pretraining. We release the training artifacts, including model checkpoints and data.
item.dc:creator: Kaustubh Ponkshe, Gyung Hyun Je, Stefan Taga, Colin Raffel, Martin Jaggi

item.title: Click and Count: Multimodal Prototype Adaptation for Class-Agnostic Object Counting
item.description: arXiv:2611.28321v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose a multimodal, class-agnostic, density-based object counting framework that specifies the object of interest through visual exemplars, a text description, or both, within a single iterative refinement pipeline. Existing counters typically fall into two groups: methods that fuse two modalities, a hand-drawn bounding box and a text description, to specify the target object, and single-modality methods that rely on either a box exemplar or text alone. A few recent methods replace the box with a point or click. We expand a single click into a precise object mask via a frozen visual-prompt segmentation model, feeding an iterative prototype-refinement process that also fuses a text description at every refinement step. We make two contributions: first, a click-derived exemplar extraction module that removes the bounding-box requirement of prior exemplar-based counters; second, a per-step text-fusion mechanism that combines visual and textual prompts throughout refinement. Combined with text guidance, our model achieves state-of-the-art counting accuracy, outperforming prior click-based counting methods across all metrics and surpassing the box-exemplar base architecture in mean absolute error. The code is available at github.com/ameniifi/Click-and-Count.
item.dc:creator: Amani Aifi, Wassim Bouachir, Ahmed Zgaren, Nizar Bouguila

item.title: Inferring Experimental Objectives in Microscopy Experiments from Decision Traces
item.description: arXiv:2611.29814v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern microscopes can acquire, analyze and act on data far faster than human operators can decide what to measure next. Exploiting this speed in automated experiments requires the instrument to follow the scientific logic of the operator, and one way to encode that logic is through reward functions that become part of the operation process. Here we explore whether such reward functions can be learned from the decision histories of microscope operators. We propose multiple frameworks in which recorded choices among alternative measurement locations serve as comparative evidence about the operator's preferences, and we compare several algorithms for reconstructing the reward including interpretable linear models built on physically meaningful image descriptors, nonlinear functions of the same descriptors, an unsupervised image representation followed by preference modeling, and a preference trained deep kernel inspired model. The result of this analysis is a spatial field of reward functions over the sample that can be used to run the instrument. We also propose a way to benchmark these approaches, based on withheld decisions and on decision histories generated with known objectives. We then examine the possibility that a decision history contains changing priorities throughout the experiment. A hidden Markov model assigns distinct rewards to recurring selection strategies, whereas a continuous-state model tracks smoothly varying preference weights. Controlled sequences generated over real microscopy candidate sets show that both concealed switches and gradual drift can be recovered. These reward functions, learned directly from recorded decisions, provide candidate objectives for future automated microscopy experiments.
item.dc:creator: Kamyar Barakati, Boris N. Slautin, Aditya Raghavan, Babita Babita, Surya Prakash Reddy, Jordan Marshall, Munireach Nannory, Stephen Puplampu, Alla Slautina, Faith M. Hines, Newsha Javanmardi, Sergei V. Kalinin

item.title: Sampling with graph wavelet kernels: optimality and adaptivity to regularity and geometry
item.description: arXiv:2611.29992v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We construct wavelet-based determinantal samplers on manifolds and geometric graphs whose approximation rates adapt to the regularity of the observable. On a Riemannian manifold of dimension $m$, our wavelet DPPs satisfy variance reduction of order $n^{1-2s/m}$ for linear statistics of both $s$-H\"older and $H^s$ observables, where $0<s\le1$. Using these samplers, we further construct unbiased quadrature rules with root mean square error $O(n^{-1/2-s/m})$ using at most $3n/2$ function evaluations, matching the classical optimal randomized integration exponent. For point clouds sampled from an $m$-dimensional manifold, we develop corresponding determinantal samplers on two standard classes of geometric random graphs: $\varepsilon$-graphs and symmetric $k$-nearest-neighbour graphs. These samplers satisfy the same variance reduction for linear statistics of $s$-H\"older observables and yield conditionally unbiased estimators of empirical averages with root mean square error $O(n^{-1/2-s/m})$, using at most $2n$ function evaluations. In both settings, the rates are governed by the intrinsic dimension $m$ and the regularity $s$ of the observable.
item.dc:creator: Pranav Gupta, Hoang-Son Tran, Subhroshekhar Ghosh

item.title: ASTERISM: Do Multimodal LLMs Actually Look at All the Images?
item.description: arXiv:2611.32316v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-image benchmarks aim to test whether a multimodal large language model (MLLM) combines evidence across images, but many of their items can be answered from a single image. Across about 33k items from 19 public benchmarks, our audit and a two-stage single-image filter find that one image or the question alone settles 24.2% of them. On these items, MLLMs recover from one image a median 78% of the accuracy that all images add over the text alone, so these items reward answering from one image, which we call the single-image shortcut. MLLMs take this shortcut even on items where one image is not enough. On such items, most of their wrong answers repeat an answer they give from one image, at a rate well above chance. We build ASTERISM, to our knowledge the largest audited multi-image benchmark, from these 19 benchmarks by keeping their items that need more than one image. Its 18.7k items, 2.0k of them corrected or rewritten, share one format, one scorer and seven task categories. We also release ASTERISM-Train with 49k training items and ASTERISM-Lite, a hard subset whose items we manually verify one by one. On ASTERISM-Lite, the strongest proprietary MLLM scores 68%. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), now common in MLLM post-training, rewards the shortcut as well, because a correct answer read off one image earns as much reward as one that combines images. In line with this, existing RLVR objectives add little to the ASTERISM score. To stop rewarding the shortcut in training as ASTERISM does in evaluation, we propose cross-image credit assignment (CICA), an extension of RLVR that moves the credit toward the tokens that need more than one image. On three open-source MLLMs, CICA raises the ASTERISM score by 2.6 to 6.0 points, more than twice the gain of each general and vision-specific RL objective trained on the same data.
item.dc:creator: Chanseul Cho, Dongwoo Kim, Noori Bae, Seungjae Moon, Seongsu Lee, Youngmin Ro

item.title: Degree-bounded Satisfiability of Local MPNNs with Sum Aggregation is NEXPTIME-hard
item.description: arXiv:2611.32595v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We prove that the following problem is NEXPTIME-hard: given a message passing neural network (MPNN) $M$ with local sum aggregation and truncated ReLU activations, and a degree bound $d$ encoded in unary, decide whether there is a pointed graph $(G,v)$ with rational node labels and degree at most $d$ that is accepted by $M$. Hardness already holds for the fixed degree bound $d=3$.
item.dc:creator: Marco S\"alzer

item.title: OmniAct: One Policy, One Million Embodiments
item.description: arXiv:2611.33158v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A single policy that controls diverse robots must not only transfer task knowledge across embodiments, but also adapt its behavior to each robot's capabilities. Existing approaches facilitate transfer through shared action representations, but these representations do not necessarily capture how differences in robot morphology should shape manipulation strategies. We introduce OmniAct, a cross-embodiment manipulation policy that conditions directly on each robot's kinematics in a specific scene to produce embodiment-specific behavior. This kinematic graph represents the robot's joint positions, motion axes, and connectivity to its visual observation, allowing the policy to account for how its embodiment related to objects and surfaces in the scene. A flow-matching policy predicts relative joint motions for each node, enabling control across robots with different degrees of freedom and kinematic configurations. To learn how physical structure shapes behavior at scale, we procedurally design and filter one million physically feasible robot embodiments; next, we develop algorithms to generate robot trajectories in simulation for all embodiments; finally, we train across diverse simulated manipulation tasks. On 2,000 embodiment-scene-held-out evaluation episodes, OmniAct achieves 63.0% success, compared to 17.8% for pi 0.5 and 57.9% for the strongest baseline; on the task families GPT-6 Astra was evaluated on, it achieves 64.7% against GPT-6 Astra's 41.1%. On a previously unseen real-world robot, it achieves nearly twice the success rate of the next best method, MolmoAct2. Beyond task success, we observe that OmniAct learns distinct manipulation strategies that exploit the capabilities and accommodate the limitations of different morphologies. Project: https://omniact.github.io/
item.dc:creator: Xiang Fan, Yuheng Wang, Jiayuan Yan, Bohan Fang, Wisdom Oluchi Ikezogwo, Ainaz Eftekhar, Max Argus, Zhongzheng Ren, Jiafei Duan, Ranjay Krishna
